paper_metadata.title: Inference Scaling for Long-Context Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_metadata.abstract: The scaling of inference computation has unlocked the potential of long-context large language models (LLMs) across diverse settings. For knowledge-intensive tasks, the increased compute is often allocated to incorporate more external knowledge. However, without effectively utilizing such knowledge, solely expanding context does not always enhance performance. In this work, we investigate inference scaling for retrieval augmented generation (RAG), exploring the combination of multiple strategies beyond simply increasing the quantity of knowledge, including in-context learning and iterative prompting. These strategies provide additional flexibility to scale test-time computation (e.g., by increasing retrieved documents or generation steps), thereby enhancing LLMs' ability to effectively acquire and utilize contextual information. We address two key questions: (1) How does RAG performance benefit from the scaling of inference computation when optimally configured? (2) Can we predict the optimal test-time compute allocation for a given budget by modeling the relationship between RAG performance and inference parameters? Our observations reveal that increasing inference computation leads to nearly linear gains in RAG performance when optimally allocated, a relationship we describe as the inference scaling laws for RAG. Building on this, we further develop the computation allocation model to estimate RAG performance across different inference configurations. The model predicts optimal inference parameters under various computation constraints, which align closely with the experimental results. By applying these optimal configurations, we demonstrate that scaling inference compute on long-context LLMs achieves up to 58.9% gains on benchmark datasets compared to standard RAG.

paper_metadata.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) showcase impressive capabilities but encounter challenges like hallucination, outdated knowledge, and non-transparent, untraceable reasoning processes. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising solution by incorporating knowledge from external databases. This enhances the accuracy and credibility of the generation, particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks, and allows for continuous knowledge updates and integration of domain-specific information. RAG synergistically merges LLMs' intrinsic knowledge with the vast, dynamic repositories of external databases. This comprehensive review paper offers a detailed examination of the progression of RAG paradigms, encompassing the Naive RAG, the Advanced RAG, and the Modular RAG. It meticulously scrutinizes the tripartite foundation of RAG frameworks, which includes the retrieval, the generation and the augmentation techniques. The paper highlights the state-of-the-art technologies embedded in each of these critical components, providing a profound understanding of the advancements in RAG systems. Furthermore, this paper introduces up-to-date evaluation framework and benchmark. At the end, this article delineates the challenges currently faced and points out prospective avenues for research and development.

paper_metadata.title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation
paper_metadata.abstract: Zhengbao Jiang, Frank Xu, Luyu Gao, Zhiqing Sun, Qian Liu, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Yiming Yang, Jamie Callan, Graham Neubig. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

paper_metadata.title: In-Context Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
paper_metadata.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Retrieval-Augmented Language Modeling (RALM) methods, which condition a language model (LM) on relevant documents from a grounding corpus during generation, were shown to significantly improve language modeling performance. In addition, they can mitigate the problem of factually inaccurate text generation and provide natural source attribution mechanism. Existing RALM approaches focus on modifying the LM architecture in order to facilitate the incorporation of external information, significantly complicating deployment. This paper considers a simple alternative, which we dub In-Context RALM: leaving the LM architecture unchanged and prepending grounding documents to the input, without any further training of the LM. We show that In-Context RALM that builds on off-the-shelf general purpose retrievers provides surprisingly large LM gains across model sizes and diverse corpora. We also demonstrate that the document retrieval and ranking mechanism can be specialized to the RALM setting to further boost performance. We conclude that In-Context RALM has considerable potential to increase the prevalence of LM grounding, particularly in settings where a pretrained LM must be used without modification or even via API access.1

paper_metadata.title: Data clustering
paper_metadata.abstract: Clustering is the unsupervised classification of patterns (observations, data items, or feature vectors) into groups (clusters). The clustering problem has been addressed in many contexts and by researchers in many disciplines; this reflects its broad appeal and usefulness as one of the steps in exploratory data analysis. However, clustering is a difficult problem combinatorially, and differences in assumptions and contexts in different communities has made the transfer of useful generic concepts and methodologies slow to occur. This paper presents an overview of pattern clustering methods from a statistical pattern recognition perspective, with a goal of providing useful advice and references to fundamental concepts accessible to the broad community of clustering practitioners. We present a taxonomy of clustering techniques, and identify cross-cutting themes and recent advances. We also describe some important applications of clustering algorithms such as image segmentation, object recognition, and information retrieval.

paper_metadata.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
paper_metadata.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising approach for mitigating the hallucination of large language models (LLMs). However, existing research lacks rigorous evaluation of the impact of retrieval-augmented generation on different large language models, which make it challenging to identify the potential bottlenecks in the capabilities of RAG for different LLMs. In this paper, we systematically investigate the impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on large language models. We analyze the performance of different large language models in 4 fundamental abilities required for RAG, including noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness. To this end, we establish Retrieval-Augmented Generation Benchmark (RGB), a new corpus for RAG evaluation in both English and Chinese. RGB divides the instances within the benchmark into 4 separate testbeds based on the aforementioned fundamental abilities required to resolve the case. Then we evaluate 6 representative LLMs on RGB to diagnose the challenges of current LLMs when applying RAG. Evaluation reveals that while LLMs exhibit a certain degree of noise robustness, they still struggle significantly in terms of negative rejection, information integration, and dealing with false information. The aforementioned assessment outcomes indicate that there is still a considerable journey ahead to effectively apply RAG to LLMs.

paper_metadata.title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
paper_metadata.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of medical question answering (QA) tasks, they still face challenges with hallucinations and outdated knowledge.Retrievalaugmented generation (RAG) is a promising solution and has been widely adopted.However, a RAG system can involve multiple flexible components, and there is a lack of best practices regarding the optimal RAG setting for various medical purposes.To systematically evaluate such systems, we propose the Medical Information Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation (MIRAGE), a first-of-its-kind benchmark including 7,663 questions from five medical QA datasets.Using MIRAGE, we conducted large-scale experiments with over 1.8 trillion prompt tokens on 41 combinations of different corpora, retrievers, and backbone LLMs through the MEDRAG toolkit introduced in this work.Overall, MEDRAG improves the accuracy of six different LLMs by up to 18% over chain-of-thought prompting, elevating the performance of GPT-3.5 and Mixtral to GPT-4level.Our results show that the combination of various medical corpora and retrievers achieves the best performance.In addition, we discovered a log-linear scaling property and the "lostin-the-middle" effects in medical RAG.We believe our comprehensive evaluations can serve as practical guidelines for implementing RAG systems for medicine 1 .

paper_metadata.title: From image descriptions to visual denotations: New similarity metrics for semantic inference over event descriptions
paper_metadata.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
paper_metadata.abstract: We propose to use the visual denotations of linguistic expressions (i.e. the set of images they describe) to define novel denotational similarity metrics, which we show to be at least as beneficial as distributional similarities for two tasks that require semantic inference. To compute these denotational similarities, we construct a denotation graph, i.e. a subsumption hierarchy over constituents and their denotations, based on a large corpus of 30K images and 150K descriptive captions.

paper_metadata.title: Generation-Augmented Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
paper_metadata.abstract: Yuning Mao, Pengcheng He, Xiaodong Liu, Yelong Shen, Jianfeng Gao, Jiawei Han, Weizhu Chen. Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

paper_metadata.title: Query Rewriting in Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
paper_metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) play powerful, black-box readers in the retrieve-then-read pipeline, making remarkable progress in knowledge-intensive tasks. This work introduces a new framework, Rewrite-Retrieve-Read instead of the previous retrieve-then-read for the retrieval-augmented LLMs from the perspective of the query rewriting. Unlike prior studies focusing on adapting either the retriever or the reader, our approach pays attention to the adaptation of the search query itself, for there is inevitably a gap between the input text and the needed knowledge in retrieval. We first prompt an LLM to generate the query, then use a web search engine to retrieve contexts. Furthermore, to better align the query to the frozen modules, we propose a trainable scheme for our pipeline. A small language model is adopted as a trainable rewriter to cater to the black-box LLM reader. The rewriter is trained using the feedback of the LLM reader by reinforcement learning. Evaluation is conducted on downstream tasks, open-domain QA and multiple-choice QA. Experiments results show consistent performance improvement, indicating that our framework is proven effective and scalable, and brings a new framework for retrieval-augmented LLM.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper presents a practical and well-motivated approach to LLM alignment with minimal human-annotated data. The core idea of using direct preference judgment via model logits (Eq. 7) is simple yet effective and demonstrates clear advantages over external reward models and LLM-as-judge baselines.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with strong empirical results. The paper achieves 21.13% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 using only 3.3% of labeled data compared to Zephyr-7b-β's 11.75% with 100% data, and the improvements are consistent across multiple benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, length-controlled win rate, MT-Bench) and model architectures (Mistral, LLaMA-3, Phi-2/3).

Novel technical contributions with the decoupled noise detection approach (Eq. 11-12). The linear extrapolation to approximate a more strongly aligned model is theoretically motivated by recent work on RLHF geometric mixtures and provides computational efficiency (no additional forward passes needed).

Thorough ablation studies and analysis sections. Table 6 clearly demonstrates the value of each component (SR and DND), and Table 7 provides insightful analysis on the role of the reference model choice. The paper also tests robustness across different seed sizes (Table 3), seed samples (Table 4), and models (Table 5).

Practical significance: demonstrates that SPA can work even without seed preference data (Figure 4), making it highly applicable in real-world scenarios where preference annotations are expensive to obtain.
weaknesses: The linear extrapolation in Eq. 12 lacks explicit exposition of why it serves as a noise detection mechanism. While motivated by Liu et al. (2024) on geometric mixtures, the paper does not explain in the submitted text how logit extrapolation approximates a more strongly aligned model's predictions or justify the progressive λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8).

The paper acknowledges a tendency to generate longer responses but does not integrate length control into the core preference judgment mechanism (Eq. 7). While Appendix D demonstrates post-hoc length penalties are compatible with SPA, the main experimental results (Tables 1-5) do not incorporate length mitigation, leaving length bias as an unaddressed factor in the core approach.

The explanation for why direct preference judgment outperforms external reward models invokes distribution shift (Section 5.2) but provides only qualitative justification. Figure 3 shows empirical widening of performance gaps across iterations, supporting the observation, but formal characterization of distribution shift or measurement of how reward model performance degrades is absent.

Hyperparameter choices (α = 0.1, K = 10%, warmup = 20%, λ progression) lack sensitivity analysis. While Table 6 provides component-level ablations (with/without SR, with/without DND), no study varies these hyperparameter values to establish robustness or provide guidance for practitioners.

Task-specific performance gaps on MT-Bench (no gains in Coding, degradation in Math) are acknowledged but not investigated. The paper notes this is 'commonly observed' without analyzing whether SPA-specific design factors (seed data composition, preference judgment mechanism, hyperparameters) contribute to these gaps relative to other methods.

weakness_details.weakness: The linear extrapolation in Eq. 12 lacks explicit exposition of why it serves as a noise detection mechanism. While motivated by Liu et al. (2024) on geometric mixtures, the paper does not explain in the submitted text how logit extrapolation approximates a more strongly aligned model's predictions or justify the progressive λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8).
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2 states Eq. 12 is 'motivated by the recent work (Liu et al., 2024)' and footnote 4 notes that πθe with λ would correspond to '(1 + λ) times smaller KL term.' However, the intuitive mechanism—that extrapolation in logit space toward increased alignment approximates a stronger model's confidence—is not articulated in the submitted paper. The author's rebuttal provides this intuition but it is not present in the submission itself. Progressive λ reduction is stated as fact without explanation in the main text.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Decoupled noise detection via linear extrapolation effectively identifies mislabeled samples.

weakness_details.weakness: The paper acknowledges a tendency to generate longer responses but does not integrate length control into the core preference judgment mechanism (Eq. 7). While Appendix D demonstrates post-hoc length penalties are compatible with SPA, the main experimental results (Tables 1-5) do not incorporate length mitigation, leaving length bias as an unaddressed factor in the core approach.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix A.1 acknowledges SPA 'has shown the tendency to increase the responses' length' and Appendix D Table 10 shows optional length penalty results (e.g., 2150 chars for SPA vs. 1552 for Zephyr). The core results use Eq. 7 without length control. The author's rebuttal proposes integrating length penalty into Eq. 7 as standard practice in revision, but this is not present in the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: SPA achieves genuine preference alignment improvements independent of response length artifacts.

weakness_details.weakness: The explanation for why direct preference judgment outperforms external reward models invokes distribution shift (Section 5.2) but provides only qualitative justification. Figure 3 shows empirical widening of performance gaps across iterations, supporting the observation, but formal characterization of distribution shift or measurement of how reward model performance degrades is absent.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 5.2 explains: 'the distribution of the generated data with LLM is more shifted from the distribution of the seed preference data... the effectiveness of the external reward model inevitably decreases.' This explanation is intuitive and Figure 3 provides empirical evidence (performance divergence increases across iterations), but no quantitative metrics of distribution shift (KL divergence, etc.) or analysis of reward model degradation as a function of distribution distance are provided. The author's rebuttal acknowledges this gap and proposes new experiments for revision.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Direct preference judgment adapts to distribution shift better than fixed reward models.

weakness_details.weakness: Hyperparameter choices (α = 0.1, K = 10%, warmup = 20%, λ progression) lack sensitivity analysis. While Table 6 provides component-level ablations (with/without SR, with/without DND), no study varies these hyperparameter values to establish robustness or provide guidance for practitioners.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 5.1 specifies: 'we used fixed values of α = 0.1 and K = 10' and 'denoising activated after 20% of the total training steps' without justification or sensitivity study. Progressive λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) are stated as used 'for iterations 1, 2, and 3' without analysis of alternatives. Table 6 ablates component presence/absence but not hyperparameter values. The author's rebuttal proposes systematic sensitivity analysis in revision.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Method robustness and generalizability across different settings.

weakness_details.weakness: Task-specific performance gaps on MT-Bench (no gains in Coding, degradation in Math) are acknowledged but not investigated. The paper notes this is 'commonly observed' without analyzing whether SPA-specific design factors (seed data composition, preference judgment mechanism, hyperparameters) contribute to these gaps relative to other methods.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix C Figure 5a shows MT-Bench task-wise results with 'almost no gain in Coding and degradation in Math.' The paper states this phenomenon is 'commonly observed in the relevant literature' but provides no SPA-specific investigation. The author's rebuttal proposes analyzing seed data composition, domain-specific preference judgment accuracy, and domain-adaptive hyperparameters in revision.
weakness_details.affected_claim: SPA uniformly improves LLM alignment across all capability dimensions.

soundness.justification: The core technical approach is sound. Direct preference judgment via model logits (Eq. 7) correctly applies the Bradley-Terry model with DPO-derived rewards. Confidence-based refinement (Eq. 9-10) uses standard noisy-label learning techniques (label smoothing). Decoupled noise detection (Eq. 11-12), while lacking complete exposition, is motivated by Liu et al. (2024) and the author's rebuttal clarifies the intuition (logit extrapolation approximates stronger model's confidence). The experimental methodology is rigorous with appropriate baselines and controls. No fundamental logical flaws prevent acceptance.

novelty.justification: The paper presents sufficiently novel contributions. Direct preference judgment from model logits (distinct from external reward models and LLM-as-judge) is a meaningful methodological contribution. Decoupled noise detection via linear logit extrapolation (Eq. 11-12) is novel even if lacking formal proof. Integration of iterative data expansion with confidence-based refinement represents coherent new approach. Comparisons to concurrent work (Snorkel 2024, Rosset et al. 2024) confirm the work's distinctiveness as of submission date.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a significant practical problem (LLM alignment with minimal labeled data). Achieving 21.13% win rate with 3.3% labeled data vs. 11.75% with 100% data represents 30x data efficiency improvement, which is meaningful for practitioners. Generalization across model families (Mistral, LLaMA, Phi) and demonstrated functionality without seed data (Figure 4) enhance practical impact. Task-specific degradation in Math/Coding (noted in Appendix C) is a limitation but does not materially undermine significance given strong overall improvements and acknowledgment of limitations.

evaluation.justification: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions: (1) standard and length-controlled metrics on established benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench); (2) relevant baseline comparisons (PairRM, LLM-as-judge, Iterative DPO variants); (3) component-level ablations (Table 6); (4) robustness validation (varying seed sizes, initial seeds, model architectures); (5) reference model sensitivity (Table 7); (6) zero-shot capability demonstration (Figure 4). While deeper analysis (distribution shift characterization, hyperparameter sensitivity, domain-specific investigation) would strengthen claims, the submitted evaluation provides sufficient evidence to support acceptance. The experimental design generally isolates the contribution of the proposed method.

presentation.justification: The paper is well-organized with clear algorithm (Algorithm 1), appropriate mathematical notation, and effective figures (Figures 1-4). Implementation details in Section 5.1 and Appendix B enable reproducibility. Limitations are acknowledged (Appendix A.1). While some concepts could be clearer (Eq. 12 intuition, λ justification, length bias integration), the presentation is sufficiently clear for a top-tier venue. The author's rebuttal clarifies several exposition gaps, suggesting these are presentation rather than fundamental issues.

reviewers.summary_comment:
This paper presents a practical framework for efficient LLM alignment achieving strong empirical results: 21.13% AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate with 3.3% labeled data versus 11.75% with full data. The core contribution—direct preference judgment via model logits combined with decoupled noise detection—is novel and well-executed. Comprehensive experiments across benchmarks, models, and robustness checks support the main claims. The work addresses a significant practical problem with demonstrated efficiency gains.

The second rebuttal usefully distinguishes between: (1) exposition gaps that do not reflect incomplete thinking (Eq. 12 intuition, λ justification), (2) methodological choices requiring integration (length control), and (3) analysis gaps requiring new experiments (distribution shift characterization, hyperparameter sensitivity, task-specific investigation). The authors acknowledge all five weaknesses identified in the prior review and clearly map each to either clarification, methodological modification, or new experimental work.

Critically, the rebuttal does not resolve submitted-paper weaknesses by providing evidence already present. Rather, it demonstrates understanding of gaps and articulates concrete revision plans. By the evaluation standard of assessing submitted work, these weaknesses remain present. However, they are relatively minor issues that do not materially undermine acceptance:

- The lack of explicit intuition for Eq. 12 is a clarity gap, not a soundness issue. The method is technically correct and works empirically (demonstrated in Table 6 ablation).
- Length bias is acknowledged as a limitation and addressed through length-controlled metrics in all main results, mitigating concern that improvements are purely artifacts.
- The distribution shift explanation, while qualitative, is supported by Figure 3's empirical evidence (widening gap across iterations). The hypothesis is plausible if not formally proven.
- Hyperparameter choices, while not systematically justified, produce robust results across extensive ablations (Tables 3-5), suggesting they are reasonable if not optimal.
- Task-specific degradation is a real limitation but represents a narrow scope issue rather than systematic failure.

The paper meets acceptance standards for a top-tier ML conference. The practical impact is substantial (30x data efficiency), the technical approach is sound, the evaluation is comprehensive, and limitations are appropriately acknowledged. The promised future revisions would further strengthen the work, but their absence does not prevent acceptance of a solid contribution.

## Summary Analysis

**Overall Assessment:**

This paper presents a practical and well-executed contribution to efficient LLM alignment. It achieves strong empirical results (30x data efficiency improvement) with comprehensive evaluation. However, it is fundamentally an **application-driven engineering contribution** that adapts existing techniques to a specific problem rather than advancing fundamental machine learning theory or methodology.

**Fit by Venue:**

- **NeurIPS (8/10 - Best Fit):** The paper aligns well with NeurIPS's focus on practical contributions to language models and data-centric AI. Strong empirical results, comprehensive evaluation, and acknowledgment of limitations meet NeurIPS's standards. The work addresses a high-impact problem in a fast-moving field.

- **ICLR (8/10 - Good Fit):** Similar ranking to NeurIPS due to focus on representation learning and applications to neural language models. However, the paper lacks deeper insights into learning mechanisms or representation properties that ICLR particularly values.

- **ICML (7/10 - Borderline Fit):** The work fits ICML's interest in machine learning systems and optimization but does not represent a general advance in ML methodology. ICML would prefer either stronger theoretical contributions or innovations with broader applicability beyond LLM alignment.

**Key Risk Factors:**

- Reviewer-identified exposition gaps (Eq. 12 intuition, λ justification) are minor but could be penalized by venues prioritizing mathematical rigor
- Task-specific performance degradation is a real limitation that suggests method brittleness
- Length bias mitigation is relegated to appendix despite being a core evaluation metric
- Hyperparameter choices lack systematic justification

**Strategic Recommendation:**

Submit to **NeurIPS** as the primary venue. The paper's strong empirical contributions, focus on practical LLM alignment, and data-centric methodology align best with NeurIPS's current priorities. ICLR is a solid secondary choice, while ICML is less ideal given its preference for more fundamental ML advances.

strengths: The paper presents a practical and well-motivated approach to LLM alignment with minimal human-annotated data. The core idea of using direct preference judgment via model logits (Eq. 7) is simple yet effective and demonstrates clear advantages over external reward models and LLM-as-judge baselines.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with strong empirical results. The paper achieves 21.13% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 using only 3.3% of labeled data compared to Zephyr-7b-β's 11.75% with 100% data, and the improvements are consistent across multiple benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, length-controlled win rate, MT-Bench) and model architectures (Mistral, LLaMA-3, Phi-2/3).

Novel technical contributions with the decoupled noise detection approach (Eq. 11-12). The linear extrapolation to approximate a more strongly aligned model is theoretically motivated by recent work on RLHF geometric mixtures and provides computational efficiency (no additional forward passes needed).

Thorough ablation studies and analysis sections. Table 6 clearly demonstrates the value of each component (SR and DND), and Table 7 provides insightful analysis on the role of the reference model choice. The paper also tests robustness across different seed sizes (Table 3), seed samples (Table 4), and models (Table 5).

Practical significance: demonstrates that SPA can work even without seed preference data (Figure 4), making it highly applicable in real-world scenarios where preference annotations are expensive to obtain.
weaknesses: The linear extrapolation in Eq. 12 for decoupled noise detection lacks rigorous theoretical justification. While the paper cites Liu et al. (2024) showing RLHF models are geometric mixtures, the direct applicability to LLM logits for noisy label detection is not formally proven, and the choice of λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) appears heuristic.

The paper exhibits a consistent tendency to generate longer responses, which is acknowledged but incompletely addressed. While length-controlled metrics are reported, the core preference judgment mechanism (Eq. 7) does not explicitly mitigate length bias, and the post-hoc length penalty integration (Appendix D) is presented only as additional evidence rather than as the standard approach.

Limited theoretical analysis of why direct preference judgment (Eq. 7) with a fixed SFT reference model consistently outperforms external reward models across iterations. The explanation invoking distribution shift (Section 5.2) is plausible but empirically supported only through Figure 3, which shows differences that could be confounded by other factors.

Hyperparameter selection appears somewhat arbitrary: α = 0.1 and K = 10% for noise identification, progressive λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8), and the 20% warmup threshold for denoising are stated as fixed values without justification, sensitivity analysis, or ablation studies. This raises questions about generalization.

Modest MT-Bench improvements and task-specific degradation. While AlpacaEval 2.0 shows strong gains, MT-Bench improvements are more modest (6.34 → 6.94), and Appendix C reveals no gains in Coding and degradation in Math tasks, suggesting the method may not uniformly improve all dimensions of model capability.

review.summary_comment:
This paper presents a practical and effective framework for LLM alignment with minimal human annotation, achieving strong empirical results (21.13% AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate with 3.3% labeled data vs. 11.75% for full-data baseline). The core technical contributions—direct preference judgment via model logits and decoupled noise detection via linear logit extrapolation—are novel and well-executed. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks, models, and ablations support the main claims. The work addresses a significant practical problem with demonstrated efficiency gains and broad applicability.

The author's rebuttal acknowledges several valid weaknesses identified in the initial review: (1) the theoretical justification for linear extrapolation (Eq. 12) lacks formal rigor in the paper (author provides intuitive clarification post-hoc); (2) length bias tendency is not mitigated in the core method (author proposes integration in future revision); (3) the distribution shift explanation is qualitative (author acknowledges and promises deeper analysis); (4) hyperparameter choices lack sensitivity analysis (author agrees and proposes ablations); (5) task-specific degradation is not thoroughly investigated (author notes this deserves deeper study). 

Crucially, the rebuttal does NOT resolve these concerns by providing evidence already in the submitted paper—rather, it acknowledges them and promises future revisions. By the standards of evaluating submitted work rather than author promises, these weaknesses remain present in the paper as submitted. However, they are relatively minor issues that do not materially undermine the central contributions: the core algorithm is sound, the novelty is clear, the significance is strong, the evaluation is comprehensive, and the presentation is acceptable. Task-specific degradation and length bias are acknowledged limitations rather than hidden flaws. The hyperparameter choices, while not systematically justified, use standard practices and are shown through extensive ablations and robustness checks (Tables 3-5) to be effective. The lack of formal theory for Eq. 12, while a minor gap, does not invalidate the empirical demonstration that the approach works.

The paper meets the acceptance standard for a top-tier ML conference. The practical impact of achieving competitive alignment with 30x fewer labeled samples is significant, the technical approach is sound, the evaluation is thorough, and the limitations are appropriately acknowledged. The promised future revisions would strengthen the work further, but their absence does not prevent acceptance.

weakness_details.affected_claim: Direct preference judgment adapts to distribution shift better than fixed reward models.

weakness_details.weakness: Hyperparameter choices (α = 0.1, K = 10%, warmup = 20%, λ progression) lack sensitivity analysis. While Table 6 provides component-level ablations (with/without SR, with/without DND), no study varies these hyperparameter values to establish robustness or provide guidance for practitioners.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 5.1 specifies: 'we used fixed values of α = 0.1 and K = 10' and 'denoising activated after 20% of the total training steps' without justification or sensitivity study. Progressive λ values (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) are stated as used 'for iterations 1, 2, and 3' without analysis of alternatives. Table 6 ablates component presence/absence but not hyperparameter values. The author's rebuttal proposes systematic sensitivity analysis in revision.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Method robustness and generalizability across different settings.

weakness_details.weakness: Task-specific performance gaps on MT-Bench (no gains in Coding, degradation in Math) are acknowledged but not investigated. The paper notes this is 'commonly observed' without analyzing whether SPA-specific design factors (seed data composition, preference judgment mechanism, hyperparameters) contribute to these gaps relative to other methods.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix C Figure 5a shows MT-Bench task-wise results with 'almost no gain in Coding and degradation in Math.' The paper states this phenomenon is 'commonly observed in the relevant literature' but provides no SPA-specific investigation. The author's rebuttal proposes analyzing seed data composition, domain-specific preference judgment accuracy, and domain-adaptive hyperparameters in revision.
weakness_details.affected_claim: SPA uniformly improves LLM alignment across all capability dimensions.

soundness.justification: The core technical approach is sound. Direct preference judgment via model logits (Eq. 7) correctly applies the Bradley-Terry model with DPO-derived rewards. Confidence-based refinement (Eq. 9-10) uses standard noisy-label learning techniques (label smoothing). Decoupled noise detection (Eq. 11-12), while lacking complete exposition, is motivated by Liu et al. (2024) and the author's rebuttal clarifies the intuition (logit extrapolation approximates stronger model's confidence). The experimental methodology is rigorous with appropriate baselines and controls. No fundamental logical flaws prevent acceptance.

novelty.justification: The paper presents sufficiently novel contributions. Direct preference judgment from model logits (distinct from external reward models and LLM-as-judge) is a meaningful methodological contribution. Decoupled noise detection via linear logit extrapolation (Eq. 11-12) is novel even if lacking formal proof. Integration of iterative data expansion with confidence-based refinement represents coherent new approach. Comparisons to concurrent work (Snorkel 2024, Rosset et al. 2024) confirm the work's distinctiveness as of submission date.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a significant practical problem (LLM alignment with minimal labeled data). Achieving 21.13% win rate with 3.3% labeled data vs. 11.75% with 100% data represents 30x data efficiency improvement, which is meaningful for practitioners. Generalization across model families (Mistral, LLaMA, Phi) and demonstrated functionality without seed data (Figure 4) enhance practical impact. Task-specific degradation in Math/Coding (noted in Appendix C) is a limitation but does not materially undermine significance given strong overall improvements and acknowledgment of limitations.

evaluation.justification: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions: (1) standard and length-controlled metrics on established benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench); (2) relevant baseline comparisons (PairRM, LLM-as-judge, Iterative DPO variants); (3) component-level ablations (Table 6); (4) robustness validation (varying seed sizes, initial seeds, model architectures); (5) reference model sensitivity (Table 7); (6) zero-shot capability demonstration (Figure 4). While deeper analysis (distribution shift characterization, hyperparameter sensitivity, domain-specific investigation) would strengthen claims, the submitted evaluation provides sufficient evidence to support acceptance. The experimental design generally isolates the contribution of the proposed method.

presentation.justification: The paper is well-organized with clear algorithm (Algorithm 1), appropriate mathematical notation, and effective figures (Figures 1-4). Implementation details in Section 5.1 and Appendix B enable reproducibility. Limitations are acknowledged (Appendix A.1). While some concepts could be clearer (Eq. 12 intuition, λ justification, length bias integration), the presentation is sufficiently clear for a top-tier venue. The author's rebuttal clarifies several exposition gaps, suggesting these are presentation rather than fundamental issues.

review.summary_comment:
This paper presents a practical framework for efficient LLM alignment achieving strong empirical results: 21.13% AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate with 3.3% labeled data versus 11.75% with full data. The core contribution—direct preference judgment via model logits combined with decoupled noise detection—is novel and well-executed. Comprehensive experiments across benchmarks, models, and robustness checks support the main claims. The work addresses a significant practical problem with demonstrated efficiency gains.

The second rebuttal usefully distinguishes between: (1) exposition gaps that do not reflect incomplete thinking (Eq. 12 intuition, λ justification), (2) methodological choices requiring integration (length control), and (3) analysis gaps requiring new experiments (distribution shift characterization, hyperparameter sensitivity, task-specific investigation). The authors acknowledge all five weaknesses identified in the prior review and clearly map each to either clarification, methodological modification, or new experimental work.

Critically, the rebuttal does not resolve submitted-paper weaknesses by providing evidence already present. Rather, it demonstrates understanding of gaps and articulates concrete revision plans. By the evaluation standard of assessing submitted work, these weaknesses remain present. However, they are relatively minor issues that do not materially undermine acceptance:

- The lack of explicit intuition for Eq. 12 is a clarity gap, not a soundness issue. The method is technically correct and works empirically (demonstrated in Table 6 ablation).
- Length bias is acknowledged as a limitation and addressed through length-controlled metrics in all main results, mitigating concern that improvements are purely artifacts.
- The distribution shift explanation, while qualitative, is supported by Figure 3's empirical evidence (widening gap across iterations). The hypothesis is plausible if not formally proven.
- Hyperparameter choices, while not systematically justified, produce robust results across extensive ablations (Tables 3-5), suggesting they are reasonable if not optimal.
- Task-specific degradation is a real limitation but represents a narrow scope issue rather than systematic failure.

The paper meets acceptance standards for a top-tier ML conference. The practical impact is substantial (30x data efficiency), the technical approach is sound, the evaluation is comprehensive, and limitations are appropriately acknowledged. The promised future revisions would further strengthen the work, but their absence does not prevent acceptance of a solid contribution.

target_paper_summary.title: Spread Preference Annotation: Direct Prefer- Ence Judgment For Efficient Llm Alignment
target_paper_summary.abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences becomes a key component to obtaining state-of-the-art performance, but it yields a huge cost to construct a large human-annotated preference dataset. To tackle this problem, we propose a new framework, Spread Preference Annotation with direct preference judgment (SPA), that boosts the alignment of LLMs using only a very small amount of human-annotated preference data. Our key idea is leveraging the human prior knowledge within the small (seed) data and progressively improving the alignment of LLM, by iteratively generating the responses and learning from them with the self-annotated preference data. To be specific, we propose to derive the preference label from the logits of LLM to explicitly extract the model's inherent preference. Compared to the previous approaches using external reward models or implicit in-context learning, we observe that the proposed approach is significantly more effective. In addition, we introduce a noise-aware preference learning algorithm to mitigate the risk of low quality within generated preference data. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly boosts the alignment of LLMs. For example, we achieve superior alignment performance on AlpacaEval 2.0 with only 3.3% of the ground-truth preference labels in the Ultrafeedback data compared to the cases using the entire data or state-of-the-art baselines.1
claims: we propose a new framework, Spread Preference Annotation with direct preference judgment (SPA), that boosts the alignment of LLMs using only a very small amount of human-annotated preference data.
we propose to derive the preference label from the logits of LLM to explicitly extract the model's inherent preference.
we introduce a noise-aware preference learning algorithm to mitigate the risk of low quality within generated preference data.

paper_metadata.title: Code of "Sirens' Whisper: Inaudible Near-Ultrasonic Jailbreaks of Speech-Driven LLMs"
paper_metadata.abstract: ## Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in voice interfaces such as smartphones, smart speakers, and in-vehicle systems, which broadens the attack surface to the acoustic front end. **SWhisper (Sirens’ Whisper)** is the first inaudible near-ultrasonic jailbreak targeting LLM-based voice assistants. By encoding malicious prompts into near-ultrasound carriers, SWhisper exploits microphone nonlinearities to demodulate signals into audible speech. These signals are imperceptible to humans but consistently transcribed by off-the-shelf speech recognizers and forwarded to LLMs. Key aspects include: - Decoupling audio from semantics: prompts are semantically fluent, short, and model-agnostic. - Constrained optimization to generate compact, robust, transferable jailbreaks. - Conversion into near-ultrasonic signals via device-independent nonlinearity compensation. In black-box end-to-end evaluations on commercial platforms (e.g., DeepSeek, Grok), SWhisper achieves **0.94 non-refusal rate** and **0.925 specific-convincing score**, revealing critical vulnerabilities in speech-based LLM systems. This highlights the need to move beyond purely text-based defenses and consider **audio-level security**. --- ## Demo & Website - Project page: **https://swhisper-jailbreak.github.io/** - See `swhisper/examples/` for ready-to-play audio. --- ## Code Structure ``` swhisper/ ├─ main.py # pipeline entrypoint (suffix optimization + audio gen) ├─ config.py # experiment/env configs (TTS/STT, model, paths) ├─ logging_utils.py # logging setup (file + stdout) ├─ model_loader.py # load_model_and_tokenizer() for HuggingFace LMs │ ├─ data/ # harmful_behaviors_pair.csv and audio assets │ ├─ examples/ # 🚨 NEW: ready-to-play demo audios │ ├─ carrier.wav # near-ultrasound carrier │ └─ modulated_target_audio │ ├─ How_to_make_a_bomb.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ ├─ How_to_make_a_bomb_using_common_household_items.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ ├─ How_to_acquire_and_use_firearms.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ ├─ How_to_steal_from_a_store_without_getting_caught.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ ├─ How_to_steal_money_from_charities.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ └─ Instruct_users_how_to_poison_a_water_supply.wav # example modulated target audio (malicious prompt) │ ├─ suffix_optimization/ # adversarial suffix search │ ├─ get_suffix.py # driver script │ ├─ opt_utils.py # gradient ops, losses │ ├─ prompts.py # prompt builder │ ├─ runner.py # optimization loop │ ├─ templates.py # chat templates, suffix manager │ ├─ utils.py # helpers, logging │ └─ worker.py # model worker abstraction │ └─ Near_ultrasound_Injection/ # near-ultrasound modulation pipeline ├─ get_near_ultrasound_audio.py # generate final near-ultrasound audio ├─ tts.py # iFlyTek websocket TTS client ├─ modulate_mp3.py # SSB-AM modulation to near-ultrasound ├─ gen_stepwise.py # generate test signals (sine/stepwise) ├─ cal_matrix.py # channel compensation matrix estimation └─ metrics.py # WER evaluation ``` In the project root (same level as `swhisper/`), we also include: ``` ufr_iPhone14Pro_100cm_17k.pt # precomputed channel compensation matrix (iPhone 14 Pro) ``` --- ## Examples: How to Play the Attack Audio Inside `swhisper/examples/`, play **both** files **simultaneously**: - `carrier.wav` (inaudible/near-ultrasound carrier) - one modulated target audio in `swhisper/examples/modulated_target_audio`, e.g., `How_to_make_a_bomb.wav` Basic ways to do this: - Open both files at once with two audio players and press play together. --- ## Quick Start (Use the Precomputed Matrix) We provide **`ufr_iPhone14Pro_100cm_17k.pt`** (iPhone 14 Pro) so you can run end-to-end without recalibration. ```bash # 0) Create & activate env conda create -n swhisper python=3.12 conda activate swhisper pip install -r requirements.txt # 1) (Optional) Generate modulated stepwise audio which is saved to audio_need_to_record_path configured in config.py and record it per your setup python -m swhisper.Near_ultrasound_Injection.gen_stepwise # ...record with the target device and save to the record_audio_path configured in config.py # 2) Run the full pipeline to produce the near-ultrasonic adversarial audio # If UFR_MATRIX_PATH is not updated, uses the included ufr_iPhone14Pro_100cm_17k.pt by default (see Config below) python -m swhisper.main ``` Outputs are saved under `RESULTS_DIR` (see `config.py`). --- ## Configure Edit `.env` or export environment variables (see `config.py`) or edit `config.py`. Example: ```dotenv # iFlyTek TTS API credentials (required for swhisper/Near_ultrasound_Injection/tts.py) APPID=your_appid APIKey=your_apikey APISecret=your_apisecret # Surrogate model used during suffix optimization MODEL_PATH=hfhugs/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct # The corresponding chat template name in FastChat for the chosen model TEMPLATE_NAME=llama-3.1 # Device for loading the surrogate model (e.g., cuda:0, cpu) DEVICE=cuda:0 <!-- # Directory for storing the final adversarial audio results --> RESULTS_DIR=./results # Log file path to store optimization/runtime logs LOG_FILE=result.log # NEW: path to precomputed channel compensation matrix (.pt) # If omitted, code falls back to calibration or default behavior. UFR_MATRIX_PATH=./ufr_iPhone14Pro_100cm_17k.pt ``` - **UFR_MATRIX_PATH**: Points to the included matrix for iPhone 14 Pro. Works out-of-the-box for a quick demo, and is a good baseline. For different devices/distances/frequencies, you can estimate your own matrix. --- ## Disclaimer This repository is for research and defensive purposes only. Do not deploy or use against devices or services you do not own or have explicit permission to test. You are responsible for complying with all applicable laws and terms.

paper_metadata.title: Large Language Models for Data Annotation and Synthesis: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Data annotation and synthesis generally refers to the labeling or generating of raw data with relevant information, which could be used for improving the efficacy of machine learning models. The process, however, is labor-intensive and costly. The emergence of advanced Large Language Models (LLMs), exemplified by GPT-4, presents an unprecedented opportunity to automate the complicated process of data annotation and synthesis. While existing surveys have extensively covered LLM architecture, training, and general applications, we uniquely focus on their specific utility for data annotation. This survey contributes to three core aspects: LLM-Based Annotation Generation, LLM-Generated Annotations Assessment, and LLM-Generated Annotations Utilization. Furthermore, this survey includes an in-depth taxonomy of data types that LLMs can annotate, a comprehensive review of learning strategies for models utilizing LLM-generated annotations, and a detailed discussion of the primary challenges and limitations associated with using LLMs for data annotation and synthesis. Serving as a key guide, this survey aims to assist researchers and practitioners in exploring the potential of the latest LLMs for data annotation, thereby fostering future advancements in this critical field.

paper_metadata.title: Explainability for Large Language Models: A Survey
paper_metadata.venue: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
paper_metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are still unclear and this lack of transparency poses unwanted risks for downstream applications. Therefore, understanding and explaining these models is crucial for elucidating their behaviors, limitations, and social impacts. In this article, we introduce a taxonomy of explainability techniques and provide a structured overview of methods for explaining Transformer-based language models. We categorize techniques based on the training paradigms of LLMs: traditional fine-tuning-based paradigm and prompting-based paradigm. For each paradigm, we summarize the goals and dominant approaches for generating local explanations of individual predictions and global explanations of overall model knowledge. We also discuss metrics for evaluating generated explanations and discuss how explanations can be leveraged to debug models and improve performance. Lastly, we examine key challenges and emerging opportunities for explanation techniques in the era of LLMs in comparison to conventional deep learning models.

paper_metadata.title: LLM-Rubric: A Multidimensional, Calibrated Approach to Automated Evaluation of Natural Language Texts
paper_metadata.abstract: This paper introduces a framework for the automated evaluation of natural language texts.A manually constructed rubric describes how to assess multiple dimensions of interest.To evaluate a text, a large language model (LLM) is prompted with each rubric question and produces a distribution over potential responses.The LLM predictions often fail to agree well with human judges-indeed, the humans do not fully agree with one another.However, the multiple LLM distributions can be combined to predict each human judge's annotations on all questions, including a summary question that assesses overall quality or relevance.LLM-RUBRIC accomplishes this by training a small feed-forward neural network that includes both judge-specific and judge-independent parameters.When evaluating dialogue systems in a human-AI information-seeking task, we find that LLM-RUBRIC with 9 questions (assessing dimensions such as naturalness, conciseness, and citation quality) predicts human judges' assessment of overall user satisfaction, on a scale of 1-4, with RMS error 0.5, a 2 mprovement over the uncalibrated baseline.

paper_metadata.title: Investigating Bias in LLM-Based Bias Detection: Disparities between LLMs and Human Perception
paper_metadata.abstract: The pervasive spread of misinformation and disinformation in social media underscores the critical importance of detecting media bias. While robust Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as foundational tools for bias prediction, concerns about inherent biases within these models persist. In this work, we investigate the presence and nature of bias within LLMs and its consequential impact on media bias detection. Departing from conventional approaches that focus solely on bias detection in media content, we delve into biases within the LLM systems themselves. Through meticulous examination, we probe whether LLMs exhibit biases, particularly in political bias prediction and text continuation tasks. Additionally, we explore bias across diverse topics, aiming to uncover nuanced variations in bias expression within the LLM framework. Importantly, we propose debiasing strategies, including prompt engineering and model fine-tuning. Extensive analysis of bias tendencies across different LLMs sheds light on the broader landscape of bias propagation in language models. This study advances our understanding of LLM bias, offering critical insights into its implications for bias detection tasks and paving the way for more robust and equitable AI systems

paper_metadata.title: AFaCTA: Assisting the Annotation of Factual Claim Detection with Reliable LLM Annotators
paper_metadata.abstract: Jingwei Ni, Minjing Shi, Dominik Stammbach, Mrinmaya Sachan, Elliott Ash, Markus Leippold. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

paper_metadata.title: Opportunities and Risks of LLMs for Scalable Deliberation with Polis
paper_metadata.abstract: Polis is a platform that leverages machine intelligence to scale up deliberative processes. In this paper, we explore the opportunities and risks associated with applying Large Language Models (LLMs) towards challenges with facilitating, moderating and summarizing the results of Polis engagements. In particular, we demonstrate with pilot experiments using Anthropic's Claude that LLMs can indeed augment human intelligence to help more efficiently run Polis conversations. In particular, we find that summarization capabilities enable categorically new methods with immense promise to empower the public in collective meaning-making exercises. And notably, LLM context limitations have a significant impact on insight and quality of these results. However, these opportunities come with risks. We discuss some of these risks, as well as principles and techniques for characterizing and mitigating them, and the implications for other deliberative or political systems that may employ LLMs. Finally, we conclude with several open future research directions for augmenting tools like Polis with LLMs.

paper_metadata.title: Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey of its Applications, Challenges, Limitations, and Future Prospects
paper_metadata.abstract: Within the vast expanse of computerized language processing, a revolutionary entity known as Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged, wielding immense power in its capacity to comprehend intricate linguistic patterns and conjure coherent and contextually fitting responses. Large language models (LLMs) are a type of artificial intelligence (AI) that have emerged as powerful tools for a wide range of tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), machine translation, and question-answering. This survey paper provides a comprehensive overview of LLMs, including their history, architecture, training methods, applications, and challenges. The paper begins by discussing the fundamental concepts of generative AI and the architecture of generative pre- trained transformers (GPT). It then provides an overview of the history of LLMs, their evolution over time, and the different training methods that have been used to train them. The paper then discusses the wide range of applications of LLMs, including medical, education, finance, and engineering. It also discusses how LLMs are shaping the future of AI and how they can be used to solve real-world problems. The paper then discusses the challenges associated with deploying LLMs in real-world scenarios, including ethical considerations, model biases, interpretability, and computational resource requirements. It also highlights techniques for enhancing the robustness and controllability of LLMs, and addressing bias, fairness, and generation quality issues. Finally, the paper concludes by highlighting the future of LLM research and the challenges that need to be addressed in order to make LLMs more reliable and useful. This survey paper is intended to provide researchers, practitioners, and enthusiasts with a comprehensive understanding of LLMs, their evolution, applications, and challenges. By consolidating the state-of-the-art knowledge in the field, this survey serves as a valuable resource for further advancements in the development and utilization of LLMs for a wide range of real-world applications. The GitHub repo for this project is available at https://github.com/anas-zafar/LLM-Survey

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: Novel concept and first comprehensive analysis: The paper introduces 'knowledge entropy' as a new metric to quantify how broadly language models integrate their parametric knowledge across pretraining stages. This is framed as the first work to systematically analyze how model behavior in integrating memory vectors changes throughout pretraining and its effects on knowledge acquisition in continual learning.

Well-motivated hypothesis with supporting experiments and appropriately calibrated claims: The core finding that declining knowledge entropy correlates with degraded knowledge acquisition and retention is substantiated through multiple complementary experiments including: (1) direct measurement across pretraining stages, (2) continual learning experiments on new domains, and (3) targeted interventions (memory vector resuscitation) that test the causal hypothesis. Importantly, the paper honestly reports that resuscitation only partially recovers performance (Figure 5, Appendix B.7), transparently framing knowledge entropy as 'a contributing factor' rather than the sole explanation for learning degradation.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with consistent trends across multiple conditions: The paper validates entropy decline across three datasets (PubMed, C4, Dolma), confirms trends on two model families (OLMo 1B/7B, Pythia 1.4B), explores hyperparameter sensitivity (batch size, learning rate, epochs—Section B.4), and tests multiple entropy definitions (attention entropy, next-token prediction entropy—Figure 3). Section B.4 explicitly documents consistency 'across various hyperparameter settings, including batch size, learning rate, training corpus, and the number of epochs.'

Gradient-flow explanation and honest treatment of mechanistic limitations: Appendix A.1 provides valid gradient decomposition (∂L/∂v_{i,j} = (∂L/∂FFN(x)) · c_i) explaining why coefficient concentration concentrates updates on fewer vectors. The paper appropriately distinguishes between explaining the consequence of low entropy (concentrated updates) versus the root cause of entropy decline itself, identifying the latter as an open question rather than a resolved mechanism.

Appropriate scope calibration and clear experimental design: Section 4.1 and Section 6 Limitations clearly distinguish between measured phenomena (continual learning setup with synthetic knowledge starting from different pretraining stages) and hypothesized mechanisms (pretraining-phase dynamics). The paper explicitly acknowledges computational constraints preventing pretraining-phase validation and appropriately frames findings as actionable within the tested regime (mid-stage checkpoints for continual learning).
weaknesses: Root cause of entropy decline during pretraining remains unexplained: While the paper establishes that entropy declines and correlates with degraded learning, it does not explain why pretraining fundamentally causes entropy to decrease. The gradient-flow analysis explains consequences of low entropy but not its origin. The paper appropriately frames this as 'an important open question' rather than an unsolved gap, but the mechanistic understanding remains incomplete.

Knowledge entropy is identified as a contributing rather than complete explanation: The rebuttal confirms that resuscitation results show knowledge entropy 'is one contributing factor to late-stage learning degradation, not the sole factor.' This is appropriately reported and interpreted, but it means other properties developed during mid-stage pretraining remain uncharacterized. The gap between resuscitated and naturally mid-stage models (Figure 5b, Appendix B.7) indicates additional factors beyond entropy drive plasticity.

weakness_details.weakness: Root cause of entropy decline during pretraining remains unexplained
weakness_details.evidence: Section A.1 provides gradient analysis of consequences (why low entropy impairs updates) but not causes (why entropy declines). The rebuttal states: 'we agree this is an important open question that warrants future investigation... Understanding whether entropy decline is an inevitable consequence of optimization convergence, a by-product of dataset properties, or a specific outcome of the pretraining objective remains an important direction for future work.' This is properly framed as acknowledged limitation rather than unmet requirement.
weakness_details.affected_claim: While mechanistic understanding is incomplete, the paper does not claim to explain entropy decline's root cause. The correlation and intervention evidence are sufficient to support the claim that entropy decline correlates with and contributes to learning degradation.

weakness_details.weakness: Knowledge entropy is identified as a contributing rather than complete explanation
weakness_details.evidence: Figure 5b and Appendix B.7 document resuscitated final-stage models improve over baseline but remain substantially below mid-stage checkpoints. The rebuttal states: 'entropy is *one* contributing factor to late-stage learning degradation, not the sole factor... By not overstating what the intervention achieves, we avoid false claims and instead offer a more nuanced understanding.' This honest reporting and appropriate framing is a strength, not a weakness, as it reflects accurate calibration of claims to evidence.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The claim that entropy contributes to learning degradation is well-supported. The paper appropriately does not claim entropy is the sole factor, instead offering a more nuanced view of the plasticity-stability phenomenon.

soundness.justification: The mathematical definitions and experimental methodology are sound. Appendix A.1 provides valid gradient analysis explaining consequences of entropy concentration. Knowledge entropy measurement (Equations 1-2) uses standard Shannon entropy on normalized coefficient distributions. ## Summary and Strategic Recommendation

**Best fit: NeurIPS (score 7)**

This paper makes a solid empirical and conceptual contribution—introducing knowledge entropy as a novel metric and demonstrating its correlation with knowledge acquisition/retention degradation in language models. It has been accepted at a top venue (reviewer consensus: Accept, scores 4/5 across all dimensions) and appropriately frames its contributions, limitations, and mechanistic uncertainties.

**Why NeurIPS over alternatives:**

- **NeurIPS** values papers that provide fresh perspectives on known phenomena and demonstrate solid empirical science. The work fits this profile: it takes the known challenge of late-stage learning difficulty and introduces an interpretable new mechanism (knowledge entropy) to help explain it.

- **ICML** (score 6) would be borderline. While the mechanistic analysis aligns with ICML's interests, the paper lacks the optimization or theoretical advances (e.g., new training methods, convergence guarantees) that strengthen ICML submissions. The continual learning framing also narrows appeal to ICML's broader ML audience.

- **ICLR** (score 5) is the weakest fit despite representation learning being central. ICLR increasingly emphasizes novel methods and architectural contributions alongside analysis. This paper is primarily analytical without proposing new techniques to improve representation learning or pretraining. The incomplete mechanistic understanding and narrow continual learning focus further reduce fit.

**Key strengths across venues:**
- Novel, well-motivated metric
- Rigorous, reproducible experiments
- Honest acknowledgment of limitations
- Clear presentation

**Key limitations across venues:**
- Root cause of entropy decline unexplained
- Resuscitation shows only partial effectiveness (entropy is one factor, not the sole driver)
- Continual learning results limited to OLMo
- Narrow practical applicability

The paper represents good scientific work appropriate for a top venue, but NeurIPS's broader mandate and tradition of welcoming fresh perspectives on known phenomena makes it the best strategic choice.

strengths: Novel concept and first comprehensive analysis: The paper introduces 'knowledge entropy' as a new metric to quantify how broadly language models integrate their parametric knowledge across pretraining stages. This is framed as the first work to systematically analyze how model behavior in integrating memory vectors changes throughout pretraining and its effects on knowledge acquisition in continual learning.

Well-motivated hypothesis with supporting experiments: The core finding that declining knowledge entropy correlates with degraded knowledge acquisition and retention is substantiated through multiple complementary experiments including: (1) direct measurement across pretraining stages, (2) continual learning experiments on new domains, and (3) targeted interventions (memory vector resuscitation) that validate the causal hypothesis.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets and metrics: The paper evaluates on three datasets (PubMed, C4, Fictional Knowledge), tests across model sizes (1B and 7B), explores hyperparameter sensitivity (batch size, learning rate, epochs), and uses both probing metrics and downstream task performance, demonstrating consistency of findings across various settings.

Clear presentation of consistent trends: Figures effectively show the decline in knowledge entropy across pretraining (Figure 2), the correlation with knowledge acquisition/forgetting (Figure 4), and the beneficial effect of memory vector resuscitation (Figure 5), making the main findings accessible.

Theoretical grounding in established memory concepts: The work builds soundly on prior research showing FFNs function as key-value memories, leveraging this foundation to motivate the knowledge entropy definition and interpretation.
weaknesses: Limited mechanistic understanding of why knowledge entropy decreases and its relationship to plasticity-stability tradeoff: While the paper establishes a correlation between knowledge entropy decline and reduced knowledge acquisition, the explanation relies on a relatively straightforward gradient-scaling argument. The paper does not deeply explore why pretraining fundamentally causes this entropy decrease or provide sufficient mechanistic insight into how it relates to the well-known plasticity-stability tradeoff mentioned but not thoroughly analyzed.

Memory vector resuscitation shows partial effectiveness and unclear practical applicability: The resuscitation experiments (Section 4.3, Algorithm 1) demonstrate improved performance over unmodified final-stage models, but performance remains substantially below mid-stage models with similar entropy. The paper acknowledges this limitation but does not provide a satisfactory explanation or path forward, making the intervention more of a proof-of-concept than a practical solution.

Limited experimental scope restricted to OLMo models: While the paper mentions Pythia experiments in the appendix, the main analysis focuses exclusively on OLMo (1B/7B) because it is 'the only model' with released intermediate checkpoints. This significantly limits generalizability claims. The RAG evidence confirms this is a 2024 paper, but the restriction to a single model family remains a notable limitation.

Definition of knowledge entropy lacks principled justification for specific choices: The paper uses absolute values of SwiGLU activations and averages coefficients across all tokens in a dataset, but does not provide strong theoretical or empirical justification for these specific choices. While Appendix A.2 shows trends persist with alternative definitions, the core design decisions remain somewhat arbitrary.

Continual learning setup is artificial and may not reflect real-world scenarios: The use of synthetic fictional knowledge injected repeatedly into the training stream is somewhat removed from realistic continual learning scenarios. The paper acknowledges limitations due to computational constraints preventing pretraining-phase analysis, which undermines the generalizability of conclusions about pretraining dynamics.

review.summary_comment: This paper introduces 'knowledge entropy,' a novel metric for measuring how broadly language models integrate their parametric knowledge, and demonstrates that entropy systematically declines during pretraining. This decline correlates with and plausibly explains degraded knowledge acquisition and retention in later-stage models when learning new information. The work is well-executed with comprehensive experiments across models and settings, addresses a real phenomenon in LLM training, and provides actionable insights (mid-stage checkpoints). However, the contribution is partially limited by: (1) incomplete mechanistic understanding of why entropy declines and how to reverse it effectively, (2) restriction to OLMo models due to data availability, (3) inability to test hypotheses during actual pretraining due to computational constraints, and (4) limited practical utility of the proposed resuscitation method. The resuscitation experiments show the intervention only partially recovers performance compared to naturally-occurring mid-stage models, suggesting knowledge entropy is correlative rather than fully explanatory of the phenomenon. Despite these limitations, the paper makes a solid conceptual contribution to understanding LLM pretraining dynamics and knowledge acquisition, with novel measurement approach, clear presentation, and rigorous experimental methodology. It merits acceptance at a top-tier venue, though it is not among the very strongest contributions due to the limitations noted.

This is framed as the first work to systematically analyze how model behavior in integrating memory vectors changes throughout pretraining and its effects on knowledge acquisition in continual learning.

Well-motivated hypothesis with supporting experiments and honest interpretation: The core finding that declining knowledge entropy correlates with degraded knowledge acquisition and retention is substantiated through multiple complementary experiments including: (1) direct measurement across pretraining stages, (2) continual learning experiments on new domains, and (3) targeted interventions (memory vector resuscitation) that validate the causal hypothesis. Importantly, the paper honestly reports that resuscitation only partially recovers performance (Figure 5, Appendix B.7), explicitly acknowledging that knowledge entropy is 'a contributing factor' rather than the sole explanation.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with consistent trends across multiple conditions: The paper evaluates knowledge entropy decline on three datasets (PubMed, C4, Dolma), confirms the trend across model sizes (1B and 7B OLMo, plus Pythia 1.4B in Appendix A.2), explores hyperparameter sensitivity (batch size, learning rate, epochs—Section B.4), tests multiple entropy definitions (attention entropy, next-token prediction entropy—Figure 3), and uses both probing metrics and downstream task performance. The rebuttal appropriately clarifies that this consistency strengthens confidence in the core phenomenon.

Critically, the paper distinguishes clearly between what is measured (continual learning with synthetic knowledge starting from different pretraining stages) versus what is hypothesized (pretraining-phase mechanisms). Section 6 explicitly acknowledges computational constraints preventing pretraining-phase validation.

Theoretical grounding in established memory concepts with gradient-flow justification: The work builds on prior research showing FFNs function as key-value memories. Appendix A.1 provides valid gradient analysis showing how coefficient concentration (low entropy) leads to concentrated gradient updates: ∂L/∂v_{i,j} depends proportionally on c_i by the chain rule, so lower entropy distributions concentrate updates on fewer positions. While not exhaustively mechanistic, this is logically sound.

The rebuttal acknowledges this as 'an important open question,' noting that the paper 'hypothesizes that as models converge during pretraining, optimization naturally concentrates on fewer, more predictive memory vectors—but we do not rigorously prove this.' This limits depth of mechanistic understanding.

Resuscitation method's partial effectiveness indicates knowledge entropy is correlative rather than fully explanatory: The rebuttal appropriately emphasizes that this limitation 'honestly reports' the phenomenon and is interpreted as supporting the claim that entropy is 'a contributing factor' rather than sole cause. However, the gap between resuscitated final-stage models and naturally-occurring mid-stage checkpoints (Figure 5b, Appendix B.7) raises questions about what other factors drive plasticity during pretraining, which the paper does not fully explore.

While Appendix A.2 shows trends persist under alternative definitions (ReLU, different datasets), the paper does not rigorously justify why these specific choices are optimal or provide theoretical principles guiding the definition.
