paper_metadata.title: Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection: A Systematic Review
paper_metadata.abstract: Anomaly detection has been used for decades to identify and extract anomalous components from data. Many techniques have been used to detect anomalies. One of the increasingly significant techniques is Machine Learning (ML), which plays an important role in this area. In this research paper, we conduct a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) which analyzes ML models that detect anomalies in their application. Our review analyzes the models from four perspectives; the applications of anomaly detection, ML techniques, performance metrics for ML models, and the classification of anomaly detection. In our review, we have identified 290 research articles, written from 2000-2020, that discuss ML techniques for anomaly detection. After analyzing the selected research articles, we present 43 different applications of anomaly detection found in the selected research articles. Moreover, we identify 29 distinct ML models used in the identification of anomalies. Finally, we present 22 different datasets that are applied in experiments on anomaly detection, as well as many other general datasets. In addition, we observe that unsupervised anomaly detection has been adopted by researchers more than other classification anomaly detection systems. Detection of anomalies using ML models is a promising area of research, and there are a lot of ML models that have been implemented by researchers. Therefore, we provide researchers with recommendations and guidelines based on this review.

paper_metadata.title: Smart anomaly detection in sensor systems: A multi-perspective review
paper_metadata.abstract: Anomaly detection is concerned with identifying data patterns that deviate remarkably from the expected behavior. This is an important research problem, due to its broad set of application domains, from data analysis to e-health, cybersecurity, predictive maintenance, fault prevention, and industrial automation. Herein, we review state-of-the-art methods that may be employed to detect anomalies in the specific area of sensor systems, which poses hard challenges in terms of information fusion, data volumes, data speed, and network/energy efficiency, to mention but the most pressing ones. In this context, anomaly detection is a particularly hard problem, given the need to find computing-energy-accuracy trade-offs in a constrained environment. We taxonomize methods ranging from conventional techniques (statistical methods, time-series analysis, signal processing, etc.) to data-driven techniques (supervised learning, reinforcement learning, deep learning, etc.). We also look at the impact that different architectural environments (Cloud, Fog, Edge) can have on the sensors ecosystem. The review points to the most promising intelligent-sensing methods, and pinpoints a set of interesting open issues and challenges.

paper_metadata.title: An Adaptable and Unsupervised TinyML Anomaly Detection System for Extreme Industrial Environments
paper_metadata.abstract: Industrial assets often feature multiple sensing devices to keep track of their status by monitoring certain physical parameters. These readings can be analyzed with machine learning (ML) tools to identify potential failures through anomaly detection, allowing operators to take appropriate corrective actions. Typically, these analyses are conducted on servers located in data centers or the cloud. However, this approach increases system complexity and is susceptible to failure in cases where connectivity is unavailable. Furthermore, this communication restriction limits the approach's applicability in extreme industrial environments where operating conditions affect communication and access to the system. This paper proposes and evaluates an end-to-end adaptable and configurable anomaly detection system that uses the Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, and Tiny-MLOps methodologies in an extreme industrial environment such as submersible pumps. The system runs on an IoT sensing Kit, based on an ESP32 microcontroller and MicroPython firmware, located near the data source. The processing pipeline on the sensing device collects data, trains an anomaly detection model, and alerts an external gateway in the event of an anomaly. The anomaly detection model uses the isolation forest algorithm, which can be trained on the microcontroller in just 1.2 to 6.4 s and detect an anomaly in less than 16 milliseconds with an ensemble of 50 trees and 80 KB of RAM. Additionally, the system employs blockchain technology to provide a transparent and irrefutable repository of anomalies.

paper_metadata.title: A survey on deep learning tools dealing with data scarcity: definitions, challenges, solutions, tips, and applications
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Data scarcity is a major challenge when training deep learning (DL) models. DL demands a large amount of data to achieve exceptional performance. Unfortunately, many applications have small or inadequate data to train DL frameworks. Usually, manual labeling is needed to provide labeled data, which typically involves human annotators with a vast background of knowledge. This annotation process is costly, time-consuming, and error-prone. Usually, every DL framework is fed by a significant amount of labeled data to automatically learn representations. Ultimately, a larger amount of data would generate a better DL model and its performance is also application dependent. This issue is the main barrier for many applications dismissing the use of DL. Having sufficient data is the first step toward any successful and trustworthy DL application. This paper presents a holistic survey on state-of-the-art techniques to deal with training DL models to overcome three challenges including small, imbalanced datasets, and lack of generalization. This survey starts by listing the learning techniques. Next, the types of DL architectures are introduced. After that, state-of-the-art solutions to address the issue of lack of training data are listed, such as Transfer Learning (TL), Self-Supervised Learning (SSL), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), Model Architecture (MA), Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), and Deep Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (DeepSMOTE). Then, these solutions were followed by some related tips about data acquisition needed prior to training purposes, as well as recommendations for ensuring the trustworthiness of the training dataset. The survey ends with a list of applications that suffer from data scarcity, several alternatives are proposed in order to generate more data in each application including Electromagnetic Imaging (EMI), Civil Structural Health Monitoring, Medical imaging, Meteorology, Wireless Communications, Fluid Mechanics, Microelectromechanical system, and Cybersecurity. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first review that offers a comprehensive overview on strategies to tackle data scarcity in DL.

paper_metadata.title: AI-Based Intrusion Detection Systems for In-Vehicle Networks: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: The Controller Area Network (CAN) is the most widely used in-vehicle communication protocol, which still lacks the implementation of suitable security mechanisms such as message authentication and encryption. This makes the CAN bus vulnerable to numerous cyber attacks. Various Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) have been developed to detect these attacks. However, the high generalization capabilities of Artificial Intelligence (AI) make AI-based IDS an excellent countermeasure against automotive cyber attacks. This article surveys AI-based in-vehicle IDS from 2016 to 2022 (August) with a novel taxonomy. It reviews the detection techniques, attack types, features, and benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the article discusses the security of AI models, necessary steps to develop AI-based IDSs in the CAN bus, identifies the limitations of existing proposals, and gives recommendations for future research directions.

paper_metadata.title: Machine Learning Threatens 5G Security
paper_metadata.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is expected to solve many challenges in the fifth generation (5G) of mobile networks. However, ML will also open the network to several serious cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Most of the learning in ML happens through data gathered from the environment. Un-scrutinized data will have serious consequences on machines absorbing the data to produce actionable intelligence for the network. Scrutinizing the data, on the other hand, opens privacy challenges. Unfortunately, most of the ML systems are borrowed from other disciplines that provide excellent results in small closed environments. The resulting deployment of such ML systems in 5G can inadvertently open the network to serious security challenges such as unfair use of resources, denial of service, as well as leakage of private and confidential information. Therefore, in this article we dig into the weaknesses of the most prominent ML systems that are currently vigorously researched for deployment in 5G. We further classify and survey solutions for avoiding such pitfalls of ML in 5G systems.

paper_metadata.title: A Survey of Networking Applications Applying the Software Defined Networking Concept Based on Machine Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: The main task of future networks is to build, as much as possible, intelligent networking architectures for intellectualization, activation, and customization. Software-defined networking (SDN) technology breaks the tight coupling between the control plane and the data plane in the traditional network architecture, making the controllability, security, and economy of network resources into a reality. As one of the important actualization methods of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), combined with SDN architecture will have great potential in areas, such as network resource management, route planning, traffic scheduling, fault diagnosis, and network security. This paper presents the network applications combined with SDN concepts based on ML from two perspectives, namely the perspective of ML algorithms and SDN network applications. From the perspective of ML algorithms, this paper focuses on the applications of classical ML algorithms in SDN-based networks, after a characteristic analysis of algorithms. From the other perspective, after classifying the existing network applications based on the SDN architecture, the related ML solutions are introduced. Finally, the future development of the ML algorithms and SDN concepts is discussed and analyzed. This paper occupies the intersection of the AI, big data, computer networking, and other disciplines; the AI itself is a new and complex interdisciplinary field, which causes the researchers in this field to often have different professional backgrounds and, sometimes, divergent research purposes. This paper is necessary and helpful for researchers from different fields to accurately master the key issues.

paper_metadata.title: A Survey on Machine-Learning Techniques for UAV-Based Communications
paper_metadata.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) will be an integral part of the next generation wireless communication networks. Their adoption in various communication-based applications is expected to improve coverage and spectral efficiency, as compared to traditional ground-based solutions. However, this new degree of freedom that will be included in the network will also add new challenges. In this context, the machine-learning (ML) framework is expected to provide solutions for the various problems that have already been identified when UAVs are used for communication purposes. In this article, we provide a detailed survey of all relevant research works, in which ML techniques have been used on UAV-based communications for improving various design and functional aspects such as channel modeling, resource management, positioning, and security.

paper_metadata.title: Decentral and Incentivized Federated Learning Frameworks: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_metadata.abstract: The advent of federated learning (FL) has sparked a new paradigm of parallel and confidential decentralized machine learning (ML) with the potential of utilizing the computational power of a vast number of Internet of Things (IoT), mobile, and edge devices without data leaving the respective device, thus ensuring privacy by design. Yet, simple FL frameworks (FLFs) naively assume an honest central server and altruistic client participation. In order to scale this new paradigm beyond small groups of already entrusted entities toward mass adoption, FLFs must be: 1) truly decentralized and 2) incentivized to participants. This systematic literature review is the first to analyze FLFs that holistically apply both, the blockchain technology to decentralize the process and reward mechanisms to incentivize participation. 422 publications were retrieved by querying 12 major scientific databases. After a systematic filtering process, 40 articles remained for an in-depth examination following our five research questions. To ensure the correctness of our findings, we verified the examination results with the respective authors. Although having the potential to direct the future of distributed and secure artificial intelligence, none of the analyzed FLFs is production ready. The approaches vary heavily in terms of use cases, system design, solved issues, and thoroughness. We provide a systematic approach to classify and quantify differences between FLFs, expose limitations of current works and derive future directions for research in this novel domain.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem of neurodegenerative disease classification from speech signals, which is a legitimate application domain.

The use of Constant Q Cepstral Coefficients (CQCC) for speech analysis is theoretically motivated by the form-invariance property of the CQT, which is properly explained with mathematical derivations.

The paper evaluates the proposed approach on two distinct datasets (Italian Parkinson's and Minsk2019 ALS databases) and compares against multiple baseline features including Jitter, Shimmer, Teager Energy, and MFCC.
weaknesses: CQCC has already been applied to pathological speech classification in prior work (Patil et al., 2023) for infant cry classification, and the current application to neurodegenerative diseases appears to be a straightforward domain transfer rather than a novel contribution.

The experimental setup has critical methodological issues: the datasets are small and heavily imbalanced (handled via SMOTE which can inflate performance estimates), the train-test split uses only 20% test data with no cross-validation, and results on multi-class classification (Table 5-6) show modest improvements (5.6-7.7%) over MFCC that may not be statistically significant given the lack of confidence intervals or significance tests.

Table 4 reveals an internally inconsistent result: SVM with CQCC achieves 63.4% accuracy on binary classification, which is worse than the Shimmer baseline at 65.3%, directly contradicting the paper's claims of consistent superiority; this critical failure is not explained or investigated in the submitted paper despite the rebuttal acknowledging it as a critical issue.

The paper lacks rigorous statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests are provided for the reported improvements; no ablation studies are conducted to understand which components of CQCC contribute to performance; and the LDA visualization in Figure 3 is qualitative without quantitative metrics.

The form-invariance property explanation (Section 3.1.1 and Appendix) is convoluted and poorly presented, with inconsistent notation (e.g., equation numbering issues, superscripts that appear to be formatting errors like '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), making it difficult to verify the theoretical claims.

The paper contains numerous writing quality issues including grammatical errors ('it;s kind' instead of 'its kind'), typos ('accosication' instead of 'association', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), incomplete sentences, and poor organization, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a top-tier venue.

weakness_details.weakness: CQCC has already been applied to pathological speech classification in prior work (Patil et al., 2023) for infant cry classification, and the current application to neurodegenerative diseases appears to be a straightforward domain transfer rather than a novel contribution.
weakness_details.evidence: The paper cites Patil et al. (2023) which demonstrated CQCC performance on pathological infant cry classification. The paper claims 'to the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first study of it;s kind on sustained vowel sounds for multi neurodegenerative disorder classification and analysis' (line 102). In the second rebuttal, the authors state: 'The submitted paper still claims to be the first study of its kind...Our rebuttal conceded this is domain transfer rather than methodological innovation since CQCC for pathological speech was already demonstrated by Patil et al. (2023). This concession does not change what the submitted paper states.' The submitted paper remains unchanged and continues to claim novelty that has been conceded as invalid.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The claim that this is 'the first study of its kind on sustained vowel sounds for multi neurodegenerative disorder classification'

weakness_details.weakness: The experimental setup has critical methodological issues: the datasets are small and heavily imbalanced (handled via SMOTE which can inflate performance estimates), the train-test split uses only 20% test data with no cross-validation, and results on multi-class classification (Table 5-6) show modest improvements (5.6-7.7%) over MFCC that may not be statistically significant given the lack of confidence intervals or significance tests.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.1 (lines 270-275) states: 'For training and testing, we used 80% and 20% of the data, respectively.' No mention of cross-validation, k-fold validation, or multiple runs appears in the submitted paper. The second rebuttal explicitly acknowledges: 'The submitted paper's Section 4.1 still specifies only: For training and testing, we used 80% and 20% of the data, respectively. No cross-validation was implemented.' Table 2 shows datasets with max ~297-300 samples, yielding test sets of approximately 44-60 samples. The rebuttal states: 'It remains a single 80-20 split on datasets with max ~300 samples, yielding test sets of ~44-60 samples—insufficient for reliable performance estimates.' These methodological flaws remain unaddressed in the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The claimed superiority of CQCC over MFCC with improvements of 5.6% and 7.7%

weakness_details.weakness: Table 4 reveals an internally inconsistent result: SVM with CQCC achieves 63.4% accuracy on binary classification, which is worse than the Shimmer baseline at 65.3%, directly contradicting the paper's claims of consistent superiority; this critical failure is not explained or investigated in the submitted paper despite the rebuttal acknowledging it as a critical issue.
weakness_details.evidence: Table 4 (line 379): SVM Accuracy with CQCC is 63.4%, while SVM with Shimmer is 65.3%. The abstract (lines 45-50) claims: 'CQCC, when integrated with Random Forest and Support Vector Machine classifiers, significantly outperform MFCC, achieving absolute improvements of 5.6% and 7.7%, respectively.' This is demonstrably false for SVM on binary classification. The second rebuttal states: 'This contradicts the abstract's claim of significantly outperform. Our rebuttal identifies this as a critical finding... We propose investigating different kernels (linear, polynomial) and hyperparameter ranges (C, γ). **However, no such investigation appears in the submitted paper.** The submitted paper provides only RBF kernel with C=1 and offers no explanation for SVM's failure.' The authors further state: 'This is not a minor issue—it represents a fundamental contradiction in the paper's central claims that remains entirely unaddressed in the submission.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The abstract's claim that CQCC with SVM 'significantly outperform' MFCC

weakness_details.weakness: The paper lacks rigorous statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests are provided for the reported improvements; no ablation studies are conducted to understand which components of CQCC contribute to performance; and the LDA visualization in Figure 3 is qualitative without quantitative metrics.
weakness_details.evidence: Tables 4, 5, 6 (lines 379-430) report single accuracy values with no error bars, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical tests. No ablation study compares individual components (CQT magnitude, resampling, DCT) in isolation. Section 4.2 specifies only 'RBF kernel and c = 1' with no justification or alternative kernel results. The second rebuttal acknowledges: 'All tables (4, 5, 6) in the submitted paper report single point estimates with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The rebuttal acknowledges: All reported improvements (5.6%, 7.7% in Tables 5-6) lack confidence intervals or significance tests. With small test sets (~60 samples), these differences may be within noise. This problem persists unchanged in the submitted paper.' The LDA analysis (Section 5.2.2, lines 410-430) remains purely visual without quantitative separability indices.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The quantitative claims about CQCC superiority

weakness_details.weakness: The form-invariance property explanation (Section 3.1.1 and Appendix) is convoluted and poorly presented, with inconsistent notation (e.g., equation numbering issues, superscripts that appear to be formatting errors like '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), making it difficult to verify the theoretical claims.
weakness_details.evidence: Equations are numbered with non-standard notation: '(ℑ)' for equation 3 (line 147), '(Σ)' for equation 5 (line 167), '(T)' for equation 7 (line 180). Equation (10) appears twice: lines 245-246 and line 269 with different content. The second rebuttal acknowledges: 'The submitted paper still contains: ... Non-standard equation numbering: (ℑ) for Eq. 3, (Σ) for Eq. 5, (T) for Eq. 7; (6) Equation (10) appears twice with different content (lines 245-246 and line 269). The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading and presentation fixes as future revisions but these are not implemented in the submitted paper.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The theoretical justification for using CQCC based on form-invariance

weakness_details.weakness: The paper contains numerous writing quality issues including grammatical errors ('it;s kind' instead of 'its kind'), typos ('accosication' instead of 'association', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), incomplete sentences, and poor organization, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a top-tier venue.
weakness_details.evidence: Line 102: 'it;s kind'; Line 118: 'accosication'; Line 267: 'aditionally'; Line 316: 'imabalce'; Section 5.1 starts discussing spectrographic analysis but connection to CQCC is unclear; Algorithm 1 notation is inconsistent with main text. The second rebuttal explicitly confirms all these errors persist: 'The submitted paper still contains typos (it;s kind, accosication, aditionally, imabalce), non-standard equation numbering (ℑ), (Σ), (T), and the duplicate equation (10). The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading as a future action—these corrections are not implemented in the current submission.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: Overall presentation quality and professionalism of the submission

soundness.justification: The experimental methodology is fundamentally unsound and remains unchanged in the submitted paper despite acknowledgment in the rebuttal. Single 80-20 train-test split without cross-validation on small datasets (max ~300 samples) with ~45-60 test samples is insufficient for reliable performance estimation. No statistical significance testing validates claimed improvements. Most critically, Table 4 demonstrates SVM with CQCC (63.4%) underperforms Shimmer baseline (65.3%), contradicting the paper's core claims of consistent superiority. The submitted paper provides no explanation or investigation of this catastrophic failure. The second rebuttal explicitly states: 'However, no such investigation appears in the submitted paper. The submitted paper provides only RBF kernel with C=1 and offers no explanation for SVM's failure. This is not a minor issue—it represents a fundamental contradiction in the paper's central claims that remains entirely unaddressed in the submission.' The form-invariance derivation contains formatting errors and notation inconsistencies that hinder verification.

novelty.justification: CQCC application to pathological speech is not new; it was demonstrated in Patil et al. (2023) for infant cries. The paper claims to be 'the first study of its kind on sustained vowel sounds for multi neurodegenerative disorder classification' but the rebuttal explicitly concedes this is 'domain transfer rather than methodological innovation.' The distinction of applying existing CQCC to sustained vowels of neurodegenerative disease versus infant cries represents an incremental variation, not a novel methodological contribution. The submitted paper continues to make this questionable novelty claim (line 102: 'it;s kind' remains uncorrected). The form-invariance property is well-established theory being reapplied. For a top-tier venue, merely applying an existing method to a different disease dataset falls short of novelty standards, particularly when the improvement margins are modest and lack statistical validation.

significance.justification: The results lack clinical or methodological significance. Claimed improvements of 5.6-7.7% on multi-class classification lack statistical validation and may be within noise given small test sets (~45-60 samples). Critically, SVM with CQCC fails catastrophically on binary classification (63.4% vs. 65.3% Shimmer baseline), suggesting the method does not generalize across classifiers. The submitted paper provides no investigation of this failure. Datasets are small (max ~300 samples per disease-control pair) and results on single 80-20 splits are unreliable. No clinical validation or expert evaluation is provided. For a top-tier venue, this work represents neither a methodological advance (acknowledged as domain transfer in rebuttal) nor a validated clinical tool. The authors' second rebuttal states: 'We acknowledge that acceptance at this time would be premature, and we appreciate the detailed guidance for substantial revision.'

evaluation.justification: Critical evaluation gaps persist in the submitted paper: (1) single 80-20 train-test split with no cross-validation or multiple runs; (2) no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; (3) SMOTE handling unspecified regarding potential test data leakage; (4) SVM underperformance (Table 4) not investigated—the submitted paper offers no explanation for why SVM achieves worse performance with CQCC than Shimmer; (5) no ablation studies isolating component contributions; (6) no sensitivity analysis of CQT parameters (B, fmin); (7) no comparison with different SVM kernels or hyperparameters; (8) LDA analysis purely visual without quantitative separability metrics; (9) spectrographic analysis qualitative without statistical validation; (10) no comparison with contemporary deep learning approaches; (11) no comparison with modern baselines like Mel-spectrograms referenced in related work. The second rebuttal explicitly confirms these gaps remain unresolved in the submitted paper.

presentation.justification: Presentation quality remains below standards for a top-tier venue. The submitted paper still contains: (1) typos and grammatical errors ('it;s kind' line 102, 'accosication' line 118, 'aditionally' line 267, 'imabalce' line 316); (2) non-standard equation numbering with symbols '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)' appearing to be formatting errors; (3) duplicate equation (10) with different content (lines 245-246 and 269); (4) convoluted and difficult-to-follow form-invariance explanation (Section 3.1.1); (5) inconsistent notation in Algorithm 1 relative to main text; (6) qualitative spectrographic analysis in Section 5.1 without quantitative metrics; (7) poor organization with spectrographic analysis disconnected from main narrative; (8) methodology details under-specified (SMOTE stratification, cross-validation strategy). The second rebuttal explicitly states: 'The submitted paper still contains typos (it;s kind, accosication, aditionally, imabalce)...The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading as a future action—these corrections are not implemented in the current submission.' These presentation issues would not by themselves warrant rejection, but combined with major methodological and evaluation flaws they prevent acceptance.

reviewers.summary_comment: The authors' second rebuttal demonstrates professional integrity by explicitly acknowledging that the submitted paper remains fundamentally unchanged despite the rebuttal's identification of critical flaws. The authors state: 'However, rebuttal statements that promise future corrections do not constitute corrections to the submitted work. A paper must be evaluated on its submitted form, not on the authors' intentions for future revision.' This statement accurately reflects the evaluation standard. The submitted paper has **zero unresolved critical issues**—all critical flaws identified in the initial review remain present and unaddressed in the current submission: (1) **Novelty**: The paper continues to claim being 'the first study of its kind' (line 102) despite the rebuttal's acknowledgment this is 'domain transfer rather than methodological innovation'; (2) **SVM Failure**: Table 4 shows SVM+CQCC (63.4%) underperforms Shimmer (65.3%), contradicting abstract claims, with no investigation or explanation in the submitted paper; (3) **Methodology**: Section 4.1 still specifies only single 80-20 split with no cross-validation, acknowledged as 'inadequate' in rebuttal but unchanged in submission; (4) **Statistical Validation**: All tables report single point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests, unchanged from initial submission; (5) **Presentation**: All typos ('it;s kind', 'accosication', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), formatting errors ('(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), and duplicate equation (10) remain in submitted paper; (6) **Ablation Studies**: Promised but not implemented; (7) **Spectrographic Analysis**: Remains qualitative without quantitative metrics. The authors' acknowledgment in the second rebuttal that 'acceptance at this time would be premature' is appropriate. The paper requires substantial new experimental work (cross-validation, statistical testing, SVM investigation, ablation studies, deep learning comparisons, quantitative analysis) that would effectively constitute a new submission. As the submitted paper stands, it does not meet acceptance standards for a selective top-tier machine learning conference.

### Summary

**Overall Assessment**: This paper is **not suitable for submission to any of these three venues** in its current form.

**Critical Issues Across All Venues**:

1. **Fundamental Methodological Flaws** (unresolved in submitted paper):
   - Single 80-20 train-test split without cross-validation on datasets with max ~300 samples
   - SVM with CQCC achieves 63.4% vs. 65.3% for Shimmer—contradiction of central claims with no explanation
   - No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars
   - Test set sizes (~45-60 samples) too small for reliable estimates

2. **Lack of Novelty** (acknowledged but unchanged in submission):
   - CQCC application to pathological speech already demonstrated in Patil et al. 2023
   - Authors' rebuttal concedes this is "domain transfer rather than methodological innovation"
   - Yet submitted paper continues claiming to be "the first study of its kind"

   - Typos: 'it;s kind', 'accosication', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'
   - Non-standard equation numbering: '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'
   - Duplicate equation (10) with conflicting definitions

4. **Venue-Specific Misalignments**:
   - **ICML**: Lacks algorithmic/systems novelty; insufficient rigor for methods conference
   - **NeurIPS**: No novel ML contribution; purely application-focused with flawed evaluation
   - **ICLR**: Employs only classical ML (RF, SVM), no deep learning or learned representations

The authors' own rebuttal statement is apt: *"acceptance at this time would be premature."* The paper requires substantial new experimental work (cross-validation, statistical testing, SVM investigation, deep learning comparisons) that would effectively constitute a new submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem of neurodegenerative disease classification from speech signals, which is a legitimate application domain.

The use of Constant Q Cepstral Coefficients (CQCC) for speech analysis is theoretically motivated by the form-invariance property of the CQT, which is properly explained with mathematical derivations.

The paper evaluates the proposed approach on two distinct datasets (Italian Parkinson's and Minsk2019 ALS databases) and compares against multiple baseline features including Jitter, Shimmer, Teager Energy, and MFCC.
weaknesses: CQCC has already been applied to pathological speech classification in prior work (Patil et al., 2023) for infant cry classification, and the current application to neurodegenerative diseases appears to be a straightforward domain transfer rather than a novel contribution.

The experimental setup has critical methodological issues: the datasets are small and heavily imbalanced (handled via SMOTE which can inflate performance estimates), the train-test split uses only 20% test data with no cross-validation, and results on multi-class classification (Table 5-6) show modest improvements (5.6-7.7%) over MFCC that may not be statistically significant given the lack of confidence intervals or significance tests.

The paper lacks rigorous statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests are provided for the reported improvements; no ablation studies are conducted to understand which components of CQCC contribute to performance; and the LDA visualization in Figure 3 is qualitative without quantitative metrics.

The form-invariance property explanation (Section 3.1.1 and Appendix) is convoluted and poorly presented, with inconsistent notation (e.g., equation numbering issues, superscripts that appear to be formatting errors like '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), making it difficult to verify the theoretical claims.

The paper contains numerous writing quality issues including grammatical errors ('it;s kind' instead of 'its kind'), typos ('accosication' instead of 'association', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), incomplete sentences, and poor organization, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a top-tier venue.

The spectrographic analysis in Section 5.1 is descriptive rather than quantitative, providing qualitative explanations of spectrograms without numerical evidence or statistical backing for the claimed differences between disease conditions.

The experimental comparison is incomplete: no comparison with other state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for speech-based disease classification; no comparison with other advanced features like spectrograms or log-mel spectrograms that are increasingly common in modern applications; and the classifier choices (RF and SVM) are dated relative to current practice.

The work would require major revisions including: rigorous cross-validation with statistical testing, comparison with modern deep learning baselines, explanation of SVM's poor performance, quantitative spectrographic analysis, and substantial presentation improvements. In its current form, it does not meet the standards of a selective top-tier machine learning conference.

The rebuttal promises 'extensive proofreading' as future work, not a fix in the current submission. For a top-tier venue, a paper must be evaluated on its current form, and this submission has critical flaws in soundness, novelty, and evaluation that would require substantial new experimental work to resolve. The rebuttal does not provide evidence of completed corrections; it acknowledges the need for corrections. Therefore, the decision to reject remains unchanged.

weakness_details.weakness: Table 4 reveals an internally inconsistent result: SVM with CQCC achieves 63.4% accuracy on binary classification, which is worse than the Shimmer baseline at 65.3%, directly contradicting the paper's claims of consistent superiority; this critical failure is not explained or investigated in the submitted paper despite the rebuttal acknowledging it as a critical issue.
weakness_details.evidence: Table 4 (line 379): SVM Accuracy with CQCC is 63.4%, while SVM with Shimmer is 65.3%. The abstract (lines 45-50) claims: 'CQCC, when integrated with Random Forest and Support Vector Machine classifiers, significantly outperform MFCC, achieving absolute improvements of 5.6% and 7.7%, respectively.' This is demonstrably false for SVM on binary classification. The second rebuttal states: 'This contradicts the abstract's claim of significantly outperform. Our rebuttal identifies this as a critical finding... We propose investigating different kernels (linear, polynomial) and hyperparameter ranges (C, γ). **However, no such investigation appears in the submitted paper.** The submitted paper provides only RBF kernel with C=1 and offers no explanation for SVM's failure.' The authors further state: 'This is not a minor issue—it represents a fundamental contradiction in the paper's central claims that remains entirely unaddressed in the submission.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The abstract's claim that CQCC with SVM 'significantly outperform' MFCC

weakness_details.weakness: The paper lacks rigorous statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, p-values, or significance tests are provided for the reported improvements; no ablation studies are conducted to understand which components of CQCC contribute to performance; and the LDA visualization in Figure 3 is qualitative without quantitative metrics.
weakness_details.evidence: Tables 4, 5, 6 (lines 379-430) report single accuracy values with no error bars, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical tests. No ablation study compares individual components (CQT magnitude, resampling, DCT) in isolation. Section 4.2 specifies only 'RBF kernel and c = 1' with no justification or alternative kernel results. The second rebuttal acknowledges: 'All tables (4, 5, 6) in the submitted paper report single point estimates with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The rebuttal acknowledges: All reported improvements (5.6%, 7.7% in Tables 5-6) lack confidence intervals or significance tests. With small test sets (~60 samples), these differences may be within noise. This problem persists unchanged in the submitted paper.' The LDA analysis (Section 5.2.2, lines 410-430) remains purely visual without quantitative separability indices.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The quantitative claims about CQCC superiority

weakness_details.weakness: The form-invariance property explanation (Section 3.1.1 and Appendix) is convoluted and poorly presented, with inconsistent notation (e.g., equation numbering issues, superscripts that appear to be formatting errors like '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), making it difficult to verify the theoretical claims.
weakness_details.evidence: Equations are numbered with non-standard notation: '(ℑ)' for equation 3 (line 147), '(Σ)' for equation 5 (line 167), '(T)' for equation 7 (line 180). Equation (10) appears twice: lines 245-246 and line 269 with different content. The second rebuttal acknowledges: 'The submitted paper still contains: ... Non-standard equation numbering: (ℑ) for Eq. 3, (Σ) for Eq. 5, (T) for Eq. 7; (6) Equation (10) appears twice with different content (lines 245-246 and line 269). The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading and presentation fixes as future revisions but these are not implemented in the submitted paper.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The theoretical justification for using CQCC based on form-invariance

weakness_details.weakness: The paper contains numerous writing quality issues including grammatical errors ('it;s kind' instead of 'its kind'), typos ('accosication' instead of 'association', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), incomplete sentences, and poor organization, suggesting insufficient proofreading for a top-tier venue.
weakness_details.evidence: Line 102: 'it;s kind'; Line 118: 'accosication'; Line 267: 'aditionally'; Line 316: 'imabalce'; Section 5.1 starts discussing spectrographic analysis but connection to CQCC is unclear; Algorithm 1 notation is inconsistent with main text. The second rebuttal explicitly confirms all these errors persist: 'The submitted paper still contains typos (it;s kind, accosication, aditionally, imabalce), non-standard equation numbering (ℑ), (Σ), (T), and the duplicate equation (10). The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading as a future action—these corrections are not implemented in the current submission.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: Overall presentation quality and professionalism of the submission

soundness.justification: The experimental methodology is fundamentally unsound and remains unchanged in the submitted paper despite acknowledgment in the rebuttal. Single 80-20 train-test split without cross-validation on small datasets (max ~300 samples) with ~45-60 test samples is insufficient for reliable performance estimation. No statistical significance testing validates claimed improvements. Most critically, Table 4 demonstrates SVM with CQCC (63.4%) underperforms Shimmer baseline (65.3%), contradicting the paper's core claims of consistent superiority. The submitted paper provides no explanation or investigation of this catastrophic failure. The second rebuttal explicitly states: 'However, no such investigation appears in the submitted paper. The submitted paper provides only RBF kernel with C=1 and offers no explanation for SVM's failure. This is not a minor issue—it represents a fundamental contradiction in the paper's central claims that remains entirely unaddressed in the submission.' The form-invariance derivation contains formatting errors and notation inconsistencies that hinder verification.

novelty.justification: CQCC application to pathological speech is not new; it was demonstrated in Patil et al. (2023) for infant cries. The paper claims to be 'the first study of its kind on sustained vowel sounds for multi neurodegenerative disorder classification' but the rebuttal explicitly concedes this is 'domain transfer rather than methodological innovation.' The distinction of applying existing CQCC to sustained vowels of neurodegenerative disease versus infant cries represents an incremental variation, not a novel methodological contribution. The submitted paper continues to make this questionable novelty claim (line 102: 'it;s kind' remains uncorrected). The form-invariance property is well-established theory being reapplied. For a top-tier venue, merely applying an existing method to a different disease dataset falls short of novelty standards, particularly when the improvement margins are modest and lack statistical validation.

significance.justification: The results lack clinical or methodological significance. Claimed improvements of 5.6-7.7% on multi-class classification lack statistical validation and may be within noise given small test sets (~45-60 samples). Critically, SVM with CQCC fails catastrophically on binary classification (63.4% vs. 65.3% Shimmer baseline), suggesting the method does not generalize across classifiers. The submitted paper provides no investigation of this failure. Datasets are small (max ~300 samples per disease-control pair) and results on single 80-20 splits are unreliable. No clinical validation or expert evaluation is provided. For a top-tier venue, this work represents neither a methodological advance (acknowledged as domain transfer in rebuttal) nor a validated clinical tool. The authors' second rebuttal states: 'We acknowledge that acceptance at this time would be premature, and we appreciate the detailed guidance for substantial revision.'

evaluation.justification: Critical evaluation gaps persist in the submitted paper: (1) single 80-20 train-test split with no cross-validation or multiple runs; (2) no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; (3) SMOTE handling unspecified regarding potential test data leakage; (4) SVM underperformance (Table 4) not investigated—the submitted paper offers no explanation for why SVM achieves worse performance with CQCC than Shimmer; (5) no ablation studies isolating component contributions; (6) no sensitivity analysis of CQT parameters (B, fmin); (7) no comparison with different SVM kernels or hyperparameters; (8) LDA analysis purely visual without quantitative separability metrics; (9) spectrographic analysis qualitative without statistical validation; (10) no comparison with contemporary deep learning approaches; (11) no comparison with modern baselines like Mel-spectrograms referenced in related work. The second rebuttal explicitly confirms these gaps remain unresolved in the submitted paper.

presentation.justification: Presentation quality remains below standards for a top-tier venue. The submitted paper still contains: (1) typos and grammatical errors ('it;s kind' line 102, 'accosication' line 118, 'aditionally' line 267, 'imabalce' line 316); (2) non-standard equation numbering with symbols '(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)' appearing to be formatting errors; (3) duplicate equation (10) with different content (lines 245-246 and 269); (4) convoluted and difficult-to-follow form-invariance explanation (Section 3.1.1); (5) inconsistent notation in Algorithm 1 relative to main text; (6) qualitative spectrographic analysis in Section 5.1 without quantitative metrics; (7) poor organization with spectrographic analysis disconnected from main narrative; (8) methodology details under-specified (SMOTE stratification, cross-validation strategy). The second rebuttal explicitly states: 'The submitted paper still contains typos (it;s kind, accosication, aditionally, imabalce)...The rebuttal promises extensive proofreading as a future action—these corrections are not implemented in the current submission.' These presentation issues would not by themselves warrant rejection, but combined with major methodological and evaluation flaws they prevent acceptance.

review.summary_comment: The authors' second rebuttal demonstrates professional integrity by explicitly acknowledging that the submitted paper remains fundamentally unchanged despite the rebuttal's identification of critical flaws. The authors state: 'However, rebuttal statements that promise future corrections do not constitute corrections to the submitted work. A paper must be evaluated on its submitted form, not on the authors' intentions for future revision.' This statement accurately reflects the evaluation standard. The submitted paper has **zero unresolved critical issues**—all critical flaws identified in the initial review remain present and unaddressed in the current submission: (1) **Novelty**: The paper continues to claim being 'the first study of its kind' (line 102) despite the rebuttal's acknowledgment this is 'domain transfer rather than methodological innovation'; (2) **SVM Failure**: Table 4 shows SVM+CQCC (63.4%) underperforms Shimmer (65.3%), contradicting abstract claims, with no investigation or explanation in the submitted paper; (3) **Methodology**: Section 4.1 still specifies only single 80-20 split with no cross-validation, acknowledged as 'inadequate' in rebuttal but unchanged in submission; (4) **Statistical Validation**: All tables report single point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests, unchanged from initial submission; (5) **Presentation**: All typos ('it;s kind', 'accosication', 'aditionally', 'imabalce'), formatting errors ('(ℑ)', '(Σ)', '(T)'), and duplicate equation (10) remain in submitted paper; (6) **Ablation Studies**: Promised but not implemented; (7) **Spectrographic Analysis**: Remains qualitative without quantitative metrics. The authors' acknowledgment in the second rebuttal that 'acceptance at this time would be premature' is appropriate. The paper requires substantial new experimental work (cross-validation, statistical testing, SVM investigation, ablation studies, deep learning comparisons, quantitative analysis) that would effectively constitute a new submission. As the submitted paper stands, it does not meet acceptance standards for a selective top-tier machine learning conference.

target_paper_summary.title: Neuroacoustic Patterns: Constant Q Cep- Stral Coefficients For The Classification Of Neurodegenerative Disorders
target_paper_summary.abstract: Early identification of neurodegenerative diseases is crucial for effective diagnosis in neurological disorders. However, the quasi-periodic nature of vocal tract sampling often results in inadequate spectral resolution in traditional spectral features, such as Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), thereby limiting their classification effectiveness. In this study, we propose the use of Constant Q Cepstral Coefficients (CQCC), which leverage geometrically spaced frequency bins to provide superior spectrotemporal resolution, particularly for capturing the fundamental frequency and its harmonics in speech signals associated with neurodegenerative disorders. Our results demonstrate that CQCC, when integrated with Random Forest and Support Vector Machine classifiers, significantly outperform MFCC, achieving absolute improvements of 5.6 % and 7.7 %, respectively. Furthermore, CQCC show enhanced performance over traditional acoustic measures, such as Jitter, Shimmer, and Teager Energy. The effectiveness of CQCC is underpinned by the form-invariance property of the Constant Q Transform (CQT), which ensures consistent feature representation across varying pitch and tonal conditions, thereby enhancing classification robustness. Furthermore, the robustness of CQCC features against MFCC features are validated using LDA plots. These findings are validated using the Italian Parkinson's database and the Minsk2019 database of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, underscoring the potential of CQCC to advance the classification of neurodegenerative disorders.
claims: we propose the use of Constant Q Cepstral Coefficients (CQCC), which leverage geometrically spaced frequency bins to provide superior spectrotemporal resolution, particularly for capturing the fundamental frequency and its harmonics in speech signals associated with neurodegenerative disorders.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: Well-motivated and thoughtful design: The paper identifies genuine pain points in LLM-based web automation (infeasible subtasks, lack of data) and proposes targeted solutions. The subgoal-guided verification idea is intuitive and addresses a real problem by enabling verification at a simpler level than task execution itself.

Strong empirical results: VeSX achieves 34.0% average success rate on WebArena, significantly outperforming prior work without human guidance (Drouin et al.: 23.5%, Koh et al.: 19.2%) and even surpassing the human-feedback-assisted method in two scenarios. The improvements are particularly substantial in Shop (47% relative gain), CMS (51%), and Red (169%).

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper provides thorough ablations for all three components (subgoal-guided verification, hierarchical self-correction, exemplar bank), demonstrating the necessity of each. The ablations are well-structured and provide actionable insights, e.g., showing that reflection has larger impact than replanning but both are needed.

Practical hierarchical approach to error correction: The reflection-then-replanning strategy is sensible—attempting to fix execution errors locally before regenerating plans—and the ablations show both components significantly contribute to performance.

Exemplar bank design addresses scalability: Using single actions rather than full trajectories as exemplars is an effective approach to handle long web tasks, and the heuristic metadata generation (abstract subtask + action context) is reasonable and shows measurable impact (+13.7% over no abstraction).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual components: Subgoal-guided verification, self-correction, and exemplar-based learning are not novel techniques in isolation. The core contribution is their combination and adaptation to web automation, but the individual mechanisms are relatively straightforward applications of existing ideas (verification has been explored in math reasoning, reflection in agent work, exemplar learning in few-shot prompting).

Critical technical details missing from submitted paper: The submitted paper lacks precise specifications for key mechanisms. Reflection prompts are not shown; replanning logic is vague; exemplar retrieval methods are underspecified; Algorithm 1 lacks iteration bounds; the self-evaluation prompt for exemplar collection is not documented. The author's rebuttal acknowledges these gaps exist and commits to adding them in future revisions, confirming they are not currently in the submitted paper.

Verification method extensibility to new domains unclear: External verification relies on pre-designed functions (check_url, check_webpage_content, check_action_history) that require domain-specific implementation. The paper provides no guidance on designing these functions for new domains, and the rebuttal only commits to adding such guidance in future work.

Exemplar bank construction relies on LLM self-evaluation with unquantified confirmation bias: The paper describes using LLM self-evaluation to judge trajectory success but does not show the evaluation prompt or report filtering statistics for all scenarios. The rebuttal acknowledges this is a reproducibility issue and commits to adding these details in revision, confirming they are absent from the submitted paper.

Evaluation limited to single benchmark without generalization evidence: Testing only on WebArena prevents claims about generalization to other interactive agent domains. The paper makes no attempt to evaluate on other benchmarks like Mind2Web, and the rebuttal provides no new experiments.

weakness_details.weakness: Limited technical novelty of individual components: Subgoal-guided verification, self-correction, and exemplar-based learning are not novel techniques in isolation. The core contribution is their combination and adaptation to web automation, but the individual mechanisms are relatively straightforward applications of existing ideas (verification has been explored in math reasoning, reflection in agent work, exemplar learning in few-shot prompting).
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4 cites prior work on verification in complex reasoning (Wang et al., 2023b; Gou et al., 2023), reflection in agent workflows, and exemplar-based prompting. The rebuttal acknowledges 'the individual components are indeed known techniques' and defends the contribution as 'their combination and adaptation to web automation.' The ablations show component necessity but not novelty of individual mechanisms.

The author's rebuttal acknowledges these gaps exist and commits to adding them in future revisions, confirming they are not currently in the submitted paper.

Section 3.1 (lines 326-330) describes the self-evaluation process but does not provide the prompt. The rebuttal's second response states: 'The reflection prompt: Not shown in Section 2.3... This should be in Appendix A.2' and 'We acknowledge these are significant gaps... In a revision, we would add...' This confirms the gaps are acknowledged as absent from the submitted paper.

The paper provides no guidance on designing these functions for new domains, and the rebuttal only commits to adding such guidance in future work.

This confirms the submitted paper lacks this guidance.

If LLM considers the whole execution trajectory to be reasonable and the final result may be correct, the actions in this trajectory will be collected as exemplars' but does not show the prompt. Only Section 3.3.3 mentions '35 trajectories that were deemed correctly completed' for Shop; statistics for other scenarios are not in the submitted paper. The rebuttal states: 'In the submitted paper, Section 3.1 states the yield rate for Shop is 35/60 ≈ 58% (though this is not explicit)... We do not provide yield rates for other scenarios. We should have: (1) shown the self-evaluation prompt explicitly, (2) reported yield rates for all scenarios' confirming these are absent from the submitted paper.

The paper makes no attempt to evaluate on other benchmarks like Mind2Web, and the rebuttal provides no new experiments.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 3.1 (lines 313-318) evaluates only on WebArena with 5 scenarios. No evaluation on Mind2Web, DigitalEnv, or other interactive benchmarks is provided. The rebuttal states: 'we have not evaluated on Mind2Web or other benchmarks' and 'We do not propose new experiments in this rebuttal... we have not conducted additional benchmarks for this submission.' This confirms no cross-benchmark evaluation exists in or will be added to the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Claims about generalization of VeSX to interactive agent tasks beyond web automation.

soundness.justification: The core framework logic is sound: subgoal-guided verification enables checking subtask completion against simpler criteria; hierarchical self-correction (reflection-then-replan) addresses both execution and planning errors; exemplar banks support in-context learning. The rebuttal's clarification that reflection attempts once, then triggers replanning if needed (preventing infinite loops) is logically complete and consistent with Algorithm 1. The ablation studies empirically validate that each component contributes to performance. While the submitted paper lacks technical details that would allow precise reproduction, the high-level approach is valid and the empirical validation is sound for the WebArena domain.

novelty.justification: Individual components (verification, reflection, exemplar learning) exist in prior work, but the rebuttal provides substantive clarification of how their combination is novel: (1) subgoal-guided verification formulates verification as a distinct, simpler problem from execution—this conceptual separation is not standard in web automation literature; (2) hierarchical reflect-then-replan is specifically designed for web environments where planning failures are common and distinct from execution failures; (3) exemplar bank using single actions with abstract subtask metadata and action context is novel to web automation (prior work uses full trajectories). The ablations (Tables 2-5) demonstrate that each component is necessary (removing any degrades performance), supporting their non-redundancy. For an applied domain paper, this level of methodological contribution is acceptable at a top-tier venue.

significance.justification: VeSX achieves 34.0% average success on WebArena, substantially outperforming prior work without human guidance (23.5% best prior) and competitive with human-guided methods (33.5%). Improvements are significant in multiple scenarios (47-169% relative gains). The framework addresses real problems in LLM agent deployment (infeasible subtasks, data scarcity). However, significance is limited by evaluation on a single benchmark; generalization beyond WebArena is undemonstrated. The contribution is solid and meaningful within the web automation domain but not transformative for the broader ML field.

evaluation.justification: The evaluation includes comprehensive baseline comparisons (5 methods), detailed ablations for all three components (Tables 2-5), and consistent improvements across all five scenarios. The experimental setup is sound (using gpt-4o consistently, temperature=0 for reproducibility). The rebuttal clarifies that exemplar collection yields 58% for Shop (35/60 tasks) and acknowledges that statistics for other scenarios are not reported in the submitted paper. The ablations thoroughly validate component contributions. However, there are gaps: (1) exemplar statistics not reported for all scenarios in submitted paper, (2) no analysis of verification accuracy or failure modes, (3) no computational cost analysis, (4) Algorithm 1 iteration bounds not specified. Overall, evaluation is adequate for claiming WebArena performance but lacks depth in understanding failure modes and generalization.

presentation.justification: The paper is well-organized with clear motivation, structured related work, and systematic explanation of three components. Figures 1 and 3 effectively illustrate the framework. However, presentation has persistent gaps acknowledged by the rebuttal as requiring revision: (1) reflection and replanning prompts not shown (required for reproducibility), (2) exemplar retrieval specifications incomplete (threshold not documented), (3) Algorithm 1 lacks iteration bounds, (4) self-evaluation prompt for exemplar collection not provided, (5) filtering statistics incomplete (only Shop reported in results section, per rebuttal). The rebuttal acknowledges these are 'significant gaps' and that the paper 'should have included these details in the original submission.' The gaps prevent precise reproduction but do not make the paper incomprehensible at a high level. Clarity is sufficient for understanding the approach but insufficient for implementation without access to authors' code or detailed prompts.

reviewers.summary_comment: VeSX proposes a well-motivated framework for LLM agents in web automation combining subgoal-guided verification, hierarchical self-correction, and exemplar banks. The empirical results are strong, achieving state-of-the-art on WebArena (34.0% vs. 23.5% prior best without human guidance) with comprehensive ablations demonstrating the necessity of each component. The core ideas are sound and appropriately combined for this application domain. However, the submitted paper has material reproducibility gaps that the rebuttal acknowledges and commits to fixing in revision: reflection prompts are not shown, replanning logic is underspecified, exemplar retrieval mechanisms lack detail, Algorithm 1 lacks iteration bounds, the self-evaluation prompt for exemplars is missing, and filtering statistics are incomplete. These gaps are not resolved by the rebuttal; rather, the rebuttal confirms their absence and explains what should be added. The paper is acceptable because: (1) the framework is sound and validated empirically on a standard benchmark, (2) the component combination is sufficiently novel for web automation, (3) ablations are thorough and show component necessity, (4) the results are significant for the domain. However, the reproducibility and technical specification gaps prevent this from being a strong accept. The work makes a solid applied contribution with strong WebArena performance, but generalization to other domains is undemonstrated and the detailed implementation cannot be reliably reproduced from the submitted paper alone. For a top-tier venue, this meets the acceptance threshold as a methodologically sound contribution to an important applied domain with convincing empirical validation, despite presentation and scope limitations.

### Detailed Reasoning

**Paper Summary:**
VeSX is a framework for LLM-based web automation agents combining three components: (1) subgoal-guided verification to validate subtask completion, (2) hierarchical self-correction (reflection for execution errors, replanning for planning errors), and (3) an exemplar bank using single actions with metadata for in-context learning. Evaluated on WebArena, VeSX achieves 34% average success rate, outperforming prior methods without human guidance.

**Reviewer Assessment:**
- **Strengths**: Strong empirical results, well-motivated design, comprehensive ablations, practical hierarchical error correction
- **Critical Weaknesses**: Limited novelty of individual components; missing technical details (prompts, retrieval specs, Algorithm 1 bounds); reproducibility gaps acknowledged in rebuttal as unfixed; single-benchmark evaluation; unquantified LLM self-evaluation bias

---

### Cross-Venue Analysis

**ICML (Score: 6/10 – Borderline/Risky)**

ICML is a strong fit for application-driven ML work with solid engineering contributions. VeSX's practical design addressing real web automation challenges aligns with ICML's "application-driven machine learning" track. The comprehensive ablations and strong WebArena results meet evaluation standards.

However, ICML expects either (1) novel ML methodology or (2) broader empirical validation. VeSX provides neither: individual components are known techniques (verification from math reasoning, reflection from agent work, exemplars from few-shot learning), and evaluation is single-benchmark. The paper reads as careful engineering of existing ideas rather than a methodological advance. The reproducibility gaps (missing prompts, underspecified Algorithm 1) particularly hurt here because ICML values systems work that can be replicated and built upon.

**Risk**: Rejection likely if reviewers emphasize novelty or reproducibility. Acceptance likely if reviewers weight strong empirical results and practical problem-solving heavily. **Verdict**: Risky submission.

---

**NeurIPS (Score: 6/10 – Borderline/Risky)**

NeurIPS's explicit interest in "AI/ML for practical applications" and "AI systems" makes this appealing. The strong results and agent-system design fit the conference's scope.

However, NeurIPS attracts world-class research across ML disciplines. This paper is domain-specific engineering rather than advancing fundamental concepts in learning, optimization, or reasoning that would have broad impact. The missing technical details and single-benchmark scope are significant concerns for a venue expecting reproducible, broadly applicable contributions. The paper doesn't clarify whether the gains come from the algorithmic contribution or from careful prompting/engineering of GPT-4o.

**Risk**: Similar to ICML—strong empirical results are offsetting factors, but limited novelty and scope make this risky. **Verdict**: Borderline, likely rejection without significant revisions addressing generalization and technical clarity.

---

**ICLR (Score: 5/10 – Weak Fit)**

ICLR focuses on representation learning, learning algorithms, and learned systems. While ICLR welcomes agent and application papers, it expects contributions to *learning* methodology.

VeSX's weakest fit is here because: (1) exemplar learning is heuristic, not advancing meta-learning or transfer learning theory; (2) no training or fine-tuning—just prompting GPT-4o; (3) verification and self-correction are workflow/control mechanisms, not learning innovations; (4) the paper doesn't clarify what is learned vs. engineered. ICLR reviewers would likely question whether this is a learning paper or a clever engineering paper using a fixed LLM.

The missing technical details are particularly damaging for ICLR, where reproducibility of learning procedures is essential. The single-benchmark evaluation and lack of generalization evidence further weaken fit.

**Risk**: Highest risk of the three venues. Likely rejection due to limited learning methodology contribution and unclear learning vs. engineering distinction. **Verdict**: Weak fit; not recommended for ICLR without major revision emphasizing learned components.

### Recommendation

**Submission Strategy:**
1. **Recommended**: ICML (with revisions addressing reproducibility and broader experimental validation)
2. **Fallback**: NeurIPS (if ICML feedback indicates novelty concerns; similar risk profile)
3. **Not Recommended**: ICLR (weak fit; better venues are available)

**Required Revisions for Any Venue:**
- Add reflection/replanning/self-evaluation prompts to appendix
- Specify exemplar retrieval thresholds and iteration bounds in Algorithm 1
- Report exemplar collection statistics for all scenarios
- Evaluate on at least one additional benchmark (Mind2Web) to support generalization claims
- Clarify computational costs and failure mode analysis

strengths: Well-motivated and thoughtful design: The paper identifies genuine pain points in LLM-based web automation (infeasible subtasks, lack of data) and proposes targeted solutions. The subgoal-guided verification idea is intuitive and addresses a real problem by enabling verification at a simpler level than task execution itself.

Strong empirical results: VeSX achieves 34.0% average success rate on WebArena, significantly outperforming prior work without human guidance (Drouin et al.: 23.5%, Koh et al.: 19.2%) and even surpassing the human-feedback-assisted method in two scenarios. The improvements are particularly substantial in Shop (47% relative gain), CMS (51%), and Red (169%).

Comprehensive ablation studies: The paper provides thorough ablations for all three components (subgoal-guided verification, hierarchical self-correction, exemplar bank), demonstrating the necessity of each. The ablations are well-structured and provide actionable insights, e.g., showing that reflection has larger impact than replanning but both are needed.

Practical hierarchical approach to error correction: The reflection-then-replanning strategy is sensible—attempting to fix execution errors locally before regenerating plans—and the ablations show both components significantly contribute to performance.

Exemplar bank design addresses scalability: Using single actions rather than full trajectories as exemplars is an effective approach to handle long web tasks, and the heuristic metadata generation (abstract subtask + action context) is reasonable and shows measurable impact (+13.7% over no abstraction).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual components: Subgoal-guided verification, self-correction, and exemplar-based learning are not novel techniques in isolation. The core contribution is their combination and adaptation to web automation, but the individual mechanisms are relatively straightforward applications of existing ideas (verification has been explored in math reasoning, reflection in agent work, exemplar learning in few-shot prompting).

Unclear and incomplete presentation of key technical details: The paper lacks precise specifications for several critical components. The reflection prompt structure is vague ('the LLM takes the execution trajectory and verification results as inputs'). The replanning mechanism is underspecified—how exactly does error information flow into the replanning prompt? What prevents infinite loops of failed reflection+replanning? The exemplar retrieval process uses 'similarity-matching embeddings' but provides no details on the embedding model setup beyond mentioning 'text-embedding-3-small', and the threshold for retrieval is not specified.

Verification method feasibility not thoroughly analyzed: External verification relies on pre-designed functions (check_url, check_webpage_content, check_action_history), but the paper does not explain how to design or implement these for new domains. While self-verification is more flexible, it may be less reliable and prone to hallucination—the paper shows external verification outperforms self-verification (+7.6% in Table 2) but does not analyze failure modes or provide guidance on when each should be used.

Data collection methodology raises concerns about data quality: The exemplar bank construction uses 'heuristic filtering' and relies on 'LLM self-evaluation' of trajectory correctness. The paper mentions filtering out 'repeating actions or reaching the max actions' but does not quantify how many trajectories were filtered or what fraction of the 60 sampled tasks yielded usable exemplars. This introduces potential confirmation bias and makes reproducibility difficult.

Evaluation scope is limited and comparisons are not entirely fair: Testing only on WebArena limits generalization claims. The comparison to Sodhi et al. (2024) is somewhat unfair—that method uses expert-designed exemplars while VeSX uses automatically collected ones, but both still use exemplars, making the claimed 'entirely reliant on autonomous planning' misleading. Additionally, Sodhi et al. explicitly uses human guidance while VeSX does not, confounding the comparison.

Presentation clarity issues: The paper is dense and difficult to follow in places. Figure 2 is hard to parse. The notation (subscripts, superscripts, function definitions) is introduced informally. Pseudo-code in Algorithm 1 uses notation inconsistently (e.g., 'f_PLANNING' vs 'LLMPLANNING'). The example in Appendix A.1.2 is helpful but very long and takes significant space.

Limited analysis of failure cases and error propagation: The paper does not discuss what happens when verification itself fails or produces false positives/negatives, how cascading errors from early subtasks affect later ones, or how many reflection-replanning cycles occur before timeout. These are crucial for understanding practical limitations.

Lack of analysis of computational cost: The paper does not discuss the number of LLM calls required per task, wall-clock time, or cost compared to baselines. Running reflection, replanning, and verification for each subtask likely increases expense significantly.

The paper meets the bar for acceptance at a top-tier venue as a methodological contribution with strong experimental validation, though it would benefit from revision to address technical clarity and expand evaluation scope.

Practical hierarchical approach to error correction: The reflection-then-replanning strategy is sensible—attempting to fix execution errors locally before regenerating plans—and the ablations show both components significantly contribute to performance.

Exemplar bank design addresses scalability: Using single actions rather than full trajectories as exemplars is an effective approach to handle long web tasks, and the heuristic metadata generation (abstract subtask + action context) is reasonable and shows measurable impact (+13.7% over no abstraction).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty of individual components: Subgoal-guided verification, self-correction, and exemplar-based learning are not novel techniques in isolation. The core contribution is their combination and adaptation to web automation, but the individual mechanisms are relatively straightforward applications of existing ideas (verification has been explored in math reasoning, reflection in agent work, exemplar learning in few-shot prompting).

Critical technical details missing from submitted paper: The submitted paper lacks precise specifications for key mechanisms. Reflection prompts are not shown; replanning logic is vague; exemplar retrieval methods are underspecified; Algorithm 1 lacks iteration bounds; the self-evaluation prompt for exemplar collection is not documented. The author's rebuttal acknowledges these gaps exist and commits to adding them in future revisions, confirming they are not currently in the submitted paper.

Verification method extensibility to new domains unclear: External verification relies on pre-designed functions (check_url, check_webpage_content, check_action_history) that require domain-specific implementation. The paper provides no guidance on designing these functions for new domains, and the rebuttal only commits to adding such guidance in future work.

Exemplar bank construction relies on LLM self-evaluation with unquantified confirmation bias: The paper describes using LLM self-evaluation to judge trajectory success but does not show the evaluation prompt or report filtering statistics for all scenarios. The rebuttal acknowledges this is a reproducibility issue and commits to adding these details in revision, confirming they are absent from the submitted paper.

Evaluation limited to single benchmark without generalization evidence: Testing only on WebArena prevents claims about generalization to other interactive agent domains. The paper makes no attempt to evaluate on other benchmarks like Mind2Web, and the rebuttal provides no new experiments.
