paper_metadata.title: RLEF: Grounding Code LLMs in Execution Feedback with Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as agents solve user-specified tasks over multiple steps while keeping the required manual engagement to a minimum. Crucially, such LLMs need to ground their generations in any feedback obtained to reliably achieve the desired outcomes. We propose an end-to-end reinforcement learning method for teaching models to leverage execution feedback in the realm of code synthesis, where state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to improve code iteratively compared to independent sampling. We benchmark on competitive programming tasks, where we achieve new state-of-the art results with both small (8B parameters) and large (70B) models while reducing the amount of samples required by an order of magnitude. Our analysis of inference-time behavior demonstrates that our method produces LLMs that effectively leverage automatic feedback over multiple steps.

paper_metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning for Generative AI: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep Generative AI has been a long-standing essential topic in the machine learning community, which can impact a number of application areas like text generation and computer vision. The major paradigm to train a generative model is maximum likelihood estimation, which pushes the learner to capture and approximate the target data distribution by decreasing the divergence between the model distribution and the target distribution. This formulation successfully establishes the objective of generative tasks, while it is incapable of satisfying all the requirements that a user might expect from a generative model. Reinforcement learning, serving as a competitive option to inject new training signals by creating new objectives that exploit novel signals, has demonstrated its power and flexibility to incorporate human inductive bias from multiple angles, such as adversarial learning, hand-designed rules and learned reward model to build a performant model. Thereby, reinforcement learning has become a trending research field and has stretched the limits of generative AI in both model design and application. It is reasonable to summarize and conclude advances in recent years with a comprehensive review. Although there are surveys in different application areas recently, this survey aims to shed light on a high-level review that spans a range of application areas. We provide a rigorous taxonomy in this area and make sufficient coverage on various models and applications. Notably, we also surveyed the fast-developing large language model area. We conclude this survey by showing the potential directions that might tackle the limit of current models and expand the frontiers for generative AI.

paper_metadata.title: Making Language Models Better Tool Learners with Execution Feedback
paper_metadata.abstract: Tools serve as pivotal interfaces that enable humans to understand and reshape the environment. With the advent of foundation models, AI systems can utilize tools to expand their capabilities and interact with the real world. Existing tool learning methodologies, encompassing supervised fine-tuning and prompt engineering approaches, often induce large language models to utilize tools indiscriminately, as complex tasks often exceed their own competencies. However, introducing tools for simple tasks, which the models themselves can readily resolve, can inadvertently propagate errors rather than enhance performance. This leads to the research question: can we teach language models when and how to use tools? To meet this need, we propose Tool leaRning wIth exeCution fEedback (TRICE), a two-stage end-to-end framework that enables the model to continually learn through feedback derived from tool execution, thereby learning when and how to use tools effectively. Experimental results, backed by further analysis, show that TRICE can make the large language model selectively use tools by improving the accuracy of tool usage while enhancing insufficient tool learning and mitigating excessive reliance on tools. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/TRICE.

paper_metadata.title: LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners
paper_metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning (ICL), a supervised learning technique that relies on adding annotated examples to the model context. We investigate a contextual bandit version of in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL), where models learn in-context, online, from external reward, instead of supervised data. We show that LLMs effectively demonstrate such learning, and provide a detailed study of the phenomena, experimenting with challenging classification tasks and models of sizes from 500M to 70B parameters. This includes identifying and addressing the instability of the process, demonstrating learning with both semantic and abstract labels, and showing scaling trends. Our findings highlight ICRL capabilities in LLMs, while also underscoring fundamental limitations in their implicit reasoning about errors.

paper_metadata.title: Octopus: Embodied Vision-Language Programmer from Environmental Feedback
paper_metadata.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved substantial progress in multimodal perception and reasoning. When integrated into an embodied agent, existing embodied VLM works either output detailed action sequences at the manipulation level or only provide plans at an abstract level, leaving a gap between high-level planning and real-world manipulation. To bridge this gap, we introduce Octopus, an embodied vision-language programmer that uses executable code generation as a medium to connect planning and manipulation. Octopus is designed to 1) proficiently comprehend an agent's visual and textual task objectives, 2) formulate intricate action sequences, and 3) generate executable code. To facilitate Octopus model development, we introduce OctoVerse: a suite of environments tailored for benchmarking vision-based code generators on a wide spectrum of tasks, ranging from mundane daily chores in simulators to sophisticated interactions in complex video games such as Grand Theft Auto (GTA) and Minecraft. To train Octopus, we leverage GPT-4 to control an explorative agent that generates training data, i.e., action blueprints and corresponding executable code. We also collect feedback that enables an enhanced training scheme called Reinforcement Learning with Environmental Feedback (RLEF). strengths: Novel integration of VAE-style amortized inference with a black-box COP solver through Fenchel-Young loss gradient estimation. The technical combination of latent variable modeling with structured reconstruction (ensuring feasible solutions) is creative and addresses a genuine problem in learning from discrete optimization solutions.

The approach naturally handles multiple agents/cost functions without requiring labels, unlike existing inverse optimization and IRL methods that typically assume a single underlying cost. This is a meaningful distinction from prior work and is well-articulated in the introduction.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (synthetic Waxman graphs, real ship routing data, TSP instances) with both qualitative and quantitative analyses. The latent space visualizations are intuitive and demonstrate meaningful structure (e.g., agent clustering in Fig. 2, ship width correlation in Fig. 3).
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction between stated optimality assumptions and real-world data applicability. The method explicitly assumes observed solutions are COP-optimal (Section 3.3, lines 247-249), yet the real ship trajectory dataset contains actual navigational behavior that is inherently noisy, suboptimal, and influenced by factors beyond cost minimization. The rebuttal acknowledges this ('real ship trajectories are not optimized under any fixed cost function') but the submitted paper contains no such caveat or robustness analysis.

Gradient estimation lacks rigorous theoretical foundation. The claim of unbiasedness (line 217) relies on expectation linearity but provides no approximation error bounds, convergence guarantees, or formal analysis of how perturbation magnitude ε affects gradient quality. Algorithm 1 Step 4 specifies only 'ε ~ N' without parameters, making full algorithm specification incomplete. The rebuttal acknowledges these are 'legitimate technical gaps' but no formal analysis appears in the submitted paper.

Severely weakened baseline comparisons undermine empirical validation. The VAE baseline completely fails to converge ('NC' in Table 2) with attribution to 'graph complexity' rather than systematic investigation. Lahoud et al. (2024)—directly addressing differentiable path inference—is cited but not experimentally compared despite being a natural competitor. The dismissive claim about its scalability is unsupported. The rebuttal acknowledges these problems but none are corrected in the submitted paper.

No direct validation that learned latent representations recover true underlying cost functions. For synthetic Waxman data where ground truth costs are known (Appendix A, lines 568-577), the paper provides only qualitative clustering visualization (Fig. 2) without quantitative cost recovery metrics. The rebuttal identifies this gap but the submitted paper lacks cost reconstruction error, ranking correlation, or visualization of learned versus true costs.

Marginal and statistically insignificant quantitative improvements. Table 2 shows IO-LVM achieves 0.873 ± 0.016 Spearman correlation vs PO's 0.813 ± 0.025 on synthetic data (~7.4% with overlapping error bars). On real ship data, the difference is explicitly acknowledged as 'not statistically significant due to high variance.' These results do not demonstrate compelling empirical advantage.

Underconstrained architecture with ad-hoc hyperparameter selection. Table 1 shows substantial performance gaps across latent dimensions (burma14 validation: 0.892 to 0.976 from 2 to 10 dims, indicating underfitting). Appendix C acknowledges overfitting at 10 dims but states 'Addressing this was beyond the scope.' Only β is systematically ablated; choices for Φ transformation, perturbation strategy, and architecture are not ablated.

soundness.justification: Multiple unresolved technical gaps undermine soundness. (1) The core optimality assumption (Section 3.3) explicitly contradicts real data characteristics (ship trajectories), and the rebuttal's acknowledgment of this does not appear in the submitted paper. No robustness analysis validates performance under violated assumptions. (2) Gradient estimation (line 217, Equation 7) relies on expectation linearity without approximation error bounds, convergence analysis, or complete algorithm specification (ε parameters missing). The rebuttal identifies these as 'legitimate technical gaps' but the paper contains no formal analysis. (3) While individual techniques (VAEs, Fenchel-Young loss from Berthet et al. 2020) are established, their integration in IO-LVM lacks sufficient theoretical rigor for the core gradient estimation step. The submitted paper does not resolve these gaps despite the rebuttal's constructive acknowledgment.

novelty.justification: The technical combination remains novel: integrating VAE-style amortized inference with black-box COP solvers through perturbed Fenchel-Young loss, with ability to handle multiple agents without labels. This distinguishes IO-LVM from prior inverse optimization work (which assumes single or context-conditioned costs). However, novelty is primarily in engineering combination of existing techniques (Berthet et al. 2020's perturbation framework, standard VAE architecture, known inverse optimization concepts). The contribution is incremental rather than foundational. Novelty gates the paper above threshold (score 3) but does not overcome other major deficiencies.

significance.justification: Significance remains severely limited for a top-tier ML venue. (1) Application scope is narrow: only small graphs (≤2513 nodes), linear objectives, discrete path/cycle problems. No evidence of scaling to practical planning systems. (2) Empirical improvements are marginal and often insignificant—7.4% on synthetic data with overlapping error bars, explicitly insignificant on real ship data. (3) Multi-agent capability is conceptually novel but demonstrated only on toy synthetic datasets. (4) No evidence that learned representations actually recover true cost functions (acknowledged in rebuttal; not addressed in paper). (5) Core optimality assumption contradicts real-world applications, limiting practical utility. The rebuttal does not present checkable evidence of greater significance—it acknowledges limitations rather than demonstrating compelling impact.

evaluation.justification: Experimental validation remains insufficient and unfair. (1) VAE baseline completely fails to converge without adequate investigation—attribution to 'graph complexity' is insufficient; systematic hyperparameter tuning is standard practice. (2) Lahoud et al. (2024), directly addressing differentiable path inference on graphs, is cited but not experimentally compared despite being a natural strong competitor. Dismissal based on unsubstantiated scalability claims violates principles of fair comparison. (3) PO baseline is a non-standard adaptation lacking detailed justification. (4) No ground truth validation of cost recovery for synthetic data despite ground truth being available (acknowledged in rebuttal; not addressed in paper). (5) Marginal improvements with high variance on real data. The rebuttal acknowledges these problems but provides no new experimental data or evidence that they have been corrected in the submission.

presentation.justification: Clarity is acceptable. The paper clearly states the problem, presents the algorithm, and includes intuitive visualizations. However, critical details remain incompletely specified: Algorithm 1 Step 4 lacks full perturbation specification; the contradiction between optimality assumptions and real data is not highlighted; major limitations are deferred to appendices. These issues do not prevent understanding core ideas but indicate insufficient transparency about assumptions and limitations in the main paper.

reviewers.summary_comment:
The second rebuttal provides a highly constructive and self-aware response to all major weaknesses. The authors accurately identify each gap, explain why it exists in the submitted paper, and outline concrete revisions needed. Critically, they demonstrate clear understanding that acknowledging problems in a rebuttal does not resolve them in the submitted paper—a key distinction the reviewers emphasized.

However, the evaluation standard requires assessment of the submitted paper as presented, not as the authors promise to revise it. The rebuttal's detailed revision plans (Section 9 Strategy, addressing optimality assumptions, adding theoretical analysis, investigating VAE failures, comparing with Lahoud et al., validating cost recovery, ablating design choices) are compelling evidence of the authors' understanding and capability, but they represent future work, not changes present in the current submission.

The submitted paper remains unchanged from the initial review:

(1) **Soundness (Score 2)**: The optimality assumption contradicts real data, and gradient estimation lacks theoretical grounding. No robustness analysis appears in the paper despite being acknowledged in rebuttal as necessary.

(2) **Evaluation (Score 2)**: VAE baseline fails without investigation, Lahoud et al. 2024 is not compared, and cost recovery is not validated on synthetic data despite ground truth availability.

(3) **Significance (Score 2)**: Narrow application scope, marginal empirical improvements, and unvalidated core claim that learned representations correspond to true cost functions.

(4) **Novelty (Score 3)**: Technical combination is novel but incremental, combining existing techniques (Berthet et al. 2020, VAEs, inverse optimization).

(5) **Clarity (Score 3)**: Acceptable but incomplete specification of critical details (perturbation parameters, optimality assumptions for real data).

The rebuttal substantially strengthens confidence in the authors' ability to produce a strong revised paper. However, for a selective top-tier venue evaluating the work as submitted, the paper does not meet the bar due to unresolved soundness gaps, unfair baseline comparisons, and lack of validation for its core claims. A revised submission addressing the rebuttal's identified gaps could become acceptable, but the current version remains below acceptance threshold.

## Summary & Recommendation

**Core Issue Across All Three Venues:**

The paper presents an interesting technical idea (combining VAE inference with black-box COP solvers via Fenchel-Young loss), but the **submitted work contains multiple unresolved fundamental gaps** that the Reviewer clearly and comprehensively documents. Critically, the author rebuttal acknowledges these gaps and outlines concrete fixes—but acknowledgment in a rebuttal does not constitute resolution in the submitted paper.

### Key Deficiencies:

1. **Soundness (Critical):** 
   - Gradient estimation lacks theoretical rigor (no error bounds, convergence guarantees)
   - Core optimality assumption directly contradicts real-world applications (ship data), yet paper provides no robustness analysis or caveat

2. **Evaluation (Critical):**
   - VAE baseline fails without investigation
   - Most relevant competitor (Lahoud et al. 2024) cited but not compared
   - No validation that learned costs recover true underlying functions despite synthetic ground truth availability

3. **Empirical Results (Significant):**
   - 7.4% improvement with overlapping error bars (synthetic data)
   - Explicitly insignificant differences on real data
   - No compelling empirical advantage demonstrated

### Venue-Specific Fit:

- **ICML (Score 4/10):** Rejects primarily due to theoretical soundness gaps, unfair baseline comparisons, and marginal empirical validation incompatible with ICML's optimization/theory focus.

- **NeurIPS (Score 5/10):** Borderline. The interdisciplinary framing and real-world application partially fit NeurIPS's broader scope, but the same fundamental gaps apply. Could work if positioned differently, but current submission fails on rigor.

- **ICLR (Score 4/10):** Rejects primarily due to lack of quantitative representation learning validation, incomplete baseline comparisons, and unresolved assumption-violation gap. ICLR specifically values rigorous representation quality analysis.

### Recommendation:

**Do not submit in current form to any of these three venues.** The rebuttal demonstrates the authors understand the problems and have a clear roadmap to fix them. Implement the revisions outlined in the rebuttal (cost recovery validation, Lahoud et al. comparison, addressing optimality assumptions, theoretical analysis) and resubmit. The revised paper could be competitive, but the current submission does not meet acceptance standards for selective top-tier venues.

Reconstruction metrics improve significantly with more latent dimensions (Table 1: 10 dims vs 2 dims), suggesting the method is underconstrained.

Unclear evidence for learning meaningful cost representations. While latent space visualizations show clustering, there is no direct evidence that learned costs y_θ actually recover true agent cost functions. The paper assumes but never validates that the learned latent space corresponds to true underlying costs. The ship width example (Fig. 3) shows correlation but not causation—learned dimensions capture patterns correlated with ship width, not necessarily the actual cost function.

The largest graph tested has only 2513 nodes with 8924 edges, which is modest by modern standards. No evidence that the approach scales to real-world planning problems of practical interest.

soundness.justification: Multiple technical gaps undermine soundness. (1) The core assumption that observed solutions are COP-optimal (line 247-249) contradicts the real-world ship data setting and is never validated. (2) Gradient estimation claims (line 217: 'unbiased estimator') lack formal proof or error analysis. (3) Perturbation strategy (distribution and magnitude) is incompletely specified. (4) No convergence guarantees or approximation error bounds for gradient estimation. While the Fenchel-Young loss framework itself is sound, its application here lacks sufficient theoretical grounding for the actual gradient estimation used in practice.

novelty.justification: The technical combination is novel: integrating VAE-style amortized inference with a black-box COP solver through Fenchel-Young loss is creative. The ability to handle multiple agents without labels distinguishes this from prior inverse optimization work (which assumes single or context-conditioned costs). However, novelty is incremental—it primarily combines existing techniques (VAEs, Berthet et al. 2020's perturbed Fenchel-Young loss, standard inverse optimization). The contribution is above the threshold for a workshop but below expectations for a top-tier venue.

significance.justification: Significance is limited for a top-tier ML conference. (1) Application scope is narrow: only small graphs (≤2513 nodes), linear objectives, discrete path/cycle problems. No evidence of practical impact on real planning systems. (2) Quantitative improvements are marginal—IO-LVM marginally outperforms PO on synthetic data but essentially ties on ship data (Section 4.4, acknowledged as insignificant). (3) The multi-agent capability, while novel, is demonstrated only on toy datasets where ground truth costs are synthetic. (4) No demonstration that learned representations are interpretable beyond visualization—no evidence that learned y_θ recovers true cost functions.

evaluation.justification: Experimental validation is insufficient. (1) VAE baseline fails completely (marked 'NC'), rendering comparison meaningless—this is a red flag suggesting baselines are inappropriately tuned or the problem setting favors IO-LVM unfairly. (2) PO baseline is a non-standard adaptation of Berthet et al. (2020) without justification; the cited Lahoud et al. (2024) work directly addresses path inference but is not compared. (3) Quantitative results are weak: Table 2 shows marginal improvements with high variance on ships; Table 1 reconstruction improves dramatically with latent dimensions, suggesting underfitting. (4) No ground truth validation for learned costs on synthetic data despite it being available. (5) Metrics are task-specific (DJS, Spearman, Recall, IoU) with no unified evaluation framework.

presentation.justification: The paper is generally well-written with clear motivation, algorithm description, and visualizations. The latent space plots are intuitive, and the problem formulation is clearly stated. However, there are minor clarity issues: (1) Algorithm 1 incompletely specifies perturbation (distribution and magnitude); (2) the assumption of COP-optimality contradicts real data but is not highlighted as a limitation; (3) ablation studies are deferred to appendices, making the main paper incomplete. Overall, clarity is acceptable for understanding the core ideas, though some technical details require interpretation.

review.summary_comment: IO-LVM presents a technically interesting combination of VAEs with Fenchel-Young loss for learning latent cost representations from observed COP solutions. The idea of handling multiple agents without labels and ensuring feasible reconstruction is valuable. However, the paper falls short of top-tier standards on multiple fronts: (1) **Significance**: Restricted to toy-scale graph problems with no evidence of real-world applicability. (2) **Evaluation**: Weak baselines (VAE fails entirely; PO is a non-standard adaptation; recent competitors like Lahoud et al. 2024 are not compared). Marginal and often insignificant improvements. (3) **Soundness**: Core assumptions (COP-optimality) contradict real data; gradient estimation lacks theoretical grounding (no error bounds, convergence analysis, or formal proofs). (4) **Ablations**: Insufficient analysis of design choices (only β studied in detail); latent dimensionality chosen ad-hoc with acknowledged overfitting. (5) **Validation of core claims**: No direct evidence that learned latent space recovers true cost functions, despite ground truth being available for synthetic data. The paper reads as a solid workshop contribution but lacks the depth, rigor, and impact expected for a top-tier conference. The work would benefit from: scaling to realistic problem sizes, fair comparisons with recent inverse optimization methods, formal analysis of gradient estimation, ground truth cost recovery validation, and more thorough ablations.

strengths: Novel integration of VAE-style amortized inference with a black-box COP solver through Fenchel-Young loss gradient estimation. The technical combination of latent variable modeling with structured reconstruction (ensuring feasible solutions) is creative and addresses a genuine problem in learning from discrete optimization solutions.

The approach naturally handles multiple agents/cost functions without requiring labels, unlike existing inverse optimization and IRL methods that typically assume a single underlying cost. This is a meaningful distinction from prior work and is well-articulated in the introduction.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (synthetic Waxman graphs, real ship routing data, TSP instances) with both qualitative and quantitative analyses. The latent space visualizations are intuitive and demonstrate meaningful structure (e.g., agent clustering in Fig. 2, ship width correlation in Fig. 3).
weaknesses: Fundamental contradiction between stated optimality assumptions and real-world data applicability. The method explicitly assumes observed solutions are COP-optimal (Section 3.3, lines 247-249), yet the real ship trajectory dataset contains actual navigational behavior that is inherently noisy, suboptimal, and influenced by factors beyond cost minimization. This contradiction is acknowledged in the rebuttal but remains unresolved in the paper itself.

Gradient estimation lacks rigorous theoretical foundation and approximation error analysis. The claim of unbiasedness (line 217) relies on expectation linearity but provides no formal error bounds relating perturbation magnitude ε to gradient approximation quality. The perturbation distribution and magnitude are incompletely specified in Algorithm 1 (Step 4 only states ε ~ N without parameters). No convergence guarantees are provided.

Severely weakened baseline comparisons undermine empirical validation. The VAE baseline completely fails to converge ('NC' in Table 2) without adequate investigation of why—attributing failure to 'graph size and complexity' rather than exploring hyperparameter tuning or architectural choices suggests unfair comparison. The PO baseline is a non-standard adaptation lacking detailed justification. Most critically, Lahoud et al. (2024)—which directly addresses differentiable path inference on graphs—is cited but not experimentally compared despite being a natural competitor.

No direct validation that learned latent representations recover true underlying cost functions. For synthetic Waxman data where ground truth costs are known (Appendix A, lines 568-577), the paper provides only qualitative clustering visualization (Fig. 2) without quantitative cost recovery metrics (e.g., cost reconstruction error, ranking correlation with true costs). The ship width example (Fig. 3) demonstrates correlation with observed features but not causation regarding true cost structure.

Marginal and often statistically insignificant quantitative improvements over baselines. Table 2 shows IO-LVM marginally outperforms PO on synthetic data (Spearman: 0.873 ± 0.016 vs 0.813 ± 0.025), but on the real ship dataset 'the difference is not statistically significant due to high variance' (lines 416-417). VAE is not a viable comparison point due to convergence failures.

Underconstrained architecture with ad-hoc hyperparameter selection and insufficient ablation studies. Table 1 shows reconstruction improves substantially from 2 to 10 latent dimensions (burma14 validation: 0.892 to 0.976), indicating underfitting at low dimensionality. Appendix C acknowledges overfitting at 10 dimensions but states 'Addressing this was beyond the scope.' Only β is systematically analyzed; choices for Φ transformation, perturbation strategy, and encoder/decoder architecture are not ablated.

The method explicitly assumes observed solutions are COP-optimal (Section 3.3, lines 247-249), yet the real ship trajectory dataset contains actual navigational behavior that is inherently noisy, suboptimal, and influenced by factors beyond cost minimization. This contradiction is acknowledged in the rebuttal but remains unresolved in the paper itself.

However, Appendix A lines 576-598 describe the ship dataset as actual AIS navigation data with gaps, segmentation heuristics, and no guarantee of optimality. The rebuttal acknowledges 'real ship trajectories are not optimized under any fixed cost function' and suggests this 'constrains practical applicability,' but the submitted paper does not contain this caveat or robustness analysis.

The claim of unbiasedness (line 217) relies on expectation linearity but provides no formal error bounds relating perturbation magnitude ε to gradient approximation quality. The perturbation distribution and magnitude are incompletely specified in Algorithm 1 (Step 4 only states ε ~ N without parameters). No convergence guarantees are provided.

This 8.4% improvement for validation indicates underfitting at 2 dims. Addressing this was beyond the scope of our current study.' Only Table 3 provides ablation (β parameter). The rebuttal acknowledges these gaps exist but notes they were not addressed in the submission.
weakness_details.affected_claim: IO-LVM is carefully designed with principled architectural choices and hyperparameter selection

soundness.justification: Multiple unresolved technical gaps undermine soundness. (1) The core optimality assumption (Section 3.3) contradicts real data characteristics, and the submitted paper does not acknowledge or relax this assumption. (2) Gradient estimation claims lack formal theoretical grounding—the 'unbiased estimator' claim (line 217) relies on expectation linearity but omits approximation error analysis, convergence guarantees, or rigorous specification of perturbation strategy. (3) The rebuttal acknowledges these gaps ('legitimate technical gaps,' 'not adequately addressed') but the submitted paper contains no corrections or analysis. While individual techniques (VAEs, Fenchel-Young loss) are established, their integration here lacks sufficient rigor for the gradient estimation step that is central to the approach.

novelty.justification: The technical combination remains novel: integrating VAE-style amortized inference with black-box COP solvers through perturbed Fenchel-Young loss, with the ability to handle multiple agents without labels. This distinguishes IO-LVM from prior inverse optimization work. However, novelty is primarily in engineering combination of existing techniques (Berthet et al. 2020's perturbation framework, standard VAE architecture, known inverse optimization ideas). The contribution is incremental rather than foundational.

significance.justification: Significance remains severely limited for a top-tier ML venue. (1) Application scope is narrow: only small graphs (≤2513 nodes), linear objectives, discrete path/cycle problems. (2) Empirical improvements are marginal and often insignificant—7.4% Spearman improvement on synthetic data, statistically insignificant on real ship data. (3) The multi-agent capability is novel conceptually but demonstrated only on toy datasets where ground truth costs are synthetic. (4) No evidence that learned representations actually recover true cost functions (acknowledged in rebuttal but not addressed in paper). (5) Core optimality assumption contradicts real-world applications, limiting practical utility. The rebuttal does not present evidence that significance has been underestimated—it acknowledges limitations rather than demonstrating compelling impact.

evaluation.justification: Experimental validation remains insufficient. (1) VAE baseline completely fails to converge without adequate investigation—attribution to 'graph complexity' is insufficient; proper hyperparameter tuning or architecture modifications should have been explored. (2) Lahoud et al. (2024), which directly addresses differentiable path inference, is not experimentally compared despite being a natural and strong competitor. The dismissive comment about scalability is unsupported. (3) PO baseline is a non-standard adaptation lacking detailed justification. (4) No ground truth validation of cost recovery for synthetic data despite availability. (5) Marginal improvements with high variance on real data. The rebuttal acknowledges these problems ('VAE baseline failing to converge is indeed problematic,' 'should either include direct comparison or remove the dismissive claim') but none are addressed in the submitted paper itself.

presentation.justification: Clarity is acceptable. The paper clearly states the problem, presents algorithm and method, and includes intuitive visualizations. However, critical details remain incompletely specified: Algorithm 1 Step 4 lacks full perturbation specification; the contradiction between optimality assumptions and real data is not highlighted; core limitations are deferred to appendices or acknowledged only in rebuttal. These issues do not prevent understanding the core ideas but indicate insufficient transparency about assumptions and limitations.

review.summary_comment:
The rebuttal constructively acknowledges all major weaknesses identified in the review, demonstrating the authors understand the gaps. However, the acknowledgment of problems in the rebuttal does not resolve them in the submitted paper. The core issues remain:

(1) **Unresolved Soundness Gap**: The method assumes COP-optimality but is applied to real data (ship trajectories) that violates this assumption. The rebuttal states this 'constrains practical applicability,' but the paper itself never acknowledges or analyzes this contradiction. Gradient estimation theory is incomplete (no approximation error bounds, convergence analysis, or full algorithm specification).

(2) **Unresolved Evaluation Gap**: The VAE baseline fails entirely; Lahoud et al. (2024) is not compared despite being a direct competitor. Rebuttal agrees these are 'fair criticisms' but they remain unchanged in the paper. No cost recovery validation exists for synthetic data despite known ground truth.

(3) **Marginal Empirical Gains**: Improvements over PO are 7.4% on synthetic data and statistically insignificant on real data. Combined with weak baselines, this fails to demonstrate meaningful empirical advantage.

(4) **Incomplete Ablations**: Architecture is underconstrained (2 dims underfit, 10 dims overfit); only β is analyzed. Other design choices (Φ, perturbation, architecture) lack ablation studies.

The paper presents a technically interesting idea combining VAEs with COP solvers, but falls short of top-tier standards due to theoretical gaps, incomplete evaluation, and limited demonstrated impact. The rebuttal's self-aware acknowledgment of limitations is appreciated but does not cure the deficits in the submission itself. For acceptance at a selective venue, the paper would require substantial revision addressing these gaps with evidence (not promises)—new experiments validating cost recovery, comparisons with recent methods, theoretical analysis of gradient estimation, and honest treatment of the optimality-assumption contradiction.

weakness_details.evidence: Table 1 burma14 with 3 unobserved features: 2 dims validation Recall 0.892, 10 dims validation Recall 0.976 (8.4% improvement indicates underfitting at 2 dims). Appendix C lines 606-614: 'With 10 latent dimensions, a slight overfitting emerges, which could be mitigated through more careful regularization and neural network architecture design. Addressing this was beyond the scope of our current study.' Only Table 3 provides systematic ablation (β parameter). No ablations documented for: Φ transformation (line 209), perturbation distribution/magnitude, encoder/decoder capacity (lines 628-630 only specify architecture, no ablation).
weakness_details.affected_claim: IO-LVM is carefully designed with principled architectural choices and hyperparameter selection.

soundness.justification: Multiple unresolved technical gaps undermine soundness. (1) The core optimality assumption (Section 3.3) explicitly contradicts real data characteristics (ship trajectories), and the rebuttal's acknowledgment of this does not appear in the submitted paper. No robustness analysis validates performance under violated assumptions. (2) Gradient estimation (line 217, Equation 7) relies on expectation linearity without approximation error bounds, convergence analysis, or complete algorithm specification (ε parameters missing). The rebuttal identifies these as 'legitimate technical gaps' but the paper contains no formal analysis. (3) While individual techniques (VAEs, Fenchel-Young loss from Berthet et al. 2020) are established, their integration in IO-LVM lacks sufficient theoretical rigor for the core gradient estimation step. The submitted paper does not resolve these gaps despite the rebuttal's constructive acknowledgment.

novelty.justification: The technical combination remains novel: integrating VAE-style amortized inference with black-box COP solvers through perturbed Fenchel-Young loss, with ability to handle multiple agents without labels. This distinguishes IO-LVM from prior inverse optimization work (which assumes single or context-conditioned costs). However, novelty is primarily in engineering combination of existing techniques (Berthet et al. 2020's perturbation framework, standard VAE architecture, known inverse optimization concepts). The contribution is incremental rather than foundational. Novelty gates the paper above threshold (score 3) but does not overcome other major deficiencies.

significance.justification: Significance remains severely limited for a top-tier ML venue. (1) Application scope is narrow: only small graphs (≤2513 nodes), linear objectives, discrete path/cycle problems. No evidence of scaling to practical planning systems. (2) Empirical improvements are marginal and often insignificant—7.4% on synthetic data with overlapping error bars, explicitly insignificant on real ship data. (3) Multi-agent capability is conceptually novel but demonstrated only on toy synthetic datasets. (4) No evidence that learned representations actually recover true cost functions (acknowledged in rebuttal; not addressed in paper). (5) Core optimality assumption contradicts real-world applications, limiting practical utility. The rebuttal does not present checkable evidence of greater significance—it acknowledges limitations rather than demonstrating compelling impact.

evaluation.justification: Experimental validation remains insufficient and unfair. (1) VAE baseline completely fails to converge without adequate investigation—attribution to 'graph complexity' is insufficient; systematic hyperparameter tuning is standard practice. (2) Lahoud et al. (2024), directly addressing differentiable path inference on graphs, is cited but not experimentally compared despite being a natural strong competitor. Dismissal based on unsubstantiated scalability claims violates principles of fair comparison. (3) PO baseline is a non-standard adaptation lacking detailed justification. (4) No ground truth validation of cost recovery for synthetic data despite ground truth being available (acknowledged in rebuttal; not addressed in paper). (5) Marginal improvements with high variance on real data. The rebuttal acknowledges these problems but provides no new experimental data or evidence that they have been corrected in the submission.

presentation.justification: Clarity is acceptable. The paper clearly states the problem, presents the algorithm, and includes intuitive visualizations. However, critical details remain incompletely specified: Algorithm 1 Step 4 lacks full perturbation specification; the contradiction between optimality assumptions and real data is not highlighted; major limitations are deferred to appendices. These issues do not prevent understanding core ideas but indicate insufficient transparency about assumptions and limitations in the main paper.

review.summary_comment:
The second rebuttal provides a highly constructive and self-aware response to all major weaknesses. The authors accurately identify each gap, explain why it exists in the submitted paper, and outline concrete revisions needed. Critically, they demonstrate clear understanding that acknowledging problems in a rebuttal does not resolve them in the submitted paper—a key distinction the reviewers emphasized.

However, the evaluation standard requires assessment of the submitted paper as presented, not as the authors promise to revise it. The rebuttal's detailed revision plans (Section 9 Strategy, addressing optimality assumptions, adding theoretical analysis, investigating VAE failures, comparing with Lahoud et al., validating cost recovery, ablating design choices) are compelling evidence of the authors' understanding and capability, but they represent future work, not changes present in the current submission.

The submitted paper remains unchanged from the initial review:

(1) **Soundness (Score 2)**: The optimality assumption contradicts real data, and gradient estimation lacks theoretical grounding. No robustness analysis appears in the paper despite being acknowledged in rebuttal as necessary.

(2) **Evaluation (Score 2)**: VAE baseline fails without investigation, Lahoud et al. 2024 is not compared, and cost recovery is not validated on synthetic data despite ground truth availability.

(3) **Significance (Score 2)**: Narrow application scope, marginal empirical improvements, and unvalidated core claim that learned representations correspond to true cost functions.

(4) **Novelty (Score 3)**: Technical combination is novel but incremental, combining existing techniques (Berthet et al. 2020, VAEs, inverse optimization).

(5) **Clarity (Score 3)**: Acceptable but incomplete specification of critical details (perturbation parameters, optimality assumptions for real data).

The rebuttal substantially strengthens confidence in the authors' ability to produce a strong revised paper. However, for a selective top-tier venue evaluating the work as submitted, the paper does not meet the bar due to unresolved soundness gaps, unfair baseline comparisons, and lack of validation for its core claims. A revised submission addressing the rebuttal's identified gaps could become acceptable, but the current version remains below acceptance threshold.

paper_metadata.title: Distorted correlations among censored data: causes, effects, and correction
paper_metadata.abstract: Data censoring occurs when researchers do not know precise values of data points (e.g., age is 55+ or concentration ≤ .001). Censoring is frequent within psychology but typically unrecognized outside of longitudinal studies. We describe five circumstances when censoring may occur, demonstrate censoring distorts correlations, and discuss how censoring can create spurious factors. Next, we explain how to use R package lava to calculate maximum likelihood estimates (Holst and Budtz-Jørgensen Computational Statistics, 28(4), 1385-1452, 2013) of correlations between uncensored variables based upon censored variables. Previous research demonstrated these estimates were more accurate than Muthén's (1984) estimate for one particular model, but no research has systematically examined their accuracy. We therefore conducted a simulation study exploring the effects of the correlation, sample size, and censoring on point and interval estimates of correlations. Based upon 80 cells in which low values of normally distributed variables were censored, we recommend the constrained regression model with Wald confidence intervals. These methods were precise and unbiased unless both variables had 70% censoring and the correlation was large and negative (e.g., -.9), in which case estimates were closer to -1 than they should be. Opposite results would occur if low values of one variable and high values of the other were censored: Estimates would be precise and unbiased unless censoring was extreme and correlations were large and positive. To estimate large correlations accurately, we recommend researchers reduce censoring by using longer longitudinal studies, using scales with more response options, and matching measures to populations to reduce floor and ceiling effects.

paper_metadata.title: Modular system programming in MINIX 3
paper_metadata.abstract: By "next-generation," I mean that MINIX is a microkernel in design and philosophy.Only the kernel runs as privileged, and all other services, including process management, file systems, networking, and all device drivers, run in their own private address spaces.Just moving device drivers out of the kernel and into their own address spaces means that they can crash without crashing the kernel.It also means that system code, including device drivers, can be tested without rebooting, and failed drivers (or servers) can be restarted.While MINIX 3 is not going to replace your desktop today, it is already a good candidate for embedded systems where robustness, reliability, and a small memory footprint are crucial.Perhaps your cell phone will be running MINIX 3 some day.

paper_metadata.title: ClusterRAID: Architecture and Prototype of a Distributed Fault-Tolerant Mass Storage System for Clusters
paper_metadata.abstract: During the past few years clusters built from commodity off-the-shelf (COTS) components have emerged as the predominant supercomputer architecture. Typically comprising a collection of standard PCs or workstations and an interconnection network, they have replaced the traditionally used integrated systems due to their better price/performance ratio. As paradigms shift from mere computing intensive to I/O intensive applications, mass storage solutions for cluster installations become a more and more crucial aspect of these systems. The inherent unreliability of the underlying components is one of the reasons why no system has been established as a standard storage solution for clusters yet. This thesis sets out the architecture and prototype implementation of a novel distributed mass storage system for commodity off-the-shelf clusters and addresses the issue of the unreliable constituent components. The key concept of the presented system is the conversion of the local hard disk drive of a cluster node into a reliable device while preserving the block device interface. By the deployment of sophisticated erasure-correcting codes, the system allows the adjustment of the number of tolerable failures and thus the overall reliability. In addition, the applied data layout considers the access behaviour of a broad range of applications and minimizes the number of required network transactions. Extensive measurements and functionality tests of the prototype, both stand-alone and in conjunction with local or distributed file systems, show the validity of the concept.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: learning across multiple families of dynamical systems with varying degrees of relatedness. The hierarchical DSR setting is well-motivated and addresses practical scenarios where manual dataset partitioning is undesirable.

The proposed MixER approach introduces a concrete alternative to gradient-based gating in MoE layers, combining K-means clustering with least-squares optimization. The core insight that context-based routing with explicit clustering can outperform vanilla gradient-based MoE routing is technically sound and clearly demonstrated in Figure 2.

The paper provides extensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains: synthetic ODE families (ODEBench), classical DSR benchmarks (LV, GO, SM), and real-world time series (SCCTS, Epilepsy2), with comparisons to several state-of-the-art meta-learning baselines (NCF, CoDA, GEPS).

The authors are transparent about limitations, explicitly acknowledging in the abstract and Section 6 that MixER underperforms task-specific meta-learners in high-data regimes on closely related data. The rebuttal further demonstrates intellectual honesty by admitting core methodological gaps without defensive argumentation.
weaknesses: The fundamental performance-relatedness tradeoff is not resolved and severely limits practical applicability. MixER only shows clear benefits on loosely related data with limited families (ODEBench-2, two families), but underperforms on closely related datasets where foundational models are most needed. This is a core contribution vs. limitation issue, not a minor scope constraint.

Experimental results contradict scalability claims. ODEBench-10B (Table 3) shows MixER-10 training performance worse than single-expert MixER-1 (0.22±0.60 vs 0.12±0.01 NCF). This directly contradicts claims of scaling to ten parametric ODEs and suggests fundamental challenges in the approach's design.

Critical ablation studies are absent. The paper describes context splitting, context shifting, and noise injection as crucial but provides no quantitative ablations isolating their individual contributions. Algorithm 1 uses L1 norm in K-means without justification or comparison to alternatives. The rebuttal confirms these design choices appear ad-hoc rather than principled.

Baseline comparisons may be biased by custom MixER-specific reimplementations. The paper removes softmax aggregation and modifies baselines for integration, but provides no evidence that standalone baseline implementations match original performance levels. CAVIA is excluded entirely due to implementation constraints, creating incomplete evaluation.

The optimization procedure lacks theoretical grounding. While referencing Li et al. (2019) for general convergence guarantees, no problem-specific analysis exists. The choice of alternating minimization (vs. joint optimization) is justified as pragmatic rather than principled. The rebuttal acknowledges this gap but confirms it remains unaddressed in the submitted work.

weakness_details.weakness: The fundamental performance-relatedness tradeoff is not resolved and severely limits practical applicability. MixER only shows clear benefits on loosely related data with limited families, but underperforms on closely related datasets where foundational models are most needed.
weakness_details.evidence: Abstract: 'However, our layer underperforms state-of-the-art meta-learners in high-data regimes.' Table 4 (LV, GO, SM) consistently shows MixER underperformance across all classical DSR benchmarks. Figure 7 (Epilepsy2) shows degraded clustering. The rebuttal acknowledges: 'This fundamentally limits significance... the practical impact is limited to scenarios where systems are loosely related... These scenarios exist in scientific computing, but they are neither the majority use case nor the most impactful for foundational models.' This admission confirms the approach lacks broad applicability.
weakness_details.affected_claim: MixER enables foundational models for DSR that learn across system hierarchies.

weakness_details.weakness: Experimental results contradict scalability claims. ODEBench-10B shows MixER-10 training performance worse than single-expert baseline, directly undermining claims of scaling to ten parametric ODEs.
weakness_details.evidence: Table 3, ODEBench-10B: NCF MIXER-1 training is 0.12±0.01 but MIXER-10 is 0.22±0.60. This is a clear performance degradation with increased expert count. The paper claims in abstract: 'demonstrating efficient training and scalability to systems of up to ten parametric ordinary differential equations.' The rebuttal explains: 'As families increase from 2 to 10, MixER performance degrades' and hypothesizes causes (clustering ambiguity, insufficient data per expert, inadequate context representation) but these failure modes are not investigated in the submitted work.
weakness_details.affected_claim: MixER demonstrates efficient training and scalability to systems of up to ten parametric ordinary differential equations.

weakness_details.weakness: Critical ablation studies are absent for design choices described as crucial. Context splitting, context shifting, and noise injection lack quantitative evaluation.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix C.1 states context splitting and shifting are 'crucial optimizations' but provides no ablations. Algorithm 1 line 7 uses L1 norm without justification or comparison to L2/L-infinity. Line 23 adds noise (σ = 10^-4) without ablation. The rebuttal confirms: 'context splitting (dividing context into m equal pieces) and context shifting (adding per-expert offsets) emerged during development as practical tricks... We should have either ablated them systematically before submission, or framed them as heuristics... We chose neither, which weakens the paper.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The proposed unsupervised routing mechanism effectively learns dynamical systems.

weakness_details.weakness: Baseline comparisons potentially biased by custom MixER-specific reimplementations without evidence of equivalence to original implementations.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix C.2: 'We perform a custom reimplementation of the baselines and incorporate them within our MixER layer.' Section 3.1 notes removal of softmax aggregation to allow independent expert operation. The paper provides: (1) no standalone baseline performance using identical architectures to isolate MixER layer effects, (2) no comparison to original paper results, (3) no mitigation for CAVIA exclusion. The rebuttal acknowledges: 'Without these, we cannot definitively claim baseline underperformance is due to the MixER framework rather than implementation differences. This is a methodological weakness we should have addressed.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: Extensive experiments validate MixER's capabilities, demonstrating efficient training and scalability compared to state-of-the-art meta-learners.

weakness_details.weakness: Optimization procedure lacks theoretical justification specific to this problem. Alternating minimization of Θ and Ξ is not proven superior to joint optimization.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 3.1 references Li et al. (2019) for general convergence guarantees but provides no problem-specific analysis for loss function (Eq. 7). No proof that alternating minimization is preferable to joint optimization. The rebuttal confirms: 'The submitted paper does not prove that alternating minimization of Θ and Ξ separately is preferable to joint optimization, nor does it analyze convergence rates for our specific loss function. We chose this optimization procedure because it decouples parameter updates... However, this is insufficient justification.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: We implement proximal alternating minimization, chosen for its proven convergence to second-order optimal solutions.

soundness.justification: While K-means and least-squares are individually sound, the paper exhibits fundamental soundness gaps: (1) No problem-specific justification for alternating minimization of Θ and Ξ vs. joint optimization; Li et al. (2019) provides only general convergence theory. (2) Algorithm 1 uses L1 norm without justification or empirical validation against L2. (3) No analysis of why context-based routing should outperform state-based routing beyond the single ODEBench-2 example. (4) Context splitting, shifting, and noise injection (critical components per Appendix C.1) are not ablated, leaving their necessity unclear. (5) Baseline implementations are modified for MixER integration without evidence this doesn't degrade their quality. The rebuttal confirms these gaps exist in the submitted work and frames them as limitations rather than providing evidence of soundness.

novelty.justification: Technical novelty remains limited. K-means clustering and least-squares optimization are classical techniques. Context-based routing instead of state-based routing is a straightforward adaptation. The paper explicitly draws from 'switch routing' (Fedus et al., 2022) with domain-specific rather than methodological innovation. The rebuttal frames this as 'adapting language modeling ideas to scientific computing' and acknowledges: 'primarily in application and problem formulation rather than algorithmic innovation.' This level of incremental novelty does not meet top-tier conference standards, especially combined with weak empirical results.

significance.justification: Practical significance is severely limited. MixER trades performance on closely related data (practical majority case) for potential benefits on loosely related data at small scale. The rebuttal explicitly states: 'the practical impact is limited to scenarios where systems are loosely related... These scenarios exist in scientific computing, but they are neither the majority use case nor the most impactful for foundational models.' ODEBench-2 (two families) shows benefits, but ODEBench-10B (ten families) shows degradation. Classical DSR benchmarks consistently underperform. The approach cannot serve as a foundational model if it fails on the practical, high-impact cases. Without resolving the performance-relatedness tradeoff, significance cannot be established.

evaluation.justification: Multiple critical evaluation gaps remain unresolved in the submitted work: (1) Baseline implementations are custom within MixER framework; standalone performance is not reported, preventing isolation of MixER layer effects. The rebuttal confirms: 'we did not provide standalone baseline performance.' (2) No ablation studies for context splitting, shifting, noise injection, or norm choices; the rebuttal confirms: 'we chose neither [to ablate them systematically or frame them as heuristics].' (3) No quantitative clustering metrics for SCCTS and Epilepsy2 beyond qualitative figures. (4) Hyperparameter choices unjustified. (5) ODEBench-10B failure modes (clustering ambiguity, insufficient data per expert) identified in rebuttal but not investigated in submitted work. (6) CAVIA excluded due to implementation constraints. These are substantive methodological weaknesses in the submitted paper.

presentation.justification: The paper is well-written with clear structure, motivated problem setting, and informative figures. Figure 1 effectively illustrates hierarchical learning. Figure 4 clearly shows gating update stages. Algorithms 1-2 are clearly presented. Section 6 transparently discusses limitations. The rebuttal demonstrates further clarity about the work's scope and limitations. While presentation quality is good, it does not overcome failures in other gates.

reviewers.summary_comment: The rebuttal demonstrates intellectual honesty but fails to resolve the core deficiencies in the submitted work. The authors acknowledge that MixER is fundamentally limited to loosely related, low-data scenarios—precisely where foundational models are least impactful. Performance degrades when scaling from two to ten families (ODEBench-10B shows worse performance for 10-expert than 1-expert configurations). Critical design choices are admitted to be ad-hoc ('practical tricks') rather than principled. Baseline comparisons are potentially biased due to custom implementations, yet no standalone baseline performance is provided. The optimization procedure's justification is pragmatic rather than principled. The rebuttal accurately characterizes these as gaps requiring "substantial additional work" to address—confirming they are not present in the submitted paper. For a top-tier ML conference, foundational model work must demonstrate strong performance across diverse regimes and scale convincingly. This submission fails both criteria. The honest rebuttal helps clarify the actual contribution (a clustering-based routing mechanism for small-scale loosely-related DSR), but this is insufficient for acceptance. The work would require: (1) demonstrating clear benefits on realistic loosely-related benchmarks at scale, (2) resolving the performance-relatedness tradeoff through algorithmic modifications, (3) providing fair baseline comparisons and comprehensive ablations, or (4) establishing theoretical foundations for the approach. None of these are present in the submitted work.

## **Summary Commentary**

This paper introduces **MixER** (Mixture of Expert Reconstructors), a novel routing mechanism for learning hierarchies of dynamical systems. While the problem is well-motivated and the paper is clearly written, it suffers from **critical methodological weaknesses and an unresolved fundamental tradeoff** that severely limits its contribution.

### **Key Issues Across All Venues:**

1. **Unresolved Performance-Relatedness Tradeoff** (Major): MixER shows benefits only on loosely related data with few families (ODEBench-2: 2 families) but **consistently underperforms on closely related datasets** where foundational models are truly needed. The abstract acknowledges this: "our layer underperforms state-of-the-art meta-learners in high-data regimes." The rebuttal confirms these are non-majority, low-impact scenarios. This is a **showstopper for claims of enabling foundational models**.

2. **Contradicted Scalability Claims** (Major): The abstract claims "scalability to systems of up to ten parametric ordinary differential equations," but Table 3 (ODEBench-10B) shows MixER-10 training performs **worse than MixER-1**. This directly contradicts the core claim and suggests fundamental design limitations not addressed in the work.

3. **Methodological Gaps** (Major):
   - Custom baseline implementations within MixER framework without standalone performance comparisons
   - No ablation studies for "crucial" design choices (context splitting, shifting, noise injection)
   - Key algorithmic choices (L1 norm in K-means) unjustified
   - Alternating minimization chosen pragmatically, not theoretically justified

4. **Limited Novelty** (Major): Reviewer rates novelty 3/10. The approach combines classical techniques (K-means, least-squares) with straightforward context-based routing adapted from language models. The contribution is primarily in application, not methodology.

5. **Significance Constraints** (Major): The rebuttal confirms practical applicability is limited to non-standard scenarios that are "neither the majority use case nor the most impactful for foundational models." This undermines the entire premise.

### **Venue-Specific Assessments:**

- **ICML (4/10)**: Poor fit. While DSR and meta-learning are ICML topics, the methodological contribution is weak, empirical results contradict claims, and practical significance is limited to edge cases. ICML expects stronger technical innovation and broader applicability for work claiming to advance foundational models.

- **NeurIPS (5/10)**: Borderline. NeurIPS's breadth on applications and interdisciplinary work provides slightly better fit than ICML. However, the same core weaknesses apply: unresolved tradeoffs, methodological gaps, and limited significance. The paper's transparency about limitations is a modest positive, but insufficient to overcome substantive issues. Application-focused work can succeed at NeurIPS, but results must be compelling or technical contribution must be novel—this achieves neither convincingly.

- **ICLR (5/10)**: Borderline. ICLR's focus on representation learning and generalization makes it a natural venue, but the paper fails to convincingly advance either. The method works poorly on the closely-related, high-data scenarios where good representations are most valuable. The missing ablations and compromised baseline comparisons are particularly problematic for a representation learning venue. The work would need significantly stronger empirical results or theoretical contributions.

### **Bottom Line:**

All three venues would likely reject this paper. The fundamental tradeoff (good on loosely-related data only) is not resolved; empirical results contradict core claims; critical ablations are missing; and practical significance is severely limited. The honest rebuttal confirms these gaps require "substantial additional work"—confirming they are absent from the submitted work. The paper would benefit from either: (1) resolving the performance tradeoff algorithmically, (2) focusing narrowly on loosely-related scenarios with compelling results, or (3) providing strong theoretical foundations for the approach. As submitted, none of these are present.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful problem: learning across multiple families of dynamical systems with varying degrees of relatedness. The hierarchical DSR setting is well-motivated and addresses practical scenarios where manual dataset partitioning is undesirable.

The proposed MixER approach introduces a concrete alternative to gradient-based gating in MoE layers, combining K-means clustering with least-squares optimization. The core insight that context-based routing with explicit clustering can outperform vanilla gradient-based MoE routing is technically sound and clearly demonstrated in Figure 2.

The paper provides extensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains: synthetic ODE families (ODEBench), classical DSR benchmarks (LV, GO, SM), and real-world time series (SCCTS, Epilepsy2), with comparisons to several state-of-the-art meta-learning baselines (NCF, CoDA, GEPS).
weaknesses: MixER consistently underperforms task-specific meta-learners on closely related datasets despite being designed for hierarchical learning. The paper explicitly acknowledges this in Sections 4.2 and 4.3, undermining the practical value of the approach for a major use case.

The experimental results are mixed and often contradict the claimed benefits. On ODEBench-10A (Table 2), adaptation performance degrades significantly for NCF and CoDA with MixER. On classical DSR datasets (Table 4), all three MixER variants underperform baselines across most metrics. The gains on loosely related data do not compensate for these systematic failures.

The paper lacks rigorous theoretical or empirical justification for core design choices. Why is K-means with L1 norm the appropriate clustering method? Why is the least-squares formulation optimal? No ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual components (context splitting, context shifting, noise injection).

The motivating example (Section 2.2) is compelling but limited in scope. It demonstrates that a single meta-learner fails on two unrelated ODEs, but the follow-up experiments don't convincingly show MixER solving this at scale. ODEBench-10B results (Table 3) show MixER-10 actually performs worse than the naive MoE baseline in many cases.

Comparison to baselines is not entirely fair. The paper reimplements baselines within the MixER framework rather than comparing against their original implementations. This means baseline performance may be degraded by forced integration into the MoE layer. CAVIA is notably excluded from MixER experiments due to its second-order optimization.

Limited novelty in the core technical contribution. Using K-means clustering for routing and least squares for gating is a straightforward application of classical techniques. The innovation over prior MoE work in NLP is incremental—the paper adopts 'switch routing' concepts from existing literature with minor adaptations for context vectors.

soundness.justification: While the core K-means and least-squares mechanisms are mathematically sound, the paper exhibits fundamental soundness issues: (1) The loss function (Eq. 7) is standard MSE with no theoretical justification for why alternating minimization on Θ and Ξ separately (rather than jointly) is appropriate for this setting. (2) The proximal alternating minimization claim lacks convergence guarantees specific to this problem. (3) The paper provides no analysis of when/why the clustering-based routing should outperform gradient-based routing beyond the motivating example. (4) The contextual routing assumption (using ξ instead of x_t for gating) lacks theoretical motivation.

The paper explicitly draws from 'switch routing' (Fedus et al., 2022) from language modeling literature, with the primary adaptation being domain-specific (DSR) rather than methodologically novel. The broader applicability to truly foundational scientific modeling remains undemonstrated.

evaluation.justification: Multiple evaluation concerns: (1) Baseline implementations are custom within the MixER framework rather than original implementations, potentially biasing results. (2) CAVIA is excluded from MixER experiments due to implementation constraints, preventing full baseline comparison. (3) No ablation studies quantify contributions of context splitting, context shifting, and noise injection. (4) Missing statistical significance testing—only error bars are provided. (5) Hyperparameter selection is not justified (e.g., why 3 experts for classical DSR, 10-20 for ODEBench?). (6) The relative L2 metric (Eq. 9) is used for model selection but only standard MSE is reported in most tables, making evaluation inconsistent. (7) On SCCTS and Epilepsy2, interpretability is evaluated qualitatively (Figures 6-7) without quantitative clustering metrics.

For a top-tier ML conference, this work needs substantial improvements: (1) fair baseline comparisons using original implementations, (2) comprehensive ablations, (3) theoretical analysis of the clustering-based routing, or (4) a fundamentally stronger empirical case showing MixER benefits on practically important regimes where it currently underperforms.

weakness_details.evidence: Section 3.1 references Li et al. (2019) for general convergence guarantees but provides no problem-specific analysis for loss function (Eq. 7). No proof that alternating minimization is preferable to joint optimization. The rebuttal confirms: 'The submitted paper does not prove that alternating minimization of Θ and Ξ separately is preferable to joint optimization, nor does it analyze convergence rates for our specific loss function. We chose this optimization procedure because it decouples parameter updates... However, this is insufficient justification.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: We implement proximal alternating minimization, chosen for its proven convergence to second-order optimal solutions.

soundness.justification: While K-means and least-squares are individually sound, the paper exhibits fundamental soundness gaps: (1) No problem-specific justification for alternating minimization of Θ and Ξ vs. joint optimization; Li et al. (2019) provides only general convergence theory. (2) Algorithm 1 uses L1 norm without justification or empirical validation against L2. (3) No analysis of why context-based routing should outperform state-based routing beyond the single ODEBench-2 example. (4) Context splitting, shifting, and noise injection (critical components per Appendix C.1) are not ablated, leaving their necessity unclear. (5) Baseline implementations are modified for MixER integration without evidence this doesn't degrade their quality. The rebuttal confirms these gaps exist in the submitted work and frames them as limitations rather than providing evidence of soundness.

novelty.justification: Technical novelty remains limited. K-means clustering and least-squares optimization are classical techniques. Context-based routing instead of state-based routing is a straightforward adaptation. The paper explicitly draws from 'switch routing' (Fedus et al., 2022) with domain-specific rather than methodological innovation. The rebuttal frames this as 'adapting language modeling ideas to scientific computing' and acknowledges: 'primarily in application and problem formulation rather than algorithmic innovation.' This level of incremental novelty does not meet top-tier conference standards, especially combined with weak empirical results.

significance.justification: Practical significance is severely limited. MixER trades performance on closely related data (practical majority case) for potential benefits on loosely related data at small scale. The rebuttal explicitly states: 'the practical impact is limited to scenarios where systems are loosely related... These scenarios exist in scientific computing, but they are neither the majority use case nor the most impactful for foundational models.' ODEBench-2 (two families) shows benefits, but ODEBench-10B (ten families) shows degradation. Classical DSR benchmarks consistently underperform. The approach cannot serve as a foundational model if it fails on the practical, high-impact cases. Without resolving the performance-relatedness tradeoff, significance cannot be established.

evaluation.justification: Multiple critical evaluation gaps remain unresolved in the submitted work: (1) Baseline implementations are custom within MixER framework; standalone performance is not reported, preventing isolation of MixER layer effects. The rebuttal confirms: 'we did not provide standalone baseline performance.' (2) No ablation studies for context splitting, shifting, noise injection, or norm choices; the rebuttal confirms: 'we chose neither [to ablate them systematically or frame them as heuristics].' (3) No quantitative clustering metrics for SCCTS and Epilepsy2 beyond qualitative figures. (4) Hyperparameter choices unjustified. (5) ODEBench-10B failure modes (clustering ambiguity, insufficient data per expert) identified in rebuttal but not investigated in submitted work. (6) CAVIA excluded due to implementation constraints. These are substantive methodological weaknesses in the submitted paper.

presentation.justification: The paper is well-written with clear structure, motivated problem setting, and informative figures. Figure 1 effectively illustrates hierarchical learning. Figure 4 clearly shows gating update stages. Algorithms 1-2 are clearly presented. Section 6 transparently discusses limitations. The rebuttal demonstrates further clarity about the work's scope and limitations. While presentation quality is good, it does not overcome failures in other gates.

review.summary_comment: The rebuttal demonstrates intellectual honesty but fails to resolve the core deficiencies in the submitted work. The authors acknowledge that MixER is fundamentally limited to loosely related, low-data scenarios—precisely where foundational models are least impactful. Performance degrades when scaling from two to ten families (ODEBench-10B shows worse performance for 10-expert than 1-expert configurations). Critical design choices are admitted to be ad-hoc ('practical tricks') rather than principled. Baseline comparisons are potentially biased due to custom implementations, yet no standalone baseline performance is provided. The optimization procedure's justification is pragmatic rather than principled. The rebuttal accurately characterizes these as gaps requiring "substantial additional work" to address—confirming they are not present in the submitted paper. For a top-tier ML conference, foundational model work must demonstrate strong performance across diverse regimes and scale convincingly. This submission fails both criteria. The honest rebuttal helps clarify the actual contribution (a clustering-based routing mechanism for small-scale loosely-related DSR), but this is insufficient for acceptance. The work would require: (1) demonstrating clear benefits on realistic loosely-related benchmarks at scale, (2) resolving the performance-relatedness tradeoff through algorithmic modifications, (3) providing fair baseline comparisons and comprehensive ablations, or (4) establishing theoretical foundations for the approach. None of these are present in the submitted work.
