review.summary_comment:
This paper makes a solid theoretical contribution by proving the first polynomial-time learnability result for multi-head linear attention networks with agnostic PAC guarantees. The technical innovation—reformulating MHLA optimization as convex regression over a lifted d^2-dimensional feature space and recovering equivalent parameters via SVD—is non-trivial and clever. The certifiable identifiability framework providing a data-dependent condition for out-of-distribution generalization is novel and useful.

The rebuttal provides helpful clarifications: (1) Algorithm 1 finds global training minima without i.i.d.; (2) the i.i.d. requirement for generalization is standard in PAC theory; (3) Lemma A.6 removes realizability when H ≥ d²; (4) autoregressive sequences are handled via union bounds (Lemma C.5, Appendix F.2). Critically, the rebuttal is honest about remaining limitations: (a) the gap between Algorithm 1 (exact OLS) and SGD practice remains unexplained theoretically, though Figure 2b provides empirical evidence; (b) this is framed as an important open question about SGD's implicit bias; (c) the authors transparently state they lack rigorous theoretical justification.

Limitations that remain unresolved in the submitted paper: (1) single-layer linear attention without softmax is simplified; (2) the theory-SGD gap is acknowledged but unresolved; (3) experiments are synthetic with d ≤ 4; (4) d^4 sample complexity is prohibitive. However, these do not prevent acceptance. The paper delivers on its core claim: the first polynomial-time algorithm for learning MHLA with provable guarantees. The limitations are understood by the authors and appropriately framed. This is a theoretical stepping stone, not a practical algorithm for modern LLMs—a distinction the authors explicitly acknowledge.

For a top-tier ML conference with emphasis on theoretical advances, this represents solid, novel, and rigorous work on an important open problem. The execution is sound, the technical approach is non-obvious, and the results extend the understanding of neural network learnability. While not groundbreaking in practical impact, the paper merits acceptance as a theoretical contribution that moves the field forward.

target_paper_summary.title: Learning Linear Attention In Polynomial Time
target_paper_summary.abstract: Previous research has explored the expressivity of Transformer models in simulating Boolean circuits or Turing machines. However, the efficient learnability of Transformers from data has remained an open question. Our study addresses this gap by providing the first polynomial-time learnability results (specifically strong, agnostic PAC learning) for single-layer Transformers with linear attention. We show that learning the optimal multi head linear attention can be recast as finding the optimal kernel predictor in a suitably defined RKHS. Moving to generalization, we construct an algorithm that, given a dataset, checks in polynomial time whether the set of best fit multi head linear attention networks on this data all perform an identical computation–a powerful notion for out of distribution generalization. We empirically validate our theoretical findings on several canonical tasks: learning random linear attention networks, key–value associations, and learning to execute finite automata. Our findings bridge a critical gap between theoretical expressivity and learnability of Transformer models.
claims: We show that learning the optimal multi head linear attention can be recast as finding the optimal kernel predictor in a suitably defined RKHS.

paper_metadata.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
paper_metadata.abstract: Multilayer neural networks trained with the back-propagation algorithm constitute the best example of a successful gradient based learning technique. Given an appropriate network architecture, gradient-based learning algorithms can be used to synthesize a complex decision surface that can classify high-dimensional patterns, such as handwritten characters, with minimal preprocessing. This paper reviews various methods applied to handwritten character recognition and compares them on a standard handwritten digit recognition task. Convolutional neural networks, which are specifically designed to deal with the variability of 2D shapes, are shown to outperform all other techniques. Real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation recognition, and language modeling. A new learning paradigm, called graph transformer networks (GTN), allows such multimodule systems to be trained globally using gradient-based methods so as to minimize an overall performance measure. Two systems for online handwriting recognition are described. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of global training, and the flexibility of graph transformer networks. A graph transformer network for reading a bank cheque is also described. It uses convolutional neural network character recognizers combined with global training techniques to provide record accuracy on business and personal cheques. It is deployed commercially and reads several million cheques per day.

paper_metadata.title: A survey on deep learning in medical image analysis
Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: This paper surveys the field of reinforcement learning from a computer-science perspective. It is written to be accessible to researchers familiar with machine learning. Both the historical basis of the field and a broad selection of current work are summarized. Reinforcement learning is the problem faced by an agent that learns behavior through trial-and-error interactions with a dynamic environment. The work described here has a resemblance to work in psychology, but differs considerably in the details and in the use of the word ``reinforcement.'' The paper discusses central issues of reinforcement learning, including trading off exploration and exploitation, establishing the foundations of the field via Markov decision theory, learning from delayed reinforcement, constructing empirical models to accelerate learning, making use of generalization and hierarchy, and coping with hidden state. It concludes with a survey of some implemented systems and an assessment of the practical utility of current methods for reinforcement learning.

paper_metadata.title: Physics-informed machine learning
Semi-Supervised Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: A comprehensive review of an area of machine learning that deals with the use of unlabeled data in classification problems: state-of-the-art algorithms, a taxonomy of the field, applications, benchmark experiments, and directions for future research. In the field of machine learning, semi-supervised learning (SSL) occupies the middle ground, between supervised learning (in which all training examples are labeled) and unsupervised learning (in which no label data are given). Interest in SSL has increased in recent years, particularly because of application domains in which unlabeled data are plentiful, such as images, text, and bioinformatics. This first comprehensive overview of SSL presents state-of-the-art algorithms, a taxonomy of the field, selected applications, benchmark experiments, and perspectives on ongoing and future research.Semi-Supervised Learning first presents the key assumptions and ideas underlying the field: smoothness, cluster or low-density separation, manifold structure, and transduction. The core of the book is the presentation of SSL methods, organized according to algorithmic strategies. After an examination of generative models, the book describes algorithms that implement the low-density separation assumption, graph-based methods, and algorithms that perform two-step learning. The book then discusses SSL applications and offers guidelines for SSL practitioners by analyzing the results of extensive benchmark experiments. Finally, the book looks at interesting directions for SSL research. The book closes with a discussion of the relationship between semi-supervised learning and transduction.

paper_metadata.title: MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Molecular machine learning has been maturing rapidly over the last few years. Improved methods and the presence of larger datasets have enabled machine learning algorithms to make increasingly accurate predictions about molecular properties. However, algorithmic progress has been limited due to the lack of a standard benchmark to compare the efficacy of proposed methods; most new algorithms are benchmarked on different datasets making it challenging to gauge the quality of proposed methods. This work introduces MoleculeNet, a large scale benchmark for molecular machine learning. MoleculeNet curates multiple public datasets, establishes metrics for evaluation, and offers high quality open-source implementations of multiple previously proposed molecular featurization and learning algorithms (released as part of the DeepChem open source library). MoleculeNet benchmarks demonstrate that learnable representations are powerful tools for molecular machine learning and broadly offer the best performance. However, this result comes with caveats. Learnable representations still struggle to deal with complex tasks under data scarcity and highly imbalanced classification. For quantum mechanical and biophysical datasets, the use of physics-aware featurizations can be more important than choice of particular learning algorithm.

paper_metadata.title: Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks: A Deep Learning Framework for Traffic Forecasting
paper_metadata.abstract: Timely accurate traffic forecast is crucial for urban traffic control and guidance. Due to the high nonlinearity and complexity of traffic flow, traditional methods cannot satisfy the requirements of mid-and-long term prediction tasks and often neglect spatial and temporal dependencies. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning framework, Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (STGCN), to tackle the time series prediction problem in traffic domain. Instead of applying regular convolutional and recurrent units, we formulate the problem on graphs and build the model with complete convolutional structures, which enable much faster training speed with fewer parameters. Experiments show that our model STGCN effectively captures comprehensive spatio-temporal correlations through modeling multi-scale traffic networks and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on various real-world traffic datasets.

paper_metadata.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
paper_metadata.abstract: Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention, gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address Transformers' computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient convolutions, we design a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode. We integrate these selective SSMs into a simplified end-to-end neural network architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (Mamba). Mamba enjoys fast inference (5$\times$ higher throughput than Transformers) and linear scaling in sequence length, and its performance improves on real data up to million-length sequences. As a general sequence model backbone, Mamba achieves state-of-the-art performance across several modalities such as language, audio, and genomics. On language modeling, our Mamba-3B model outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream evaluation.

paper_metadata.title: On the approximability of minimizing nonzero variables or unsatisfied relations in linear systems
paper_metadata.abstract: We investigate the computational complexity of two closely related classes of combinatorial optimization problems for linear systems which arise in various fields such as machine learning, operations research and pattern recognition. In the first class (Min ULR) one wishes, given a possibly infeasible system of linear relations, to find a solution that violates as few relations as possible while satisfying all the others. In the second class (Min RVLS) the linear system is supposed to be feasible and one looks for a solution with as few nonzero variables as possible. For both Min ULR and Min RVLS the four basic types of relational operators =, ⩾, > and ≠ are considered. While Min RVLS with equations was mentioned to be NP-hard in (Garey and Johnson, 1979), we established in (Amaldi; 1992; Amaldi and Kann, 1995) that min ULR with equalities and inequalities are NP-hard even when restricted to homogeneous systems with bipolar coefficients. The latter problems have been shown hard to approximate in (Arora et al., 1993). In this paper we determine strong bounds on the approximability of various variants of Min RVLS and min ULR, including constrained ones where the variables are restricted to take binary values or where some relations are mandatory while others are optional. The various NP-hard versions turn out to have different approximability properties depending on the type of relations and the additional constraints, but none of them can be approximated within any constant factor, unless P = NP. Particular attention is devoted to two interesting special cases that occur in discriminant analysis and machine learning. In particular, we disprove a conjecture of van Horn and Martinez (1992) regarding the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm to design linear classifiers (or perceptrons) that involve a close-to-minimum number of features.

paper_metadata.title: On the Sample Complexity of Reinforcement Learning
paper_metadata.venue: OpenGrey (Institut de l'Information Scientifique et Technique)
paper_metadata.abstract: This thesis is a detailed investigation into the following question: how much data must an agent collect in order to perform "reinforcement learning" successfully? This question is analogous to the classical issue of the sample complexity in supervised learning, but is harder because of the increased realism of the reinforcement learning setting. This thesis summarizes recent sample complexity results in the reinforcement learning literature and builds on these results to provide novel algorithms with strong performance guarantees. We focus on a variety of reasonable performance criteria and sampling models by which agents may access the environment. For instance, in a policy search setting, we consider the problem of how much simulated experience is required to reliably choose a "good" policy among a restricted class of policies II (as in Kearns, Mansour, and Ng [2000]). In a more online setting, we consider the case in which an agent is placed in an environment and must follow one unbroken chain of experience with no access to "offline" simulation (as in Kearns and Singh [1998]). We build on the sample based algorithms suggested by Kearns, Mansour, and Ng [2000]. Their sample complexity bounds have no dependence on the size of the state space, an exponential dependence on the planning horizon time, and linear dependence on the complexity of II. We suggest novel algorithms with more restricted guarantees whose sample complexities are again independent of the size of the state space and depend linearly on the complexity of the policy class II, but have only a polynomial dependence on the horizon time. We pay particular attention to the tradeoffs made by such algorithms.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: class imbalance in federated class-incremental learning (FCIL), which is a practical and important challenge combining federated learning with continual learning. The two-module design (GDR and TTS) is complementary and well-justified.

The Global-perspective Data Replay (GDR) module is technically sound, using SVD-based feature encryption to construct globally-informed pseudo features while preserving privacy. The use of leverage scores to guide class-balanced sampling is principled and represents a novel approach for federated settings.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) with multiple heterogeneity levels (β ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}), task splits, and client configurations. The ablation studies clearly demonstrate the contribution of each component. Consistent 2-15% improvements over six state-of-the-art baselines are substantial.

The paper includes thorough analysis beyond accuracy metrics: per-class sample distribution visualization (Figure 5), gradient-CAM visualizations (Figure 6), incremental task performance curves (Figure 3), and sensitivity analyses for hyperparameters (Figure 4). The per-task accuracy breakdown (Table 9) shows FedCBDR achieves 49.59% average on CIFAR100 versus 44.00% for LANDER, demonstrating overall superiority.

Scalability analysis is provided, including experiments with 50/100 clients, computational complexity analysis (O(n_k d²) and O(Nd²)), and communication overhead measurements. The hyperparameter configuration generalizes across three diverse datasets, suggesting reasonable robustness.
weaknesses: The privacy claim relies on practical feature encryption without formal differential privacy analysis. The paper claims 'privacy-preserving' but does not prove the encrypted features cannot be inverted or provide formal privacy guarantees. The rebuttal clarifies this is empirical privacy through not transmitting raw data, but the abstract overstates the privacy contribution without such caveats.

The Task-aware Temperature Scaling (TTS) module is empirically effective (Table 4: +2-5% improvements) but lacks formal theoretical justification. The rebuttal acknowledges no convergence proofs are provided. However, the empirical validation through ablation and sensitivity analysis adequately supports the contribution.

The method introduces multiple hyperparameters requiring tuning. While the reported ranges are tight and the same configuration generalizes across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet, the paper provides limited guidance beyond these specific values. Figure 4 shows performance sensitivity, particularly for τ_new and ω_new.

weakness_details.weakness: The privacy claim relies on practical feature encryption without formal differential privacy analysis. The paper claims 'privacy-preserving' but does not prove the encrypted features cannot be inverted or provide formal privacy guarantees.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.1 and Abstract claim privacy-preserving behavior through ISVD encryption with unknown matrices P_k^(i) and Q^(i). The rebuttal clarifies this provides 'empirical privacy' through feature encryption rather than formal guarantees. This is a minor overstatement of privacy claims rather than unsound technical approach. The method does not transmit raw data, which is standard practice in federated learning and acceptable for the venue.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The GDR module 'reconstructs global representations of prior tasks in a privacy-preserving manner' (abstract)

weakness_details.weakness: The Task-aware Temperature Scaling (TTS) module lacks formal theoretical justification beyond intuition, though empirical validation is provided.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2 provides intuitive reasoning but no formal convergence analysis. However, Table 4 shows consistent +2-5% improvements with +TTS alone across multiple datasets, and Figure 4 provides sensitivity analysis. The rebuttal correctly notes empirical validation adequately supports the contribution despite lack of formal proof.
weakness_details.affected_claim: TTS 'adaptively adjusts temperature based on task dynamics, reducing the model's overconfidence in majority classes while enhancing its sensitivity to minority classes' (abstract)

weakness_details.weakness: Limited guidance for hyperparameter selection on new domains beyond the specific tested ranges. Figure 4 shows performance sensitivity, particularly for τ_new and ω_new.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 5.1 specifies ranges (τ_old ∈ {0.8,0.9}, τ_new ∈ {1.1,1.2}, ω_old ∈ {1.1,1.4}, ω_new ∈ {0.7,0.9}) but provides no algorithmic selection procedure. However, the same configuration (τ_old=0.9, τ_new=1.1, ω_old=1.1, ω_new=0.9) works well across three datasets, suggesting reasonable transferability.
weakness_details.affected_claim: FedCBDR achieves robust improvements across 'complex settings' (Section 5.2)

soundness.justification: The core technical approach is sound and correctly implemented. SVD-based feature encryption, leverage score computation, and temperature-scaled loss formulations are mathematically coherent. Algorithm 1 clearly describes the pipeline. The rebuttal clarifies that privacy is achieved through feature encryption (practical obfuscation) rather than formal privacy proofs, which is acceptable for federated learning work. Experimental methodology is rigorous with proper statistical reporting. The rebuttal's distinction between empirical privacy (feature encryption) and formal privacy guarantees is a reasonable clarification that does not reduce the soundness of the technical approach.

novelty.justification: The paper combines existing techniques (SVD, leverage scores, temperature scaling, class-balanced sampling) in a novel way tailored to FCIL. The GDR module's application of leverage scores for globally-informed sampling in federated settings is novel compared to prior work (Re-Fed, GLFC). The integration of TTS with class-balanced replay is also new. The rebuttal does not contradict this assessment.

significance.justification: The problem of class imbalance in FCIL is practically important. The paper addresses inter-client and intra-task imbalance with 2-15% improvements over baselines. Table 9 shows FedCBDR achieves 49.59% average accuracy on CIFAR100 versus 44.00% for LANDER and 36.46% for Re-Fed, demonstrating meaningful advances. The rebuttal's clarification that the single CIFAR100 β=1.0 underperformance case (52.06% vs 52.77%, within 1.3 difference) represents a single outlier among many successes is reasonable and does not undermine significance.

evaluation.justification: Comprehensive experiments across three datasets with varying heterogeneity levels, multiple task splits, ablation studies isolating component contributions, analysis of per-class distributions and performance evolution, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, scalability tests with 50/100 clients, and qualitative Grad-CAM analysis. The rebuttal correctly notes that the CIFAR100 (5 tasks, β=1.0) underperformance is a single case (52.06% vs 52.77%, ~1.3% difference) that falls within the standard deviation ranges reported (±1.5-2.7%), and does not materially undermine the overall evaluation. Results across Tables 2 and 3 show FedCBDR achieves best or competitive performance in 8 out of 9 primary settings and best performance in all 9 settings in Table 3 (harder 5/10/20 splits).

presentation.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear motivation, methodology, and experimental design. Figures and tables effectively communicate the approach and findings. Algorithm 1 clearly describes the pipeline. Writing is generally clear. The comprehensive appendix strengthens the presentation. The rebuttal's clarification that privacy is achieved through empirical feature encryption (not formal guarantees) provides a useful precision to the presentation, though ideally this should have been clearer in the original abstract/introduction.

reviewers.summary_comment: After reviewing the author's second rebuttal, I maintain my Accept decision. The rebuttal appropriately and honestly clarifies the limitations without overstating what has been addressed in the submitted work. Key assessment updates: (1) Privacy concern (minor, not major): The rebuttal clarifies that the privacy contribution is empirical—achieved through not transmitting raw data and feature encryption—rather than formal differential privacy guarantees. This is a reasonable clarification that somewhat reduces the severity of the concern. The stated privacy claim in the abstract is slightly imprecise but not misleading in the context of federated learning practice. (2) TTS theoretical justification (remains minor): The rebuttal acknowledges the lack of formal convergence proofs but emphasizes the empirical validation (Table 4: consistent +2-5% improvements). This is acceptable for a machine learning paper; empirical validation of neural network techniques without formal theory is common in the field. (3) Hyperparameter sensitivity (remains minor): The rebuttal notes the same hyperparameter configuration (τ_old=0.9, τ_new=1.1, ω_old=1.1, ω_new=0.9) generalizes across three diverse datasets, which is a reasonable response. The ranges are tight (0.1 apart for temperature values), suggesting reasonable stability. (4) CIFAR100 underperformance (correctly contextualized as minor): The rebuttal clarifies this is a single outlier (52.06% vs 52.77%, 1.3% difference) within statistical noise (std dev ±1.5-2.7%), with FedCBDR achieving superior average performance (49.59% vs 44.00% for LANDER in Table 9). This contextualization is fair and does not undermine the overall claims. Overall, the submitted paper makes solid contributions to federated class-incremental learning through well-executed techniques addressing a real problem. The experimental evaluation is rigorous, comprehensive, and appropriately honest about limitations. The 2-15% consistent improvements, combined with thorough ablation studies, justify publication at a top-tier venue despite the acknowledged limitations around formal privacy analysis, theoretical justification for TTS, and hyperparameter selection guidelines. These are areas for future work but do not invalidate the core contributions.

## Summary and Strategic Recommendation

**Overall Assessment:**

This paper presents a well-executed engineering solution to class imbalance in federated class-incremental learning (FCIL). The work combines existing techniques (SVD, leverage scores, temperature scaling) in a novel way and demonstrates solid empirical improvements (2-15% gains) with comprehensive experiments.

**Venue Fit Analysis:**

We can revise the abstract and Section 4.1 to more precisely state that the method achieves privacy through feature encryption rather than claiming formal privacy-preserving guarantees without substantiation.

**2. Theoretical Justification for TTS (Minor Concern):**

The submitted paper does not provide formal convergence analysis or loss landscape characterization for the TTS module. However, the empirical evidence in Table 4 shows consistent improvements: ablation study with +TTS alone yields 2-5% gains over Finetune on multiple datasets and heterogeneity levels. This demonstrates that the temperature scaling mechanism is effective in practice.

The submitted paper *does* provide intuitive reasoning: using lower temperature τ_old for old classes increases prediction sharpness/discriminability, while higher temperature τ_new for new classes provides regularization. This intuition is sound in the context of class-imbalanced learning literature, though we acknowledge it lacks formal theoretical proof. The empirical validation through ablation (Table 4) and sensitivity analysis (Figure 4) supports the contribution.

**3. Hyperparameter Selection (Minor Concern):**

You correctly note that the submitted paper does not provide principled hyperparameter selection guidelines for new domains. Figure 4 shows sensitivity, particularly for τ_new and ω_new. However, we emphasize that: (a) the reported ranges are relatively tight (e.g., τ_old ∈ {0.8, 0.9} is only 0.1 apart); (b) performance is reasonably stable within each reported range; (c) the best configuration (ω_old=1.1, ω_new=0.9, τ_old=0.9, τ_new=1.1) provides a principled starting point.

For practitioners, the submitted paper provides these specific hyperparameter values that work well across three datasets and multiple heterogeneity levels (β ∈ {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}). The fact that the same hyperparameter configuration generalizes across CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet (different data sources and complexities) suggests the approach is reasonably robust. We can add clarification in the paper noting that these hyperparameters should be used as starting values for new domains, with grid search validation.

**4. CIFAR100 Underperformance Case (Minor Concern):**

You are right that the submitted paper does not investigate the CIFAR100 (5 tasks, β=1.0) case where FedCBDR (52.06%) slightly underperforms LANDER (52.77%). This is a single outlier among many successful comparisons across Tables 2 and 3. Several observations support this not undermining the paper:

- In Table 2 (main results, 3/5/10 task splits), FedCBDR achieves the best or competitive performance in 8 out of 9 settings. The CIFAR100 β=1.0 case is the only suboptimal result.
- In the more challenging "5/10/20" task split (Table 3), FedCBDR again achieves best performance across all settings.
- Per-task analysis (Table 9) shows FedCBDR achieves 49.59% average on CIFAR100 vs. 44.00% for LANDER, demonstrating overall superiority.
- The difference is small (52.06% vs 52.77%, approximately 1.3%), within the margin of statistical noise given standard deviations reported in Table 2 (±1.5 to ±2.7%).

While deeper analysis of this case would be informative, its absence does not materially affect the paper's contributions, which are validated across comprehensive experiments.

**Summary:**

The submitted paper has legitimate limitations that we acknowledge: formal privacy guarantees are absent (relying instead on practical feature encryption), theoretical analysis of TTS is limited (relying on intuition and empirical validation), hyperparameter selection guidelines are not algorithmically specified, and the single CIFAR100 underperformance case is not investigated. However, these limitations do not invalidate the core contributions:

1. The GDR module's use of leverage scores for globally-informed balanced sampling is technically sound and novel in the federated setting.
2. The empirical improvements (2-15% across baselines) are substantial and consistent across three datasets with multiple heterogeneity levels.
3. The ablation studies (Table 4) clearly demonstrate that each component (GDR and TTS) contributes meaningfully to performance.
4. The experimental evaluation is rigorous with proper statistical reporting and includes scalability analysis (50/100 clients) and comprehensive sensitivity analysis.

We are grateful for your careful attention to distinguishing between the submitted work and the rebuttal's explanations. This feedback will guide improvements in any future revision."

target_paper_summary.title: Class-Wise Balancing Data Replay For Federated Class-Incremental Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract:
Federated Class Incremental Learning (FCIL) aims to collaboratively process continuously increasing incoming tasks across multiple clients. Among various approaches, data replay has become a promising solution, which can alleviate forgetting by reintroducing representative samples from previous tasks. However, their performance is typically limited by class imbalance, both within the replay buffer due to limited global awareness and between replayed and newly arrived classes. To address this issue, we propose a class-wise balancing data replay method for FCIL (FedCBDR), which employs a global coordination mechanism for class-level memory construction and reweights the learning objective to alleviate the aforementioned imbalances. Specifically, FedCBDR has two key components:
1) the global-perspective data replay module reconstructs global representations of prior task in a privacy-preserving manner, which then guides a class-aware and importance-sensitive sampling strategy to achieve balanced replay; 2) Subsequently, to handle class imbalance across tasks, the task-aware temperature scaling module adaptively adjusts the temperature of logits at both class and instance levels based on task dynamics, which reduces the model's overconfidence in majority classes while enhancing its sensitivity to minority classes. Experimental results verified that FedCBDR achieves balanced class-wise sampling under heterogeneous data distributions and improves generalization under task imbalance between earlier and recent tasks, yielding a 2%-15% Top-1 accuracy improvement over six stateof-the-art methods.
claims: we propose a class-wise balancing data replay method for FCIL (FedCBDR), which employs a global coordination mechanism for class-level memory construction and reweights the learning objective to alleviate the aforementioned imbalances.

paper_metadata.title: Class-Incremental Learning: A Survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep models, e.g., CNNs and Vision Transformers, have achieved impressive achievements in many vision tasks in the closed world. However, novel classes emerge from time to time in our ever-changing world, requiring a learning system to acquire new knowledge continually. Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) enables the learner to incorporate the knowledge of new classes incrementally and build a universal classifier among all seen classes. Correspondingly, when directly training the model with new class instances, a fatal problem occurs -- the model tends to catastrophically forget the characteristics of former ones, and its performance drastically degrades. There have been numerous efforts to tackle catastrophic forgetting in the machine learning community. In this paper, we survey comprehensively recent advances in class-incremental learning and summarize these methods from several aspects. We also provide a rigorous and unified evaluation of 17 methods in benchmark image classification tasks to find out the characteristics of different algorithms empirically. Furthermore, we notice that the current comparison protocol ignores the influence of memory budget in model storage, which may result in unfair comparison and biased results. Hence, we advocate fair comparison by aligning the memory budget in evaluation, as well as several memory-agnostic performance measures. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhoudw-zdw/CIL_Survey/

paper_metadata.title: Combined Federated and Split Learning in Edge Computing for Ubiquitous Intelligence in Internet of Things: State-of-the-Art and Future Directions
paper_metadata.abstract: Federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) are two emerging collaborative learning methods that may greatly facilitate ubiquitous intelligence in the Internet of Things (IoT). Federated learning enables machine learning (ML) models locally trained using private data to be aggregated into a global model. Split learning allows different portions of an ML model to be collaboratively trained on different workers in a learning framework. Federated learning and split learning, each have unique advantages and respective limitations, may complement each other toward ubiquitous intelligence in IoT. Therefore, the combination of federated learning and split learning recently became an active research area attracting extensive interest. In this article, we review the latest developments in federated learning and split learning and present a survey on the state-of-the-art technologies for combining these two learning methods in an edge computing-based IoT environment. We also identify some open problems and discuss possible directions for future research in this area with the hope of arousing the research community's interest in this emerging field.

paper_metadata.title: A Survey on Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Federated learning, which allows multiple client devices in a network to jointly train a machine learning model without direct exposure of clients' data, is an emerging distributed learning technique due to its nature of privacy preservation. However, it has been found that models trained with federated learning usually have worse performance than their counterparts trained in the standard centralized learning mode, especially when the training data is imbalanced. In the context of federated learning, data imbalance may occur either locally one one client device, or globally across many devices. The complexity of different types of data imbalance has posed challenges to the development of federated learning technique, especially considering the need of relieving data imbalance issue and preserving data privacy at the same time. Therefore, in the literature, many attempts have been made to handle class imbalance in federated learning. In this paper, we present a detailed review of recent advancements along this line. We first introduce various types of class imbalance in federated learning, after which we review existing methods for estimating the extent of class imbalance without the need of knowing the actual data to preserve data privacy. After that, we discuss existing methods for handling class imbalance in FL, where the advantages and disadvantages of the these approaches are discussed. We also summarize common evaluation metrics for class imbalanced tasks, and point out potential future directions.

paper_metadata.title: A Machine Learning-Oriented Survey on Tiny Machine Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: The emergence of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) has positively revolutionized the field of Artificial Intelligence by promoting the joint design of resource-constrained IoT hardware devices and their learning-based software architectures. TinyML carries an essential role within the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions in helping societies, economies, and individuals employ effective AI-infused computing technologies (e.g., smart cities, automotive, and medical robotics). Given its multidisciplinary nature, the field of TinyML has been approached from many different angles: this comprehensive survey wishes to provide an up-to-date overview focused on all the learning algorithms within TinyML-based solutions. The survey is based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodological flow, allowing for a systematic and complete literature survey. In particular, firstly, we will examine the three different workflows for implementing a TinyML-based system, i.e., ML-oriented, HW-oriented, and co-design. Secondly, we propose a taxonomy that covers the learning panorama under the TinyML lens, examining in detail the different families of model optimization and design, as well as the state-of-the-art learning techniques. Thirdly, this survey will present the distinct features of hardware devices and software tools that represent the current state-of-the-art for TinyML intelligent edge applications. Finally, we discuss the challenges and future directions.

paper_metadata.title: A Data-Free Approach to Mitigate Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Class Incremental Learning for Vision Tasks
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep learning models often suffer from forgetting previously learned information when trained on new data. This problem is exacerbated in federated learning (FL), where the data is distributed and can change independently for each user. Many solutions are proposed to resolve this catastrophic forgetting in a centralized setting. However, they do not apply directly to FL because of its unique complexities, such as privacy concerns and resource limitations. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a framework for $\textbf{federated class incremental learning}$ that utilizes a generative model to synthesize samples from past distributions. This data can be later exploited alongside the training data to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. To preserve privacy, the generative model is trained on the server using data-free methods at the end of each task without requesting data from clients. Moreover, our solution does not demand the users to store old data or models, which gives them the freedom to join/leave the training at any time. Additionally, we introduce SuperImageNet, a new regrouping of the ImageNet dataset specifically tailored for federated continual learning. We demonstrate significant improvements compared to existing baselines through extensive experiments on multiple datasets.

paper_metadata.title: Federated Class-Incremental Learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Federated learning (FL) has attracted growing attention via data-private collaborative training on decentralized clients. However, most existing methods unrealistically assume object classes of the overall framework are fixed over time. It makes the global model suffer from significant catastrophic forgetting on old classes in real-world scenarios, where local clients often collect new classes continuously and have very limited storage memory to store old classes. Moreover, new clients with unseen new classes may participate in the FL training, further aggravating the catastrophic forgetting of the global model. To address these challenges, we develop a novel Global-Local Forgetting Compensation (GLFC) model, to learn a global class incremental model for alleviating the catastrophic forgetting from both local and global perspectives. Specifically, to address local forgetting caused by class imbalance at the local clients, we design a class-aware gradient compensation loss and a class-semantic relation distillation loss to balance the forgetting of old classes and distill consistent inter-class relations across tasks. To tackle the global forgetting brought by the non-i.i.d class imbalance across clients, we propose a proxy server that selects the best old global model to assist the local relation distillation. Moreover, a prototype gradient-based communication mechanism is developed to protect privacy. Our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 4.4%-15.1% in terms of average accuracy on representative benchmark datasets.

paper_metadata.title: Cross-Class Feature Augmentation for Class Incremental Learning
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
paper_metadata.abstract: We propose a novel class incremental learning approach, which incorporates a feature augmentation technique motivated by adversarial attacks. We employ a classifier learned in the past to complement training examples of previous tasks. The proposed approach has an unique perspective to utilize the previous knowledge in class incremental learning since it augments features of arbitrary target classes using examples in other classes via adversarial attacks on a previously learned classifier. By allowing the Cross-Class Feature Augmentations (CCFA), each class in the old tasks conveniently populates samples in the feature space, which alleviates the collapse of the decision boundaries caused by sample deficiency for the previous tasks, especially when the number of stored exemplars is small. This idea can be easily incorporated into existing class incremental learning algorithms without any architecture modification. Extensive experiments on the standard benchmarks show that our method consistently outperforms existing class incremental learning methods by significant margins in various scenarios, especially under an environment with an extremely limited memory budget.

paper_metadata.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Convolutions in Deep Learning: Applications, Challenges, and Future Trends
paper_metadata.abstract: In today’s digital age, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), a subset of Deep Learning (DL), are widely used for various computer vision tasks such as image classification, object detection, and image segmentation. There are numerous types of CNNs designed to meet specific needs and requirements, including 1D, 2D, and 3D CNNs, as well as dilated, grouped, attention, depthwise convolutions, and NAS, among others. Each type of CNN has its unique structure and characteristics, making it suitable for specific tasks. It’s crucial to gain a thorough understanding and perform a comparative analysis of these different CNN types to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Furthermore, studying the performance, limitations, and practical applications of each type of CNN can aid in the development of new and improved architectures in the future. We also dive into the platforms and frameworks that researchers utilize for their research or development from various perspectives. Additionally, we explore the main research fields of CNN like 6D vision, generative models, and meta-learning. This survey paper provides a comprehensive examination and comparison of various CNN architectures, highlighting their architectural differences and emphasizing their respective advantages, disadvantages, applications, challenges, and future trends.

paper_metadata.title: Domain generalization through meta-learning: a survey
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Deep neural networks (DNNs) have revolutionized artificial intelligence but often lack performance when faced with out-of-distribution data, a common scenario due to the inevitable domain shifts in real-world applications. This limitation stems from the common assumption that training and testing data share the same distribution-an assumption frequently violated in practice. Despite their effectiveness with large amounts of data and computational power, DNNs struggle with distributional shifts and limited labeled data, leading to overfitting and poor generalization across various tasks and domains. Meta-learning presents a promising approach by employing algorithms that acquire transferable knowledge across various tasks for fast adaptation, eliminating the need to learn each task from scratch. This survey paper delves into the realm of meta-learning with a focus on its contribution to domain generalization. We first clarify the concept of meta-learning for domain generalization and introduce a novel taxonomy based on the feature extraction strategy and the classifier learning methodology, offering a granular view of methodologies. Additionally, we present a decision graph to assist readers in navigating the taxonomy based on data availability and domain shifts, enabling them to select and develop a proper model tailored to their specific problem requirements. Through an exhaustive review of existing methods and underlying theories, we map out the fundamentals of the field. Our survey provides practical insights and an informed discussion on promising research directions.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: The paper introduces a unified and formally principled framework that generalizes beyond permutation symmetries to encompass permutations, semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and invertible maps. This hierarchical organization (Table 1) clearly articulates how different symmetry classes relate to specific neural network components, providing theoretical grounding that subsumes prior work like Git Re-Basin as special cases.

Achieving linear mode connectivity (LMC) with zero or near-zero loss barriers for independently trained Vision Transformers and GPT-2 models is a substantial empirical advance on vision tasks (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet) and Tiny Shakespeare. The results demonstrate this is possible even across width-heterogeneous architectures (Figure 3c), extending prior results which required 32× width increases for ResNets. The multi-model alignment results (Figure 4) further demonstrate the approach generalizes beyond pairwise merging within its validated scope.

The paper provides three complementary alignment strategies (activation matching, weight matching, and learned matching) with clear algorithmic descriptions. The learned matching method (Algorithm 1) elegantly handles discrete symmetries through straight-through estimators and continuous symmetries via differentiable projections, while weight matching offers a practical data-free alternative. The analysis in Section 6 identifying where gaps arise between weight and learned matching provides useful insights for future optimization.

The mathematical framework in Section 3 and Appendix E rigorously characterizes symmetries in Transformers component-by-component (feed-forward layers with permutation, multi-head attention with semi-permutation and invertibility, residual streams with orthogonal symmetry). The derivation showing how orthogonal transformations preserve RMSNorm and enable width-heterogeneous alignment (equations 6-8) is technically sound and novel.
weaknesses: Experimental evaluation uses small-scale models and datasets that do not validate the claimed architecture-agnostic nature of the framework. ViTs use embedding dimensions 256-384 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet; GPT-2 on BookCorpus is trained for only 5 epochs. While the authors appropriately acknowledge this in Appendix A and their rebuttal explains the framework is theoretically scale-invariant, the submitted paper provides no empirical evidence from contemporary-scale models (ViT-Base/Large, GPT-2-medium/large) to substantiate claims about practical generalization. Vision results are robust within their scope; language results are limited to Tiny Shakespeare and problematic on BookCorpus.

The BookCorpus language modeling results exhibit a loss barrier of 0.42 ± 0.01, substantially higher than vision tasks (near-zero) and contradicting the narrative of universal Transformer connectivity. The authors attribute this to potentially different learned strategies but provide no direct empirical evidence in the submitted paper—such as representation analysis (CCA, SVCCA), diagnostic probing, or loss landscape characterization—to support or refute this hypothesis. This remains unresolved in the submission, creating ambiguity about whether the failure reflects alignment limitations or genuine solution diversity.

Reparameterizations required for the framework (RMSNorm reparameterization per Appendix E equations 6-8, treating QK/OV circuits as canonical) are not explicitly characterized in the main submission as one-time preprocessing operations. The submitted Section 3.2.3 and Appendix A acknowledge these operations alter the network architecture but do not clearly state they are absorbed into adjacent layers with negligible overhead. This lack of clarity creates potential confusion about practical implementation costs.

ViTs use embedding dimensions 256-384 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet; GPT-2 on BookCorpus is trained for only 5 epochs. While the authors appropriately acknowledge this in Appendix A and their rebuttal explains the framework is theoretically scale-invariant, the submitted paper provides no empirical evidence from contemporary-scale models (ViT-Base/Large, GPT-2-medium/large) to substantiate claims about practical generalization. Vision results are robust within their scope; language results are limited to Tiny Shakespeare and problematic on BookCorpus.
weakness_details.evidence: Appendix B Table 3 specifies ViT embedding dimensions 256-384 with 6-8 layers on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet; GPT-2 on BookCorpus uses 6 layers, 512 embedding dimension, trained for only 5 epochs with batch size 64. Appendix A acknowledges: 'empirical results for language models were based on a smaller version of GPT-2 language models with reduced parameters due to resource constraints...indicating the need for evaluation on larger, more contemporary language models.' The rebuttal clarifies the framework is 'architecture-agnostic' in formulation and notes the symmetry classes apply across scales in principle, but the submitted paper itself contains no evidence from larger models. The rebuttal appropriately acknowledges: 'we provide proof-of-concept on small models' and 'we fully agree that validation on standard-scale models is essential for practical impact.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: That the approach generalizes to modern Transformer architectures and achieves practical significance for contemporary language/vision models.

weakness_details.weakness: The BookCorpus language modeling results exhibit a loss barrier of 0.42 ± 0.01, substantially higher than vision tasks (near-zero) and contradicting the narrative of universal Transformer connectivity. The authors attribute this to potentially different learned strategies but provide no direct empirical evidence in the submitted paper—such as representation analysis (CCA, SVCCA), diagnostic probing, or loss landscape characterization—to support or refute this hypothesis. This remains unresolved in the submission, creating ambiguity about whether the failure reflects alignment limitations or genuine solution diversity.

Juneja et al. [2023] show that...models using the same strategy might be linearly connected, linear paths across strategies exhibit barriers.' The rebuttal acknowledges: 'the submitted paper provides no representation analysis, probing studies, or loss landscape characterization to support the hypothesis that BookCorpus models learned fundamentally different strategies' and characterizes it as 'an open question.' The rebuttal proposes diagnostic probing and representation analysis as solutions but notes these would require new experiments. No such analysis appears in the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: That the framework enables LMC across diverse Transformer architectures and tasks; that findings generalize to language modeling.

weakness_details.weakness: Reparameterizations required for the framework (RMSNorm reparameterization per Appendix E equations 6-8, treating QK/OV circuits as canonical) are not explicitly characterized in the main submission as one-time preprocessing operations. The submitted Section 3.2.3 and Appendix A acknowledge these operations alter the network architecture but do not clearly state they are absorbed into adjacent layers with negligible overhead. This lack of clarity creates potential confusion about practical implementation costs.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 3.2.3 describes RMSNorm reparameterization; Appendix E provides technical derivations (equations 6-8). Appendix A states: 'requires reparameterization (e.g., RMSNorm reparameterization or multiplying out intra-head dependencies). Although it preserves functional equivalence, it alters the underlying network architecture.' The submitted paper does not explicitly state that these operations are absorbed into adjacent linear layers (W₀' = OW₀, W₁' = W₁O^T) with one-time preprocessing cost. The rebuttal clarifies: 'we absorb the orthogonal transformation O into adjacent linear layers...which requires no additional forward/backward pass cost' and proposes adding this clarification in Section 3.2.3. This clarification is reasonable but does not appear in the submitted work.
weakness_details.affected_claim: That the framework is practically implementable without hidden computational overhead; clarity about one-time vs. recurring costs.

soundness.justification: The mathematical framework is rigorous and sound. The symmetry hierarchy (Section 3, Appendix E) correctly characterizes component-specific symmetries with formal derivations (RMSNorm orthogonal invariance, QK/OV circuit invertibility, semi-permutation decomposability). Optimization objectives (Equations 1-2) are well-defined. Alignment algorithms (Hungarian algorithm, SVD, STE, Sinkhorn) are sound and correctly applied. The rebuttal does not identify any mathematical errors in the framework; the authors agree with all technical concerns raised and appropriately characterize remaining issues as empirical scope and clarity rather than fundamental soundness problems. No mathematical or logical flaws undermining the core framework have been identified or contested.

novelty.justification: The unified symmetry framework extending beyond permutations to semi-permutations, orthogonal, and invertible transformations is novel and not present in prior work (Git Re-Basin, OT fusion, Sinkhorn Re-Basin). The key insight that Transformers' component-specific symmetries (semi-permutation for multi-head attention inter-head mixing, orthogonal for residual streams with RMSNorm) enable better alignment than permutation-only approaches is new. Achieving zero-barrier LMC for independently trained ViTs and GPT-2 on vision and Tiny Shakespeare is novel for Transformers, advancing beyond prior ResNet results. The multi-model merging via universe matching in this setting is new. While soft permutations build on Sinkhorn-based ideas, their integration into the learned matching framework is novel. The component-specific symmetry analysis for Transformers, though bounded in empirical scope, represents genuine intellectual novelty.

significance.justification: Significance is solid but appropriately bounded by empirical scope. The theoretical contribution—a formal hierarchy of symmetries applicable to neural network components—advances understanding of loss landscape geometry and parameterization redundancy. This framework is conceptually important and provides a lens for analyzing modern architectures. The empirical contribution—zero-barrier LMC for Transformers on vision tasks and Tiny Shakespeare—demonstrates the framework's utility within its tested domain. The practical contribution—three alignment methods with clear algorithives—has utility for model merging, federated learning, and ensemble construction. However, significance is moderated by: (1) vision-centric validation (4 of 5 datasets are vision-related); (2) failure on BookCorpus without satisfactory explanation, limiting confidence in language generalization; (3) small-scale models preventing assessment of scalability to contemporary practice. For a top-tier venue, the theoretical framework and proof-of-concept results on vision are sufficient for acceptance; the work opens important research directions but does not represent a transformative empirical advance. The rebuttal appropriately reframes this as 'establishing proof-of-concept' rather than universal validation.

evaluation.justification: Evaluation is methodologically sound within its scope. Strengths: (1) multiple vision datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny ImageNet) with consistent near-zero results; (2) language datasets (Tiny Shakespeare near-zero, BookCorpus 0.42); (3) three alignment methods enabling fair comparison; (4) ablation studies on sampling strategies (Figure 6) and initialization (Figure 8); (5) convergence analysis (Figure 7); (6) loss surface visualization (Figures 3-4); (7) gap analysis between weight and learned matching (Section 6). Limitations: (1) small models and brief training prevent generalization claims; (2) BookCorpus failure not investigated; (3) ablations limited to single architecture/dataset (CIFAR-10); (4) no comparison to recent Transformer-specific methods beyond Verma & Elbayad (2024). The rebuttal appropriately acknowledges these limitations. The vision results (3 datasets, consistent zero barriers) are convincing within their scope; language results are limited. For acceptance, the robust vision validation plus Tiny Shakespeare success establish proof-of-concept; the BookCorpus anomaly remains concerning but not disqualifying given transparent reporting.

presentation.justification: Presentation is clear and well-organized. Strengths: (1) clear motivation (Figure 1); (2) Table 1 clearly summarizes symmetry hierarchy; (3) Section 3 systematically covers each symmetry class with component examples; (4) Figure 2 effectively illustrates reparameterizations in Transformers; (5) Algorithms 1 is clearly written; (6) Section 6 provides interpretable analysis of methods' differences. Appendices are comprehensive and appropriately detailed (B: experimental setup, C: ablations, D: soft permutations, E: theoretical foundations). Minor areas for improvement noted in submission: (1) reparameterization costs not explicitly stated as one-time preprocessing in main text (Appendix E and rebuttal clarify this, but not Section 3.2.3); (2) semi-permutation definition (linear decomposability) could be introduced earlier; (3) QK/OV circuit notation is dense; (4) Section 4.3 on multi-model merging is somewhat rushed. The rebuttal acknowledges the first issue and proposes adding a clarifying paragraph to Section 3.2.3. Overall, presentation meets standards for a top-tier venue.

reviewers.summary_comment:
This paper makes solid theoretical and empirical contributions to understanding Transformer loss landscape geometry through a unified symmetry framework. The key innovation—formalizing a hierarchy of symmetry classes (permutation ⊂ semi-permutation ⊂ orthogonal ⊂ invertible) tailored to Transformer components—is novel and rigorously developed in Section 3 and Appendix E. The demonstration of zero-barrier linear mode connectivity (LMC) between independently trained ViTs and GPT-2 models on vision tasks (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet) and Tiny Shakespeare represents genuine empirical progress, particularly the width-heterogeneous alignment (Figure 3c). The three alignment strategies are well-motivated and clearly described, with useful analysis of their differences (Section 6).

The work's scope is appropriately bounded and the authors are commendably transparent about limitations. The main limitations are: (1) small-scale experiments (ViT embedding 256-384, GPT-2 with 5 epochs on BookCorpus) that do not validate the claimed architecture-agnostic framework on contemporary models; (2) unresolved BookCorpus language modeling result (0.42 barrier) with no direct investigation to distinguish between alignment failure and genuine solution diversity; (3) lack of explicit clarification in the main text that reparameterizations are one-time preprocessing operations. The rebuttal appropriately characterizes the first as a resource constraint yielding proof-of-concept rather than universal validation, acknowledges the second as an open question warranting future investigation, and proposes straightforward text clarifications for the third.

The authors' second rebuttal demonstrates intellectual honesty by accepting all major concerns without defensive reasoning. They appropriately distinguish between what is demonstrated (vision LMC on small models) and what remains open (language model alignment, scalability to contemporary models). This framing is appropriate for acceptance: the theoretical framework is sound and novel, the vision results are robust within their scope, and the work opens important research directions. The evaluation score of 3 (rather than 4) reflects that the experiments convincingly support claims within their scope but do not provide evidence for the broadest claims about modern Transformers. This is not a weakness disqualifying the paper, but rather an accurate calibration of significance given the empirical domain.

The paper merits acceptance based on its theoretical contributions, proof-of-concept results on vision tasks, and rigorous treatment of a central problem in deep learning. The natural follow-up—validation on larger models and investigation of language model alignment—represents clear and valuable future work for the community. For a top-tier venue, the combination of novel framework and convincing (if limited-scope) empirical validation is sufficient.

## Summary

**Recommended Submission Venue: NeurIPS (fit_score: 8)**

This paper presents a novel theoretical framework and empirical study of neural network loss landscape geometry through symmetry-aware model alignment. It makes solid contributions to understanding Transformers' loss landscapes and demonstrates zero-barrier linear mode connectivity on vision tasks—findings that resonate strongly with NeurIPS's interdisciplinary, foundational research culture.

### Key Findings:

- **ICML (7/10):** Good fit on theoretical grounds and optimization focus, but limited practical scope and unresolved language modeling anomalies weaken its position for a venue valuing real-world applications.

- **NeurIPS (8/10):** Best fit. The paper's breadth (vision + language, multiple datasets, theoretical + empirical), surprising empirical results, and engagement with foundational questions about neural network solutions align well with NeurIPS's multidisciplinary mission and appreciation for proof-of-concept research.

- **ICLR (6/10):** Borderline. While the paper is on-topic for deep learning, the small-scale experiments, Transformer-specific contributions, unresolved language modeling results, and incomplete soft permutation methods create friction with ICLR's expectations for contemporary scale and general applicability.

### Strategic Recommendation:

**Submit to NeurIPS.** The paper is well-executed within its scope, makes novel theoretical and empirical contributions, and the reviewer feedback is constructively supportive (Accept decision). NeurIPS values proof-of-concept results on foundational questions and the interdisciplinary breadth this work demonstrates. The acknowledged limitations (small scale, language modeling failure) are appropriately transparent and do not disqualify the work—they represent clear directions for future research that the community can build upon.

strengths: The paper introduces a unified and formally principled framework that generalizes beyond permutation symmetries to encompass permutations, semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and invertible maps. This hierarchical organization (Table 1) clearly articulates how different symmetry classes relate to specific neural network components, providing theoretical grounding that subsumes prior work like Git Re-Basin as special cases.

Achieving linear mode connectivity (LMC) with zero or near-zero loss barriers for independently trained Vision Transformers and GPT-2 models is a substantial empirical advance. The results demonstrate this is possible even across width-heterogeneous architectures (Figure 3c), extending prior results which required 32× width increases for ResNets. The multi-model alignment results (Figure 4) further demonstrate the approach generalizes beyond pairwise merging.

The paper provides three complementary alignment strategies (activation matching, weight matching, and learned matching) with clear algorithmic descriptions. The learned matching method (Algorithm 1) elegantly handles discrete symmetries through straight-through estimators and continuous symmetries via differentiable projections, while weight matching offers a practical data-free alternative. The analysis in Section 6 identifying where gaps arise between weight and learned matching provides useful insights for future optimization.

The mathematical framework in Section 3 and Appendix E rigorously characterizes symmetries in Transformers component-by-component (feed-forward layers with permutation, multi-head attention with semi-permutation and invertibility, residual streams with orthogonal symmetry). The derivation showing how orthogonal transformations preserve RMSNorm and enable width-heterogeneous alignment (equations 6-8) is technically sound and novel.
weaknesses: Experimental evaluation is limited to small-scale models and datasets. Vision Transformers use embedding dimension 256-384 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet; GPT-2 models are significantly smaller than standard GPT-2 (small/medium/large) and trained on only 5 epochs on BookCorpus. The authors acknowledge these constraints in Appendix A but do not validate whether findings scale to modern model sizes or more realistic training regimes, which is critical for establishing practical significance.

The BookCorpus results exhibit substantially higher loss barriers (0.42 ± 0.01) compared to vision tasks (near-zero), and the paper attributes this to potentially 'fundamentally different solutions' rather than alignment failure. However, this explanation lacks rigorous evidence—no analysis of learned representations, generalization strategies, or solution geometry is provided to support or refute this claim. This unresolved discrepancy undermines confidence in the generality of the approach.

The reparameterization required for theoretical guarantees (e.g., RMSNorm reparameterization in Section 3.2.3, multiplying out QK/OV circuits in attention) alters the network architecture and loses the original parameterization. While functional equivalence is preserved, the paper does not quantify computational overhead, memory requirements, or practical implications of these reparameterizations in real deployment scenarios.

Limited analysis of when and why the approach fails. Besides BookCorpus, there is minimal investigation into failure modes, computational complexity of the alignment algorithms (especially iterative weight matching and Hungarian algorithm for large models), or guidance on hyperparameter selection (e.g., initialization sensitivity shown in Figure 8 but not fully explored across architectures).

soundness.justification: The mathematical framework is rigorous. The symmetry hierarchy (Section 3, Appendix E) correctly characterizes component-specific symmetries. The claim that function-preserving transformations exist under these symmetries is formally justified through detailed derivations (e.g., RMSNorm orthogonal invariance, QK/OV circuit invertibility). The optimization objectives (Equations 1-2) are well-defined. Alignment algorithms (weight matching, learned matching) use sound optimization techniques (Hungarian algorithm, SVD, straight-through estimators, Sinkhorn normalization). The experimental protocol (measuring loss barriers along interpolation paths) is standard and appropriate. No mathematical errors are evident. The main soundness concern is limited scope and missing failure-mode analysis, which is addressed in weaknesses but does not undermine core technical correctness.

novelty.justification: The unified symmetry framework extending beyond permutations to semi-permutations, orthogonal, and invertible transformations is novel. While Git Re-Basin (Ainsworth et al., 2022) and OT fusion (Singh & Jaggi, 2020) handle permutations, this work's formal hierarchy and application to Transformers' richer symmetries is new. The key novel insight is that multi-head attention and residual streams admit semi-permutation and orthogonal symmetries respectively, enabling better alignment. Achieving zero-barrier LMC for independently trained ViTs and GPT-2 is, to the authors' knowledge, the first such result for Transformers—a significant advance over prior work requiring 32× widening for ResNets. Multi-model merging via universe matching in the Transformer setting is novel. While soft permutations (Appendix D) build on Sinkhorn-based methods (Peña et al., 2022), their integration into the learned matching framework is new. The work subsumes prior approaches as special cases while providing genuine extensions.

significance.justification: The work makes three significant contributions: (1) theoretical—a formal framework unifying symmetry classes in neural networks with clear hierarchical organization, advancing understanding of loss landscape geometry; (2) empirical—demonstrating LMC in Transformers for the first time, with implications for model merging, ensembling, and federated learning; (3) practical—providing data-free (weight matching) and supervised (learned matching) alignment methods applicable to real settings. The findings challenge the view of Transformer loss landscapes as fragmented and suggest a more connected geometry under proper symmetry alignment. The multi-model results hint at shared low-loss manifolds. However, significance is somewhat limited by small-scale experiments and unresolved questions about language model alignment. For a top-tier ML venue, the theoretical novelty and empirical advances on Transformers are substantial, but the experimental scope constrains impact. The work opens avenues for future research on model interoperability and understanding modern architectures.

evaluation.justification: The experimental evaluation is methodologically sound but limited in scope. Strengths: (1) multiple datasets (CIFAR-10/100, Tiny ImageNet, Tiny Shakespeare, BookCorpus); (2) multiple alignment methods (activation, weight, learned matching) enabling fair comparisons; (3) ablation studies (Appendix C) on sampling strategies, initialization, iterations; (4) visualization of loss surfaces (Figure 3, 4); (5) analysis of weight/learned matching gap (Section 6). Limitations: (1) small model sizes and datasets; (2) only 5 epochs for BookCorpus (unusual and potentially confounding); (3) no comparison to recent Transformer-specific merging methods (only Verma & Elbayad 2024 mentioned); (4) no error bars or significance tests reported for some results; (5) reproducibility concerns—hyperparameter choices for learned matching not fully justified. The BookCorpus failure lacks root-cause analysis. Results are convincing for vision tasks but inconclusive for language. Wider evaluation on larger models and standard LLM benchmarks would strengthen claims. Overall, evaluation adequately supports central claims but falls short of comprehensive validation at scale.

Appendices are comprehensive and well-organized (B: experimental details, C: ablations, D: soft permutations, E: theory). Notational consistency is maintained. Some areas could be improved: (1) semi-permutation definition (linear decomposability) could be introduced earlier; (2) QK/OV circuit notation is dense; (3) multi-model merging (Section 4.3) feels rushed; (4) connection between soft and hard symmetries in Appendix D could be better integrated. Overall, the paper is accessible to researchers familiar with transformers and model alignment, though deep engagement with Appendix E is needed for full understanding. Presentation quality is suitable for a top-tier venue.

review.summary_comment: This paper makes solid theoretical and empirical contributions to understanding neural network loss landscape geometry through a unified symmetry framework. The three alignment strategies (activation, weight, learned matching) are well-motivated and the analysis isolating where weight and learned matching diverge is insightful. However, the work is constrained by evaluation on small-scale models (ViT embedding dim 256-384, GPT-2 with 5 epochs on BookCorpus), unresolved questions about language model alignment (barrier=0.42), and limited discussion of failure modes and computational complexity. The BookCorpus results suggest the approach may not generalize universally, with the paper's explanation (fundamentally different solutions) being speculative without supporting evidence. The required reparameterizations (RMSNorm, multiplying out circuits) alter architecture but practical implications are unexplored. For a top-tier ML conference, the theoretical framework and empirical advance on Transformers constitute a meaningful contribution, but the limited experimental scope and unresolved questions prevent this from being a strong accept. The work would benefit from evaluation on standard-scale models (ViT-base/large, GPT-2 medium/large) and deeper investigation of when/why the method fails. Nevertheless, the core contributions are sound, novel, and advance our understanding of modern neural network geometry.

strengths: The paper introduces a unified and formally principled framework that generalizes beyond permutation symmetries to encompass permutations, semi-permutations, orthogonal transformations, and invertible maps. This hierarchical organization (Table 1) clearly articulates how different symmetry classes relate to specific neural network components, providing theoretical grounding that subsumes prior work like Git Re-Basin as special cases.

The results demonstrate this is possible even across width-heterogeneous architectures (Figure 3c), extending prior results which required 32× width increases for ResNets. The multi-model alignment results (Figure 4) further demonstrate the approach generalizes beyond pairwise merging.

The learned matching method (Algorithm 1) elegantly handles discrete symmetries through straight-through estimators and continuous symmetries via differentiable projections, while weight matching offers a practical data-free alternative. The analysis in Section 6 identifying where gaps arise between weight and learned matching provides useful insights for future optimization.

The derivation showing how orthogonal transformations preserve RMSNorm and enable width-heterogeneous alignment (equations 6-8) is technically sound and novel.
weaknesses: Experimental evaluation uses small-scale models and datasets, limiting evidence for practical applicability to contemporary architectures. ViTs use embedding dimensions 256-384 on CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet; GPT-2 on BookCorpus is trained for only 5 epochs. The rebuttal argues the framework is scale-invariant in formulation and notes consistent vision results across three datasets, but this does not provide evidence from larger models, only theoretical reasoning about why they should work.
