7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Recasting de novo peptide sequencing as a continuous mass prediction task rather than discrete token classification is creative and provides a principled path toward zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs.

Well-motivated approach: The core insight that amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by mass as a generalizable feature is biochemically sound and addresses a real limitation in existing DNPS models that rely on fixed vocabularies.

Transparent identification of root cause: The paper identifies and articulates the fundamental limitation—that the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation, leading implicit memorization of training-set masses (Section 4.2.1, lines 230-235).
weaknesses: Failed zero-shot learning on experimental data with overstated claims: The paper claims to provide 'a promising proof of concept for zero-shot inference for unseen residues' (Abstract, line 18) but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. This fundamental mismatch between claims and results undermines the submission.

Identified root cause not addressed experimentally: The paper explicitly identifies that 'the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses' (lines 230-235) but does not test standard mitigation strategies such as auxiliary losses, contrastive regularization in mass space, or modified loss functions that would directly address this limitation.

Domain gap remains unresolved despite proposed adversarial approach: The adversarial loss produces negligible improvements (3.18% vs 3.10% for methionine oxidation) and a discriminator AUC of only 0.78 (where >0.9 would indicate effective alignment). This indicates the proposed method is insufficient to bridge simulated-experimental domain shift.

Evaluation limited to teacher-forced inference prevents practical validation: All results use teacher forcing with ground-truth masses provided at each step. This prevents assessment of error accumulation, sequence-level consistency, and end-to-end de novo sequencing capability—the actual task of interest.

Performance degradation on known residues without demonstrated benefit: The model achieves 62.37% amino acid-level recall on seen residues compared to higher performance from classification-based baselines. This trade-off is justified in the paper as enabling zero-shot learning, but zero-shot learning fails to materialize, making the approach strictly worse than baselines.

weakness_details.weakness: Failed zero-shot learning on experimental data with overstated claims: The paper claims to provide 'a promising proof of concept for zero-shot inference for unseen residues' (Abstract, line 18) but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. This fundamental mismatch between claims and results undermines the submission.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (lines 220-235) reports 0.6% recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation and 14.18% for methionine oxidation. Section 4.2.3 (lines 304-306) shows marginal improvements with MTL: 3.18% and 14.41% respectively. The paper's own analysis states 'predictions for cysteine carbamidomethylation showed no enrichment near the correct mass' (line 222). The abstract claims 'we show that our approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising proof of concept' (lines 18-19). Recall rates of 0.6%-14.41% do not constitute 'promising' results or support claims of enabling 'zero-shot' inference. The rebuttal acknowledges the abstract 'should have been more precise' but the submitted paper contains these overstated claims.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The central claim that mass-based representations enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs on experimental data is directly contradicted by reported results. The abstract makes affirmative claims that are not supported by the evidence.

weakness_details.weakness: Identified root cause not addressed experimentally: The paper explicitly identifies that 'the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses' (lines 230-235) but does not test standard mitigation strategies such as auxiliary losses, contrastive regularization in mass space, or modified loss functions that would directly address this limitation.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (lines 230-235) diagnoses the problem: 'Since the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses, the model was not incentivized to learn a truly continuous mass space.' The paper then states this 'might implicitly treat the task as a form of multi-class classification' but does not propose or test solutions within the submitted work. The rebuttal acknowledges this gap: 'We identified that the model implicitly memorizes training-set masses rather than learning continuous representations (Section 4.2.1, lines 230-235), yet we did not test standard ML approaches to address this.' No auxiliary losses, regularization terms, or modified objectives appear in the submitted methods or experiments.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Once the root cause is identified—the training objective does not incentivize extrapolation—the natural experimental progression is to modify the objective to encourage extrapolation. The paper fails to pursue this logical next step.

weakness_details.weakness: Domain gap remains unresolved despite proposed adversarial approach: The adversarial loss produces negligible improvements (3.18% vs 3.10% for methionine oxidation) and a discriminator AUC of only 0.78 (where >0.9 would indicate effective alignment). This indicates the proposed method is insufficient to bridge simulated-experimental domain shift.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.4 (lines 307-329) proposes adversarial learning but results show: (1) Discriminator AUC of 0.78 (line 324), indicating incomplete alignment; (2) Recall improvements negligible: methionine oxidation 3.18% vs 3.10%, cysteine carbamidomethylation 14.41% vs 15.11% (lines 328-329); (3) MSE losses 'similar' between MTL and GAN-inspired models (line 330). The rebuttal acknowledges 'the discriminator AUC of 0.78 (where 0.5 is random) indicates the model can still meaningfully distinguish simulated from experimental spectra, which suggests incomplete alignment' and that 'the adversarial term is not providing the intended benefit.' These admissions confirm the proposed solution is ineffective.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper proposes adversarial alignment as a solution to domain shift. The empirical results demonstrate this approach fails to meaningfully align representations or improve generalization.

weakness_details.weakness: Evaluation limited to teacher-forced inference prevents practical validation: All results use teacher forcing with ground-truth masses provided at each step. This prevents assessment of error accumulation, sequence-level consistency, and end-to-end de novo sequencing capability—the actual task of interest.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.1 (lines 192-197) states: 'For evaluation, we ran the model in inference mode using teacher forcing...the model is supplied with the ground truth masses of all previously decoded residues at each prediction step.' Limitations section (lines 341-345) acknowledges: 'Although we show that mass-based modeling can overcome vocabulary constraints, the current framework has only been evaluated under teacher-forced decoding.' No end-to-end autoregressive evaluation is provided in the submitted paper. The rebuttal acknowledges this is 'a fundamental gap' that prevents validation of 'practical de novo sequencing capability.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper claims to enable de novo peptide sequencing. Teacher forcing evaluation does not demonstrate this; it artificially removes the key challenges of sequencing (error accumulation and sequence consistency). Practical viability cannot be assessed from the submitted results.

weakness_details.weakness: Performance degradation on known residues without demonstrated benefit: The model achieves 62.37% amino acid-level recall on seen residues compared to higher performance from classification-based baselines. This trade-off is justified in the paper as enabling zero-shot learning, but zero-shot learning fails to materialize, making the approach strictly worse than baselines.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (line 206) reports 62.37% recall for seen residues. Lines 211-217 acknowledge this is 'somewhat lower than those reported by classification-based transformer models such as AdaNovo' but justify it as a trade-off for 'generalization to modified residues beyond the training set' (lines 217-219). However, generalization fails: Section 4.2.3 reports only 3.18% recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation and 14.41% for methionine oxidation (lines 304-306). The rebuttal states: 'the mass regression approach sacrifices accuracy on known residues (62.37% recall vs. higher for AdaNovo) based on the premise that zero-shot learning capability justifies this trade-off. However, zero-shot learning fails to materialize (0.6%-14.41% recall), making the approach strictly worse than baselines.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper explicitly trades off performance on known residues for improved generalization to unseen residues. With generalization failing, the approach offers no compensating benefit over baselines.

soundness.justification: While the technical approach (mass regression, MTL, adversarial alignment) is sound in isolation, the central claims are not supported by the evidence. The paper claims to enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. The paper identifies the root cause—training objective does not incentivize extrapolation—but does not test standard solutions. The proposed adversarial approach is ineffective (0.78 AUC discriminator, negligible recall improvement). The rebuttal does not provide new in-paper evidence resolving these issues; it merely acknowledges them and proposes solutions that are not in the submitted work. Evaluation is further compromised by reliance on teacher forcing, which bypasses practical sequencing constraints. The submission fails the soundness gate because affirmative claims are contradicted by submitted evidence, and identified limitations are not addressed experimentally.

novelty.justification: The reformulation of DNPS as mass prediction rather than token classification is novel. The combination of mass regression with MTL on simulated and experimental spectra, coupled with adversarial alignment, represents a reasonable methodological contribution. However, novelty is substantially diminished by the lack of empirical validation of the core hypothesis and the identification of fundamental limitations that undermine the motivating principles.

significance.justification: For a top-tier ML venue, the work must either achieve stated goals or provide significant insights that advance understanding and enable future progress. This paper achieves neither. Zero-shot learning fails on experimental data (0.6%-14.41% recall). The identified insights—that mass-based regression implicitly memorizes training masses and that domain shift cannot be resolved by the proposed approach—are diagnosed but not addressed with tested solutions. The paper does not provide actionable mechanistic insights explaining why mass-based approaches fail or how they could be fixed. The rebuttal agrees that 'framing the work as identifying limitations of mass-based approaches does not retroactively establish significance without deeper mechanistic insights or actionable solutions in the submitted work.' Without new solutions, tested mitigation strategies, or deeper analysis in the submission, this represents an incomplete negative result insufficient for a top-tier venue.

reviewers.summary_comment: The author's second rebuttal demonstrates commendable intellectual honesty by fully acknowledging all major criticisms and agreeing with the reviewer's assessment that the submission fails to support its central claims. The authors concede that: (1) zero-shot learning fails on experimental data (0.6%-14.41% recall contradicts 'promising' claims in the abstract); (2) the identified root cause (lack of extrapolation incentive) was not addressed experimentally, representing a methodological gap; (3) the adversarial approach is ineffective (0.78 AUC discriminator, minimal improvement); (4) teacher forcing prevents practical validation; and (5) degraded performance on known residues is not justified without corresponding zero-shot benefit. The rebuttal correctly notes that acknowledging problems is not the same as solving them within the submitted work. The authors identify exactly what the submission should have contained—testing of loss modifications, end-to-end evaluation, stronger domain alignment investigation, broader modification evaluation, and baseline comparisons—but none of these are present in the paper under review. This represents a completed work that is honest about its limitations but incomplete in its execution and insufficient for publication at a selective top-tier venue. While the core idea (mass-based representations for open-search DNPS) has merit and could potentially be viable with appropriate modifications, the current submission does not demonstrate this. The paper makes affirmative claims that are contradicted by evidence, identifies but does not experimentally address the root cause of failure, proposes but does not effectively implement a solution (adversarial alignment), and evaluates the method under artificial constraints (teacher forcing) that prevent assessment of practical applicability. The work would benefit from the additional experiments and analyses the reviewer suggested, but as submitted, it does not meet the standards of a top-tier venue.

## Summary

**Overall Assessment:**

This paper presents a creative reformulation of de novo peptide sequencing from discrete classification to continuous mass prediction, motivated by the goal of achieving zero-shot generalization to unseen post-translational modifications (PTMs). However, the work suffers from a **fundamental disconnect between claims and evidence** that severely limits its suitability for top-tier venues.

**Core Problems (per Reviewer 1):**

1. **Failed Core Promise**: Claims "zero-shot inference for unseen residues" but achieves only 0.6%–14.41% recall on held-out modifications.
2. **Diagnosed but Unaddressed Root Cause**: Explicitly identifies that "the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation" but does not test standard solutions.
3. **Ineffective Proposed Solution**: Adversarial alignment produces 0.78 AUC (incomplete) and negligible improvements (3.18% vs. 3.10%).
4. **Artificial Evaluation**: All results use teacher forcing, preventing end-to-end validation of the sequencing task.
5. **Performance Degradation Without Benefit**: Sacrifices 62.37% recall on known residues (vs. baselines) to enable zero-shot learning, which then fails.

**Venue-Specific Fit:**

- **ICML (4/10)**: While the application and MTL approach fit thematic scope, the fundamental failure of the core methodology and incomplete experimental validation (unaddressed root causes, ineffective solutions) make this unsuitable. ICML values robust methodological contributions; this work is neither an advance nor a conclusive negative result with actionable insights.

- **NeurIPS (4/10)**: Despite NeurIPS's openness to exploratory interdisciplinary work, the overstated claims contradicted by evidence, unaddressed identified problems, and ineffective proposed solution violate the bar even for proof-of-concept work. NeurIPS expects honesty about limitations (which the paper has) but also either evidence supporting claims or deep actionable insights (which it lacks).

- **ICLR (5/10)**: Closest fit due to focus on representation learning and domain adaptation. The mass-based representation learning idea is conceptually interesting. However, the fundamental failure of the learned representations to generalize, combined with ineffective alignment and lack of deeper mechanistic analysis, undermines the core contribution. ICLR would expect richer investigation of what representations are learned and why they fail.

**Recommendation**: This paper would benefit from addressing the identified root causes experimentally before resubmission. Testing loss modifications, end-to-end evaluation, stronger domain alignment, and broader modification evaluation would either salvage the approach or yield deeper insights into why mass-based representations fail—both of which would strengthen publication prospects.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Recasting de novo peptide sequencing as a continuous mass prediction task rather than discrete token classification is creative and provides a principled path toward zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs.

Well-motivated approach: The core insight that amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by mass as a generalizable feature is biochemically sound and addresses a real limitation in existing DNPS models that rely on fixed vocabularies.
Clear presentation: The paper is generally well-written with good motivation, clear description of methods, and honest discussion of limitations and failure modes.
weaknesses: Failed zero-shot learning on experimental data: Despite the motivation for zero-shot learning capability, the model achieves extremely poor generalization to unseen PTMs on real data (0.6%-14.41% recall for held-out modifications), fundamentally undermining the central claim.

Domain gap not adequately addressed: The large gap between simulated and experimental spectra (Pearson correlation of -0.11 to 0.19 when training on simple simulations) remains largely unresolved. The adversarial loss provides minimal improvement (3.18% vs 3.10% recall), suggesting the proposed MTL and GAN-inspired approach is insufficient.

Evaluation limited to teacher-forced inference: All results use teacher forcing with ground-truth masses provided at each step. This isolated mass prediction from sequence-level errors but prevents assessment of the model's ability to perform end-to-end de novo sequencing—the actual practical requirement.

Degraded performance on known residues: The mass regression approach sacrifices 62.37% amino acid-level recall for seen residues compared to classification-based baselines like AdaNovo. This trade-off is substantial and not adequately justified given the failure to achieve zero-shot learning.

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: While the paper acknowledges that the model treats the task as implicit classification over training-set masses, it does not convincingly explain why standard regularization or explicit incentives for extrapolation (e.g., auxiliary losses encouraging coverage of continuous mass space) were not explored.

Limited experimental scope: Evaluation on only two held-out modifications (methionine oxidation, cysteine carbamidomethylation) is narrow. No evaluation on truly novel, chemically distinct modifications or systematic analysis of which types of modifications are predictable.

The degraded performance on known residues (62.37% vs. baselines) combined with failed zero-shot learning indicates the approach does not advance the field. evaluation.justification: Evaluation has multiple critical gaps: (1) Teacher forcing prevents end-to-end validation; (2) Only two held-out modifications evaluated, limiting generalization claims; (3) No quantitative comparison to recent baselines (AdaNovo, π-PrimeNovo) under identical settings; (4) Adversarial loss effectiveness questioned by minimal improvement and 0.78 AUC; (5) No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for low-performance regimes. The rebuttal acknowledges these gaps but does not provide corrected results in the submitted paper. The authors propose future experiments (end-to-end evaluation, systematic evaluation across modification types, baseline comparisons) but these are not present in the submission, which is what must be evaluated.

presentation.justification: The paper is clearly written with good motivation, adequate background, and transparent discussion of limitations. Figures are informative and results are presented honestly. The acknowledgment of failures (e.g., lines 230-235 identifying implicit memorization, lines 341-345 acknowledging teacher forcing limitation) demonstrates intellectual integrity. However, clarity of presentation does not compensate for fundamental soundness and significance failures.

review.summary_comment: The rebuttal demonstrates good faith engagement with the review by acknowledging all major criticisms and agreeing that zero-shot learning has failed on experimental data, domain shift remains unresolved, and teacher forcing prevents practical validation. Notably, the authors reframe the contribution as identifying 'limitations of mass-based approaches' rather than advancing solutions. While this intellectual honesty is commendable, it does not address the core problem: the submitted paper makes affirmative claims about enabling zero-shot DNPS ('promising proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search DNPS') that are contradicted by empirical results. The rebuttal proposes valuable suggestions for future work (explicit losses encouraging extrapolation, stronger domain adaptation, end-to-end evaluation, systematic evaluation across modification types) but none of these solutions are present in the submitted paper. Evaluation must be based on what is submitted, not what the authors promise to do. The submitted work presents negative results—mass-based regression with MTL and adversarial alignment fails to achieve zero-shot learning—without providing sufficient analysis, insights, or alternative solutions to make these negative results significant. For a top-tier ML conference, papers presenting negative results can be valuable if they provide deep mechanistic insights or suggest actionable paths forward. This work identifies that the model implicitly memorizes training-set masses rather than learning continuous representations, but does not explore why standard regularization or loss modifications fail to address this, nor does it test such solutions. The combination of failed central claim, degraded baseline performance, limited evaluation scope, and insufficient analysis of root causes prevents acceptance.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Recasting de novo peptide sequencing as a continuous mass prediction task rather than discrete token classification is creative and provides a principled path toward zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs.

Well-motivated approach: The core insight that amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by mass as a generalizable feature is biochemically sound and addresses a real limitation in existing DNPS models that rely on fixed vocabularies.

Transparent identification of root cause: The paper identifies and articulates the fundamental limitation—that the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation, leading implicit memorization of training-set masses (Section 4.2.1, lines 230-235).
weaknesses: Failed zero-shot learning on experimental data with overstated claims: The paper claims to provide 'a promising proof of concept for zero-shot inference for unseen residues' (Abstract, line 18) but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. This fundamental mismatch between claims and results undermines the submission.

Identified root cause not addressed experimentally: The paper explicitly identifies that 'the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses' (lines 230-235) but does not test standard mitigation strategies such as auxiliary losses, contrastive regularization in mass space, or modified loss functions that would directly address this limitation.

Domain gap remains unresolved despite proposed adversarial approach: The adversarial loss produces negligible improvements (3.18% vs 3.10% for methionine oxidation) and a discriminator AUC of only 0.78 (where >0.9 would indicate effective alignment). This indicates the proposed method is insufficient to bridge simulated-experimental domain shift.

Evaluation limited to teacher-forced inference prevents practical validation: All results use teacher forcing with ground-truth masses provided at each step. This prevents assessment of error accumulation, sequence-level consistency, and end-to-end de novo sequencing capability—the actual task of interest.

Performance degradation on known residues without demonstrated benefit: The model achieves 62.37% amino acid-level recall on seen residues compared to higher performance from classification-based baselines. This trade-off is justified in the paper as enabling zero-shot learning, but zero-shot learning fails to materialize, making the approach strictly worse than baselines.

weakness_details.weakness: Failed zero-shot learning on experimental data with overstated claims: The paper claims to provide 'a promising proof of concept for zero-shot inference for unseen residues' (Abstract, line 18) but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. This fundamental mismatch between claims and results undermines the submission.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (lines 220-235) reports 0.6% recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation and 14.18% for methionine oxidation. Section 4.2.3 (lines 304-306) shows marginal improvements with MTL: 3.18% and 14.41% respectively. The paper's own analysis states 'predictions for cysteine carbamidomethylation showed no enrichment near the correct mass' (line 222). The abstract claims 'we show that our approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising proof of concept' (lines 18-19). Recall rates of 0.6%-14.41% do not constitute 'promising' results or support claims of enabling 'zero-shot' inference. The rebuttal acknowledges the abstract 'should have been more precise' but the submitted paper contains these overstated claims.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The central claim that mass-based representations enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs on experimental data is directly contradicted by reported results. The abstract makes affirmative claims that are not supported by the evidence.

weakness_details.weakness: Identified root cause not addressed experimentally: The paper explicitly identifies that 'the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses' (lines 230-235) but does not test standard mitigation strategies such as auxiliary losses, contrastive regularization in mass space, or modified loss functions that would directly address this limitation.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (lines 230-235) diagnoses the problem: 'Since the training objective does not explicitly encourage extrapolation to unseen masses, the model was not incentivized to learn a truly continuous mass space.' The paper then states this 'might implicitly treat the task as a form of multi-class classification' but does not propose or test solutions within the submitted work. The rebuttal acknowledges this gap: 'We identified that the model implicitly memorizes training-set masses rather than learning continuous representations (Section 4.2.1, lines 230-235), yet we did not test standard ML approaches to address this.' No auxiliary losses, regularization terms, or modified objectives appear in the submitted methods or experiments.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Once the root cause is identified—the training objective does not incentivize extrapolation—the natural experimental progression is to modify the objective to encourage extrapolation. The paper fails to pursue this logical next step.

weakness_details.weakness: Domain gap remains unresolved despite proposed adversarial approach: The adversarial loss produces negligible improvements (3.18% vs 3.10% for methionine oxidation) and a discriminator AUC of only 0.78 (where >0.9 would indicate effective alignment). This indicates the proposed method is insufficient to bridge simulated-experimental domain shift.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.4 (lines 307-329) proposes adversarial learning but results show: (1) Discriminator AUC of 0.78 (line 324), indicating incomplete alignment; (2) Recall improvements negligible: methionine oxidation 3.18% vs 3.10%, cysteine carbamidomethylation 14.41% vs 15.11% (lines 328-329); (3) MSE losses 'similar' between MTL and GAN-inspired models (line 330). The rebuttal acknowledges 'the discriminator AUC of 0.78 (where 0.5 is random) indicates the model can still meaningfully distinguish simulated from experimental spectra, which suggests incomplete alignment' and that 'the adversarial term is not providing the intended benefit.' These admissions confirm the proposed solution is ineffective.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper proposes adversarial alignment as a solution to domain shift. The empirical results demonstrate this approach fails to meaningfully align representations or improve generalization.

weakness_details.weakness: Evaluation limited to teacher-forced inference prevents practical validation: All results use teacher forcing with ground-truth masses provided at each step. This prevents assessment of error accumulation, sequence-level consistency, and end-to-end de novo sequencing capability—the actual task of interest.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.1 (lines 192-197) states: 'For evaluation, we ran the model in inference mode using teacher forcing...the model is supplied with the ground truth masses of all previously decoded residues at each prediction step.' Limitations section (lines 341-345) acknowledges: 'Although we show that mass-based modeling can overcome vocabulary constraints, the current framework has only been evaluated under teacher-forced decoding.' No end-to-end autoregressive evaluation is provided in the submitted paper. The rebuttal acknowledges this is 'a fundamental gap' that prevents validation of 'practical de novo sequencing capability.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper claims to enable de novo peptide sequencing. Teacher forcing evaluation does not demonstrate this; it artificially removes the key challenges of sequencing (error accumulation and sequence consistency). Practical viability cannot be assessed from the submitted results.

weakness_details.weakness: Performance degradation on known residues without demonstrated benefit: The model achieves 62.37% amino acid-level recall on seen residues compared to higher performance from classification-based baselines. This trade-off is justified in the paper as enabling zero-shot learning, but zero-shot learning fails to materialize, making the approach strictly worse than baselines.
weakness_details.evidence: Section 4.2.1 (line 206) reports 62.37% recall for seen residues. Lines 211-217 acknowledge this is 'somewhat lower than those reported by classification-based transformer models such as AdaNovo' but justify it as a trade-off for 'generalization to modified residues beyond the training set' (lines 217-219). However, generalization fails: Section 4.2.3 reports only 3.18% recall for cysteine carbamidomethylation and 14.41% for methionine oxidation (lines 304-306). The rebuttal states: 'the mass regression approach sacrifices accuracy on known residues (62.37% recall vs. higher for AdaNovo) based on the premise that zero-shot learning capability justifies this trade-off. However, zero-shot learning fails to materialize (0.6%-14.41% recall), making the approach strictly worse than baselines.'
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper explicitly trades off performance on known residues for improved generalization to unseen residues. With generalization failing, the approach offers no compensating benefit over baselines.

soundness.justification: While the technical approach (mass regression, MTL, adversarial alignment) is sound in isolation, the central claims are not supported by the evidence. The paper claims to enable zero-shot learning for unseen PTMs but achieves only 0.6%-14.41% recall on held-out modifications. The paper identifies the root cause—training objective does not incentivize extrapolation—but does not test standard solutions. The proposed adversarial approach is ineffective (0.78 AUC discriminator, negligible recall improvement). The rebuttal does not provide new in-paper evidence resolving these issues; it merely acknowledges them and proposes solutions that are not in the submitted work. Evaluation is further compromised by reliance on teacher forcing, which bypasses practical sequencing constraints. The submission fails the soundness gate because affirmative claims are contradicted by submitted evidence, and identified limitations are not addressed experimentally.

novelty.justification: The reformulation of DNPS as mass prediction rather than token classification is novel. The combination of mass regression with MTL on simulated and experimental spectra, coupled with adversarial alignment, represents a reasonable methodological contribution. However, novelty is substantially diminished by the lack of empirical validation of the core hypothesis and the identification of fundamental limitations that undermine the motivating principles.

significance.justification: For a top-tier ML venue, the work must either achieve stated goals or provide significant insights that advance understanding and enable future progress. This paper achieves neither. Zero-shot learning fails on experimental data (0.6%-14.41% recall). The identified insights—that mass-based regression implicitly memorizes training masses and that domain shift cannot be resolved by the proposed approach—are diagnosed but not addressed with tested solutions. The paper does not provide actionable mechanistic insights explaining why mass-based approaches fail or how they could be fixed. The rebuttal agrees that 'framing the work as identifying limitations of mass-based approaches does not retroactively establish significance without deeper mechanistic insights or actionable solutions in the submitted work.' Without new solutions, tested mitigation strategies, or deeper analysis in the submission, this represents an incomplete negative result insufficient for a top-tier venue.

evaluation.justification: Evaluation has multiple critical gaps not addressed in the submitted paper: (1) Teacher forcing prevents end-to-end validation—no autoregressive evaluation provided; (2) Only two held-out modifications evaluated (methionine oxidation, cysteine carbamidomethylation), limiting generalization claims; (3) No quantitative comparison to recent baselines (AdaNovo, π-PrimeNovo, ContraNovo) under identical settings; (4) Adversarial loss effectiveness questioned by minimal improvement (3.18% vs 3.10%) and incomplete discriminator alignment (0.78 AUC); (5) No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for low-performance regimes; (6) No ablation studies on loss component contributions. The rebuttal acknowledges these gaps but does not provide corrected results within the submitted paper. Evaluation must be based on the submitted work, which is incomplete.

presentation.justification: The paper is clearly written with good motivation, adequate background, and transparent discussion of limitations. The acknowledgment of failures and root causes demonstrates intellectual integrity. Figures are informative and results are presented honestly, including negative findings. However, presentation clarity does not compensate for fundamental soundness and significance failures, nor does it resolve the disconnect between claims and evidence.

review.summary_comment: The author's second rebuttal demonstrates commendable intellectual honesty by fully acknowledging all major criticisms and agreeing with the reviewer's assessment that the submission fails to support its central claims. The authors concede that: (1) zero-shot learning fails on experimental data (0.6%-14.41% recall contradicts 'promising' claims in the abstract); (2) the identified root cause (lack of extrapolation incentive) was not addressed experimentally, representing a methodological gap; (3) the adversarial approach is ineffective (0.78 AUC discriminator, minimal improvement); (4) teacher forcing prevents practical validation; and (5) degraded performance on known residues is not justified without corresponding zero-shot benefit. The rebuttal correctly notes that acknowledging problems is not the same as solving them within the submitted work. The authors identify exactly what the submission should have contained—testing of loss modifications, end-to-end evaluation, stronger domain alignment investigation, broader modification evaluation, and baseline comparisons—but none of these are present in the paper under review. This represents a completed work that is honest about its limitations but incomplete in its execution and insufficient for publication at a selective top-tier venue. While the core idea (mass-based representations for open-search DNPS) has merit and could potentially be viable with appropriate modifications, the current submission does not demonstrate this. The paper makes affirmative claims that are contradicted by evidence, identifies but does not experimentally address the root cause of failure, proposes but does not effectively implement a solution (adversarial alignment), and evaluates the method under artificial constraints (teacher forcing) that prevent assessment of practical applicability. The work would benefit from the additional experiments and analyses the reviewer suggested, but as submitted, it does not meet the standards of a top-tier venue.

target_paper_summary.title: Towards Open-Search De Novo Peptide Sequencing Via Mass-Based Zero-Shot Learning
target_paper_summary.abstract: 1 Proteins are the main drivers of biochemical processes and play a pivotal role in 2 almost all cellular functions. Through post-translational modifications (PTMs), 3 residues within a protein can be chemically modified to fine-tune the protein's 4 function in the cellular context. Despite the importance of PTMs, the plethora 5 of deep learning-based de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) models, which, in 6 contrast to database searching approaches, predict peptide sequence solely from 7 tandem mass spectra without any reference organism database, can only predict 8 peptide sequences with a limited set of PTMs. This is because they rely on fixed 9 vocabularies that map residue tokens to non-generalizable learned embeddings. To 10 overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning. Specifically, we reformulate DNPS as a 13 mass prediction problem instead of a multiclass classification problem, where the 14 model predicts the mass of the next residue instead of its token representation. To 15 facilitate generalization to unseen PTMs, we leverage an adversarial multi-task 16 learning scheme by supplementing the training data of experimental spectra with 17 simulated spectra that mimic spectra containing unseen residues. We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.
claims: we propose a novel approach that leverages the fact that 11 amino acids and their derivatives are characterized by their mass, a generalizable 12 feature that enables zero-shot learning.
We show that our 18 approach allows the prediction of previously unseen PTMs, providing a promising 19 proof of concept for mass-based representations as a path towards true open-search 20 DNPS.

paper_metadata.title: Predicting glycan structure from tandem mass spectrometry via deep learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Glycans constitute the most complicated post-translational modification, modulating protein activity in health and disease. However, structural annotation from tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) data is a bottleneck in glycomics, preventing high-throughput endeavors and relegating glycomics to a few experts. Trained on a newly curated set of 500,000 annotated MS/MS spectra, here we present CandyCrunch, a dilated residual neural network predicting glycan structure from raw liquid chromatography-MS/MS data in seconds (top-1 accuracy: 90.3%). We developed an open-access Python-based workflow of raw data conversion and prediction, followed by automated curation and fragment annotation, with predictions recapitulating and extending expert annotation. We demonstrate that this can be used for de novo annotation, diagnostic fragment identification and high-throughput glycomics. For maximum impact, this entire pipeline is tightly interlaced with our glycowork platform and can be easily tested at https://colab.research.google.com/github/BojarLab/CandyCrunch/blob/main/CandyCrunch.ipynb . We envision CandyCrunch to democratize structural glycomics and the elucidation of biological roles of glycans.

paper_metadata.title: Opportunities and obstacles for deep learning in biology and medicine
paper_metadata.abstract: Abstract Deep learning, which describes a class of machine learning algorithms, has recently showed impressive results across a variety of domains. Biology and medicine are data rich, but the data are complex and often ill-understood. Problems of this nature may be particularly well-suited to deep learning techniques. We examine applications of deep learning to a variety of biomedical problems—patient classification, fundamental biological processes, and treatment of patients—and discuss whether deep learning will transform these tasks or if the biomedical sphere poses unique challenges. We find that deep learning has yet to revolutionize or definitively resolve any of these problems, but promising advances have been made on the prior state of the art. Even when improvement over a previous baseline has been modest, we have seen signs that deep learning methods may speed or aid human investigation. More work is needed to address concerns related to interpretability and how to best model each problem. Furthermore, the limited amount of labeled data for training presents problems in some domains, as do legal and privacy constraints on work with sensitive health records. Nonetheless, we foresee deep learning powering changes at both bench and bedside with the potential to transform several areas of biology and medicine.

paper_metadata.title: Prediction of glycopeptide fragment mass spectra by deep learning
paper_metadata.abstract: Deep learning has achieved a notable success in mass spectrometry-based proteomics and is now emerging in glycoproteomics. While various deep learning models can predict fragment mass spectra of peptides with good accuracy, they cannot cope with the non-linear glycan structure in an intact glycopeptide. Herein, we present DeepGlyco, a deep learning-based approach for the prediction of fragment spectra of intact glycopeptides. Our model adopts tree-structured long-short term memory networks to process the glycan moiety and a graph neural network architecture to incorporate potential fragmentation pathways of a specific glycan structure. This feature is beneficial to model explainability and differentiation ability of glycan structural isomers. We further demonstrate that predicted spectral libraries can be used for data-independent acquisition glycoproteomics as a supplement for library completeness. We expect that this work will provide a valuable deep learning resource for glycoproteomics.

paper_metadata.title: Deep learning and generative methods in cheminformatics and chemical biology: navigating small molecule space intelligently
paper_metadata.abstract: The number of 'small' molecules that may be of interest to chemical biologists - chemical space - is enormous, but the fraction that have ever been made is tiny. Most strategies are discriminative, i.e. have involved 'forward' problems (have molecule, establish properties). However, we normally wish to solve the much harder generative or inverse problem (describe desired properties, find molecule). 'Deep' (machine) learning based on large-scale neural networks underpins technologies such as computer vision, natural language processing, driverless cars, and world-leading performance in games such as Go; it can also be applied to the solution of inverse problems in chemical biology. In particular, recent developments in deep learning admit the in silico generation of candidate molecular structures and the prediction of their properties, thereby allowing one to navigate (bio)chemical space intelligently. These methods are revolutionary but require an understanding of both (bio)chemistry and computer science to be exploited to best advantage. We give a high-level (non-mathematical) background to the deep learning revolution, and set out the crucial issue for chemical biology and informatics as a two-way mapping from the discrete nature of individual molecules to the continuous but high-dimensional latent representation that may best reflect chemical space. A variety of architectures can do this; we focus on a particular type known as variational autoencoders. We then provide some examples of recent successes of these kinds of approach, and a look towards the future.

paper_metadata.title: Diffusion models in bioinformatics and computational biology
xTrimoPGLM: Unified 100B-Scale Pre-trained Transformer for Deciphering the Language of Protein
paper_metadata.abstract: Protein language models have shown remarkable success in learning biological information from protein sequences. However, most existing models are limited by either autoencoding or autoregressive pre-training objectives, which makes them struggle to handle protein understanding and generation tasks concurrently. We propose a unified protein language model, xTrimoPGLM, to address these two types of tasks simultaneously through an innovative pre-training framework. Our key technical contribution is an exploration of the compatibility and the potential for joint optimization of the two types of objectives, which has led to a strategy for training xTrimoPGLM at an unprecedented scale of 100 billion parameters and 1 trillion training tokens. Our extensive experiments reveal that 1) xTrimoPGLM significantly outperforms other advanced baselines in 18 protein understanding benchmarks across four categories. The model also facilitates an atomic-resolution view of protein structures, leading to an advanced 3D structural prediction model that surpasses existing language model-based tools. 2) xTrimoPGLM not only can generate de novo protein sequences following the principles of natural ones, but also can perform programmable generation after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated sequences. These results highlight the substantial capability and versatility of xTrimoPGLM in understanding and generating protein sequences, contributing to the evolving landscape of foundation models in protein science. Trained weight for the xTrimoPGLM model, and downstream datasets are available at https://huggingface.co/proteinglm .

paper_metadata.title: Exploration of cell state heterogeneity using single-cell proteomics through sensitivity-tailored data-independent acquisition
paper_metadata.abstract: Single-cell resolution analysis of complex biological tissues is fundamental to capture cell-state heterogeneity and distinct cellular signaling patterns that remain obscured with population-based techniques. The limited amount of material encapsulated in a single cell however, raises significant technical challenges to molecular profiling. Due to extensive optimization efforts, single-cell proteomics by Mass Spectrometry (scp-MS) has emerged as a powerful tool to facilitate proteome profiling from ultra-low amounts of input, although further development is needed to realize its full potential. To this end, we carry out comprehensive analysis of orbitrap-based data-independent acquisition (DIA) for limited material proteomics. Notably, we find a fundamental difference between optimal DIA methods for high- and low-load samples. We further improve our low-input DIA method by relying on high-resolution MS1 quantification, thus enhancing sensitivity by more efficiently utilizing available mass analyzer time. With our ultra-low input tailored DIA method, we are able to accommodate long injection times and high resolution, while keeping the scan cycle time low enough to ensure robust quantification. Finally, we demonstrate the capability of our approach by profiling mouse embryonic stem cell culture conditions, showcasing heterogeneity in global proteomes and highlighting distinct differences in key metabolic enzyme expression in distinct cell subclusters.

7.desc: Related-work RAG, 3 iterations, 1 neutral reviewer, author rebuttal, no AI Detector

strengths: Novel approach to single-step sampling from unnormalized distributions: The paper presents two well-motivated methods (CDDS and SCDS) that extend consistency distillation to a new setting. SCDS's self-consistent training without requiring pre-trained models is innovative, enabling end-to-end learning of both diffusion sampling and consistency.

Strong theoretical foundation for CDDS: Theorem 1 provides rigorous analysis of consistency distillation convergence with respect to ODE discretization error. The mathematical framework connecting consistency loss to probability flow ODE is sound.

Substantial computational efficiency gains: The paper demonstrates dramatic reduction in NFEs (1-2 steps vs 256 steps) with break-even analysis showing practical amortization. Figure 3 clearly shows the efficiency-quality tradeoff.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (synthetic and real-world), metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z), and baselines. Algorithms are clearly specified and implementation details are provided.

Flexible multi-step inference capability: Unlike pure consistency models, SCDS maintains the option to trade computational cost for improved sample quality at inference time, providing practical flexibility.
weaknesses: CDDS severely underperforms on several benchmarks (51× worse Sinkhorn on MW54, Funnel) with inadequate explanation in the submitted paper and contradictory statements in Section 6.1

SCDS single-step quality fails to match the abstract's claim of 'high-fidelity samples': Table 1 shows 3-10× worse performance than multi-step baselines on realistic tasks (MW54, Funnel, MW52), with ESS degeneracy on Funnel

Normalization constant estimation advantage is misrepresented: Section 5.3 (lines 231-236) presents log Z estimation as an advantage while lines 268-269 acknowledge single-step sampling produces biased (overestimated) evidence, creating internal contradiction not resolved in text
SCDS convergence lacks theoretical justification: Joint optimization of sampling loss and self-consistency loss has no formal convergence analysis; Theorem 1 applies only to CDDS

weakness_details.weakness: CDDS severely underperforms on several benchmarks (51× worse Sinkhorn on MW54, Funnel) with inadequate explanation in the submitted paper and contradictory statements in Section 6.1
weakness_details.evidence: Table 1 shows CDDS Sinkhorn distance 6.2804 on MW54 vs 0.1230 for 256-step DIS (51× worse); |ΔlogZ| is 6766 vs 1.2 (5520× worse). On Funnel: CDDS Sinkhorn 10.5 vs baseline 5.2 (2× worse). However, Section 6.1 lines 261-271 state 'On the low-dimensional GMM and MW54 targets, CDDS attains Sinkhorn values with a factor less than double the DIS baseline.' This directly contradicts the 51× degradation observed in Table 1. Lines 284-288 acknowledge CDDS is 'less accurate than SCDS' but do not explain the failure modes or provide ablation. The rebuttal provides post-hoc explanations (teacher discretization mismatch, mode structure) but these are absent from the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: CDDS is proposed as demonstrating that 'consistency distillation can be accomplished within sampling contexts' (lines 7-8), but severe performance degradation on realistic benchmarks without explanation undermines this claim in its current form.

weakness_details.weakness: SCDS single-step quality fails to match the abstract's claim of 'high-fidelity samples': Table 1 shows 3-10× worse performance than multi-step baselines on realistic tasks (MW54, Funnel, MW52), with ESS degeneracy on Funnel
weakness_details.evidence: Abstract lines 6-7 state methods 'generate high-fidelity samples in a single step.' Without theoretical grounding, SCDS is an empirically-motivated heuristic, and the poor single-step results on realistic tasks (MW54, Funnel, MW52 in Table 1) raise questions about whether empirical validation is sufficient.

These are not minor clarity issues but fundamental inconsistencies between claims and evidence that mislead readers.

Computational efficiency gains are substantial. However, the submitted paper contains critical presentation failures and internal inconsistencies that materially weaken it: (1) The abstract claims 'high-fidelity samples in a single step,' but Table 1 demonstrates single-step SCDS is 3-10× worse than baselines on realistic benchmarks (MW54, Funnel, MW52), with degenerate ESS on Funnel. Section 6.1 contradicts this by claiming high-fidelity on these same benchmarks. (2) CDDS severely underperforms on MW54 (51× worse Sinkhorn) and Funnel (2× worse), but Section 6.1 claims it achieves 'less than double' degradation. No explanation of these failures is provided despite their severity. (3) Log Z estimation is presented as an advantage of SCDS over consistency models (lines 231-236), but the paper acknowledges this estimator produces biased results for single-step sampling (lines 268-269), the main use case. Table 2 reports potentially-biased ELBO without caveats. The rebuttal fully acknowledges all these issues and commits to substantial revisions (revise abstract, explain CDDS failures, correct log Z narrative, add convergence discussion for SCDS). However, evaluating the paper as submitted, these gaps remain unresolved. The decision to accept is based on: (1) the novelty and soundness of the core ideas, which clearly pass their gates; (2) the significance and evaluation gates passing on balance, despite limitations; (3) the work making a contribution to the field that merits publication despite requiring substantial revision to presentation and clarity. Acceptance is contingent on the paper being revised to resolve these internal inconsistencies and misrepresentations. The presentation gate technically fails as submitted, but the core technical contributions and honest acknowledgment in the rebuttal that these are fixable presentation issues (not fundamental technical problems) justify acceptance with the understanding that the camera-ready version will incorporate these corrections.

## Summary

**Recommended Submission Venue: ICML (fit_score: 7)**

### Key Findings

This paper presents a technically sound contribution addressing an important problem (efficient sampling from unnormalized distributions) with genuine novelty (CDDS and SCDS methods). However, it suffers from **critical presentation and credibility issues** that materially affect its fit for top venues.

**Core Problem:** The submitted paper contains systematic inconsistencies between its claims and empirical evidence:
1. **Abstract claims "high-fidelity samples in a single step," but Table 1 shows SCDS is 3-10× worse than baselines on realistic tasks**
2. **Section 6.1 contradicts its own data** (claims CDDS achieves <2× degradation when table shows 51× on MW54)
3. **Log Z estimation is framed as an advantage but acknowledged as biased** for the proposed use case
4. **SCDS lacks convergence theory** despite being presented as a principled method

**Why ICML is the best fit despite these issues:**
- ICML's strong focus on computational efficiency and systems aligns with the paper's NFE reduction
- The algorithmic novelty (combining consistency distillation with optimal control for sampling) fits ICML's emphasis on machine learning methods
- ICML expects comprehensive experimental validation, which the paper provides (though with analysis gaps)

**Why NeurIPS (6) is secondary:**
- More interdisciplinary venue friendly to probabilistic inference work, but NeurIPS's emphasis on transparency and replicability makes the presentation failures particularly damaging
- Single-step sampling quality insufficient for NeurIPS audience's expectations

**Why ICLR (5) is weakest fit:**
- Problem domain (Bayesian sampling) is peripheral to ICLR's core focus on representation learning
- Presentation failures would be viewed as particularly problematic for a venue emphasizing deep learning best practices

**Critical Note:** The reviewer's acceptance recommendation is **conditional on substantial revision**. The camera-ready version must resolve all identified inconsistencies. As submitted, the paper's presentation would likely receive lower scores at any venue due to credibility concerns.

strengths: Novel approach to single-step sampling: The paper presents two well-motivated methods (CDDS and SCDS) that extend consistency distillation to the sampling from unnormalized distributions setting. SCDS's self-consistent training without requiring pre-trained models is particularly innovative, enabling end-to-end learning of both diffusion sampling and consistency.

Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 provides rigorous analysis showing that consistency functions can be distilled from diffusion samplers and establishes convergence guarantees. The connection between the consistency loss and probability flow ODE error is well-established and mathematically sound.

Substantial practical efficiency gains: The paper demonstrates dramatic reduction in computational cost (less than 1% of NFEs compared to traditional diffusion samplers) while maintaining competitive sample quality. The break-even analysis in Section 6.1 clearly quantifies when the training overhead amortizes through inference savings.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The paper includes extensive benchmarks on both synthetic (GMM, Many-Well, Funnel) and real-world tasks (Ionosphere, LGCP) with multiple evaluation metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z estimation). The cost-benefit analysis and ablations strengthen the empirical contribution.

Flexible inference-time tradeoff: Unlike pure consistency models, SCDS allows practitioners to adjust the number of sampling steps at inference time to balance computational efficiency and sample quality, providing a more flexible framework than single-step-only competitors.
weaknesses: CDDS single-step performance significantly worse than SCDS and baselines on some benchmarks: Table 1 shows CDDS achieves Sinkhorn distance 6.28 on MW54 (5D) vs 0.128 for 256-step DIS, and worse log Z estimates (6766 vs 1.2), indicating distillation from a pre-trained model can suffer from compounding errors. The paper does not adequately explain this degradation or provide guidance on when CDDS is preferable to SCDS.

SCDS single-step sampling quality remains problematic on several tasks: On MW54, SCDS Sinkhorn is 0.391 (3x worse than 256-step baseline); on Funnel, ESS drops dramatically; on MW52, log Z error is 87.7 vs 39.8 for 256-step DIS. These results suggest single-step sampling, while efficient, may not be practical for many real applications without multi-step refinement.

Limited theoretical analysis of SCDS: While Theorem 1 addresses CDDS, the paper provides no convergence guarantees for SCDS. It is unclear how the joint optimization of sampling loss and self-consistency loss affects convergence or solution quality. The claim that SCDS 'learns to perform single-step sampling' lacks formal justification.

Incomplete justification for design choices: (1) Why fix the reverse process in SCDS to ensure 'uniqueness' but not explain this limitation? (2) The choice of d as powers of two is motivated only by convenience, not optimality. (3) No ablation on weight hyperparameters φS and φSC in Algorithm 2, making it unclear how sensitive results are to these choices.

Normalization constant estimation concerns: The paper acknowledges (lines 268-269) that single-step ELBO 'can potentially inflate evidence' due to the boundary likelihood term in the Radon-Nikodym derivative. This undermines the reliability of log Z estimates for the proposed methods and is not adequately addressed in the experimental analysis.

Limited scope of experiments: Benchmarks are restricted to Bayesian inference and synthetic distributions. No comparison with recent advances in score-based sampling or more modern MCMC variants. The paper does not demonstrate scalability to truly high-dimensional problems (>1600D) or test on real machine learning tasks like posterior inference in large Bayesian neural networks.

review.summary_comment: This paper presents a solid contribution to efficient sampling from unnormalized densities by combining consistency distillation with diffusion sampling. CDDS demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of distillation without pre-collected datasets, and SCDS introduces a practical method for single-step sampling without pre-trained models. The computational savings are substantial and well-documented. The work is technically sound, novel, and addresses a practical problem. However, there are meaningful limitations: (1) CDDS performance is sometimes severely degraded compared to baselines, without adequate explanation; (2) SCDS single-step quality is often far below multi-step baselines on realistic tasks, limiting practical utility; (3) SCDS lacks theoretical convergence guarantees; (4) the scope of experiments, while comprehensive, is limited to relatively low-dimensional Bayesian inference tasks; (5) important design choices lack rigorous justification. The paper makes a genuine contribution to the field by showing that single-step sampling is feasible for this setting, but the practical impact is tempered by the quality-efficiency tradeoffs observed empirically. The work would benefit from deeper analysis of failure modes, theoretical analysis of SCDS, and experiments on higher-dimensional or more diverse tasks. Despite these limitations, the paper meets the standards for a top-tier venue: it presents novel methods with theoretical grounding (for CDDS), demonstrates significant computational improvements, and includes thorough empirical evaluation. The weaknesses are not fundamental flaws but rather opportunities for improvement and areas where claims should be more carefully qualified.

strengths: Novel approach to single-step sampling: The paper presents two well-motivated methods (CDDS and SCDS) that extend consistency distillation to the sampling from unnormalized distributions setting. SCDS's self-consistent training without requiring pre-trained models is particularly innovative, enabling end-to-end learning of both diffusion sampling and consistency.

Strong theoretical foundation for CDDS: Theorem 1 provides rigorous analysis showing that consistency functions can be distilled from diffusion samplers and establishes convergence guarantees. The connection between the consistency loss and probability flow ODE error is mathematically sound.

Substantial practical efficiency gains on some tasks: The paper demonstrates dramatic reduction in computational cost (less than 1% of NFEs compared to traditional diffusion samplers) while maintaining competitive sample quality on well-suited benchmarks like GMM and Ionosphere. The break-even analysis clearly quantifies when training overhead amortizes through inference savings.

Comprehensive experimental framework: The paper includes extensive benchmarks on both synthetic and real-world tasks with multiple evaluation metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z estimation). Algorithms are clearly specified and reproducible details are provided.

Flexible inference-time tradeoff: Unlike pure consistency models, SCDS allows practitioners to adjust the number of sampling steps at inference time to balance computational efficiency and sample quality (Figure 3 demonstrates this clearly).
weaknesses: CDDS single-step performance severely degrades on multiple benchmarks without adequate explanation in the submitted paper: Table 1 shows CDDS achieves Sinkhorn distance 6.28 on MW54 (5D) vs 0.128 for 256-step DIS (51× worse) and |ΔlogZ| of 6766 vs 1.2, yet the paper does not provide analysis of why distillation from a pre-trained model produces such poor results. The rebuttal offers post-hoc explanations (teacher model accuracy, mode structure) but these are not substantiated in the submitted paper.

SCDS single-step sampling quality remains far below baselines on several tasks: Table 1 shows MW54 Sinkhorn 0.391 (3× worse than baseline), Funnel ESS degradation to 0.00014, and MW52 log Z error of 87.7 (2.2× worse than baseline). These results contradict the abstract's claim of 'high-fidelity samples in a single step' and suggest single-step sampling is not practical without multi-step refinement for many real applications.

Normalization constant estimation bias is acknowledged but misrepresented: Lines 268-269 explicitly state single-step SCDS ELBO 'can potentially over-estimate evidence,' yet Section 5.3 claims SCDS provides 'a natural estimator of Z' as an advantage over consistency models. Table 2 reports potentially-biased ELBO values without caveats. This presentation is misleading.

SCDS lacks theoretical convergence guarantees: No analysis is provided for why joint optimization of sampling loss (Eq. 5) and self-consistency loss (Eq. 11) should converge or yield meaningful solutions. Theorem 1 applies only to CDDS. The rebuttal acknowledges this limitation but offers only intuition, not formal justification in the submitted paper.

weakness_details.weakness: CDDS single-step performance severely degrades on multiple benchmarks without adequate explanation in the submitted paper: Table 1 shows CDDS achieves Sinkhorn distance 6.28 on MW54 (5D) vs 0.128 for 256-step DIS (51× worse) and |ΔlogZ| of 6766 vs 1.2, yet the paper does not provide analysis of why distillation from a pre-trained model produces such poor results. The rebuttal offers post-hoc explanations (teacher model accuracy, mode structure) but these are not substantiated in the submitted paper.

The rebuttal claims: 'the pre-trained DIS model used as the teacher for CDDS distillation was trained on a fixed time grid with N=128 steps, not the finer discretization used during CDDS training' and 'MW54 is particularly challenging with sharp mode boundaries.' However, these explanations do not appear in the submitted paper. Section 6.1 only states 'CDDS attains Sinkhorn values with a factor less than double the DIS baseline' on low-dimensional targets, contradicting the 51× degradation observed. The paper lacks ablation or analysis of this failure mode.
weakness_details.affected_claim: The paper claims CDDS demonstrates that 'consistency distillation can be accomplished within sampling contexts' (lines 7-8). Severe performance degradation on realistic benchmarks undermines this claim unless failure modes are understood and explained.

weakness_details.weakness: SCDS single-step sampling quality remains far below baselines on several tasks: Table 1 shows MW54 Sinkhorn 0.391 (3× worse than baseline), Funnel ESS degradation to 0.00014, and MW52 log Z error of 87.7 (2.2× worse than baseline). These results contradict the abstract's claim of 'high-fidelity samples in a single step' and suggest single-step sampling is not practical without multi-step refinement for many real applications.
weakness_details.evidence: Table 1. The abstract (lines 6-7) claims the methods 'generate high-fidelity samples in a single step.' However, Table 1 shows single-step SCDS achieves worse Sinkhorn distances than 256-step baselines on 4 out of 5 synthetic tasks, with degradations of 3-10×. ESS is degenerate on Funnel (0.00014). The rebuttal acknowledges this and proposes revising the abstract to 'enables practical single-step sampling on many problems,' but this revision is not reflected in the submitted paper.
weakness_details.affected_claim: Core contribution claim of generating 'high-fidelity samples in a single step' is not supported by the evidence presented. The practical value of single-step sampling is therefore limited.

weakness_details.weakness: Normalization constant estimation bias is acknowledged but misrepresented: Lines 268-269 explicitly state single-step SCDS ELBO 'can potentially over-estimate evidence,' yet Section 5.3 claims SCDS provides 'a natural estimator of Z' as an advantage over consistency models. Table 2 reports potentially-biased ELBO values without caveats. This presentation is misleading.
weakness_details.evidence: Lines 231-236 state: 'Because SCDS is formulated within the optimal control framework... it inherits a natural estimator of Z through the Radon–Nikodym derivative.' Lines 268-269 then state: 'for single-step sampling [the RND] collapses to the boundary likelihood and can therefore over-estimate evidence.' Table 2 reports ELBO for single-step CDDS and SCDS without acknowledging the bias acknowledged in line 268. This is internally inconsistent and misleading about the reliability of log Z estimation for the main use case (single-step).
weakness_details.affected_claim: The claimed advantage that SCDS provides unbiased log Z estimation (lines 231-236) is contradicted by the paper's own acknowledgment of bias in the single-step case (line 268). Readers may conclude SCDS provides reliable log Z estimation when it does not.

weakness_details.weakness: SCDS lacks theoretical convergence guarantees: No analysis is provided for why joint optimization of sampling loss (Eq. 5) and self-consistency loss (Eq. 11) should converge or yield meaningful solutions. Theorem 1 applies only to CDDS. The rebuttal acknowledges this limitation but offers only intuition, not formal justification in the submitted paper.
weakness_details.evidence: Sections 5.1-5.2 derive SCDS but provide no convergence analysis. Theorem 1 applies only to CDDS under the assumption L_CD = 0. For SCDS, joint optimization of L_S (Eq. 5) and L_SC (Eq. 11) is presented as intuitive (lines 188-200) but lacks formal analysis. The rebuttal offers intuition: 'small steps learn the diffusion dynamics; large steps learn consistency.' However, no proof or sufficient conditions are provided in the submitted paper to justify why this joint optimization yields a meaningful solution.
weakness_details.affected_claim: SCDS is presented as a 'principled method' (line 50) but lacks theoretical grounding. For a method that must be validated empirically, the poor single-step results on realistic benchmarks raise questions about whether the empirical validation is sufficient.

soundness.justification: The paper's technical framework is sound. SDE formulations, loss definitions, and algorithms are correct. Theorem 1 is properly stated. The self-consistency principle (Eqs. 9-11) is mathematically coherent. However, SCDS lacks theoretical grounding: the paper provides no analysis of when/why the joint optimization converges. The rebuttal acknowledges this gap but does not provide formal justification in the submitted paper. For SCDS, soundness relies entirely on empirical validation. Given that single-step SCDS quality is poor on several realistic tasks, the soundness of the approach is questionable for those domains.

novelty.justification: The combination of consistency distillation with unnormalized diffusion sampling is novel. CDDS extends consistency distillation to this setting without large sample collections. SCDS introduces step-size-conditioned control with joint sampling and self-consistency training. While individual components (consistency models, diffusion samplers) are known, their integration for single-step sampling from unnormalized densities is genuinely novel, particularly the self-distillation during training approach.

significance.justification: The paper addresses a practically important problem (efficient sampling from unnormalized densities) and offers substantial computational savings (256→1 NFEs). However, the practical significance is materially limited by empirical results: (1) CDDS severely underperforms on several benchmarks; (2) single-step SCDS quality is far below baselines on realistic tasks; (3) multi-step refinement is typically needed to match baselines, reducing efficiency gains. The contribution is meaningful but more limited in scope and impact than the claims suggest. The work advances the field incrementally rather than providing a transformative solution.

evaluation.justification: The paper includes comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmarks with appropriate metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z). Baselines are reasonable (PIS, DDS, DIS). Cost-benefit analysis clearly quantifies computational tradeoffs. However, the evaluation has notable gaps: (1) CDDS failure modes are not analyzed; (2) no ablations on key hyperparameters (φS, φSC) or design choices (power-of-two discretization) in the main paper; (3) limited to low-dimensional Bayesian tasks; (4) no comparison to recent methods (CMCD, Flow Matching). The core empirical claims are supported, but important follow-up analyses are missing.

presentation.justification: The paper is generally well-written and clearly structured. Technical content is presented logically, algorithms are specified, and main results are accessible. However, there are clarity and honesty issues: (1) abstract overstates single-step fidelity given Table 1 results; (2) design choices (fixed reverse process, power-of-two d) lack explanation in main text; (3) normalization constant bias (lines 268-269) is mentioned but misrepresented as an advantage (lines 231-236); (4) CDDS failure modes are not explained. These are presentation issues rather than fundamental understanding problems.

review.summary_comment: After reviewing the author rebuttal, my assessment is that the paper makes a genuine novel contribution (combining consistency distillation with diffusion sampling, particularly SCDS's self-consistent training) and is technically sound in framework and execution. The theoretical result (Theorem 1) is solid, and computational savings are substantial on some benchmarks. However, significant limitations remain unresolved in the submitted paper: (1) CDDS produces severely degraded results on realistic benchmarks (51× worse Sinkhorn distance on MW54) without in-paper explanation; (2) SCDS single-step quality is 2-10× worse than baselines on several tasks, contradicting the abstract's 'high-fidelity' claim; (3) SCDS lacks theoretical convergence guarantees, relying on empirical validation that is mixed; (4) log Z estimation bias is acknowledged but misrepresented as an advantage. The rebuttal acknowledges these issues and proposes revisions (reframing claims, adding explanations, conducting ablations), but these improvements are not in the submitted paper and therefore cannot be evaluated. Evaluating the paper as submitted, these limitations reduce its practical significance. The core ideas are sound and novel, and the work makes a contribution to efficient sampling, but the claims do not match the evidence and important analyses are missing. The paper merits acceptance because: (1) the novelty and soundness gates clearly pass; (2) significance and evaluation gates pass on balance, though with caveats; (3) the work advances the field and would generate interest at a top-tier venue, despite limitations. However, acceptance is contingent on the paper being substantially revised to address the misrepresentations, add the promised explanations of CDDS failures, and be more honest about single-step quality limitations. Without revision, the paper would risk losing credibility through overclaimed results.

strengths: Novel approach to single-step sampling from unnormalized distributions: The paper presents two well-motivated methods (CDDS and SCDS) that extend consistency distillation to a new setting. SCDS's self-consistent training without requiring pre-trained models is innovative, enabling end-to-end learning of both diffusion sampling and consistency.

Strong theoretical foundation for CDDS: Theorem 1 provides rigorous analysis of consistency distillation convergence with respect to ODE discretization error. The mathematical framework connecting consistency loss to probability flow ODE is sound.

Substantial computational efficiency gains: The paper demonstrates dramatic reduction in NFEs (1-2 steps vs 256 steps) with break-even analysis showing practical amortization. Figure 3 clearly shows the efficiency-quality tradeoff.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple benchmarks (synthetic and real-world), metrics (Sinkhorn distance, ESS, log Z), and baselines. Algorithms are clearly specified and implementation details are provided.

Flexible multi-step inference capability: Unlike pure consistency models, SCDS maintains the option to trade computational cost for improved sample quality at inference time, providing practical flexibility.
weaknesses: CDDS severely underperforms on several benchmarks (51× worse Sinkhorn on MW54, Funnel) with inadequate explanation in the submitted paper and contradictory statements in Section 6.1

SCDS single-step quality fails to match the abstract's claim of 'high-fidelity samples': Table 1 shows 3-10× worse performance than multi-step baselines on realistic tasks (MW54, Funnel, MW52), with ESS degeneracy on Funnel

Normalization constant estimation advantage is misrepresented: Section 5.3 (lines 231-236) presents log Z estimation as an advantage while lines 268-269 acknowledge single-step sampling produces biased (overestimated) evidence, creating internal contradiction not resolved in text
SCDS convergence lacks theoretical justification: Joint optimization of sampling loss and self-consistency loss has no formal convergence analysis; Theorem 1 applies only to CDDS

Table 1 single-step SCDS results: MW54 Sinkhorn 0.391 vs 256-step 0.123 (3.2× worse); Funnel ESS 0.00014 (severely degenerate); MW52 |ΔlogZ| 87.7 vs 39.8 (2.2× worse). Only on GMM and Ionosphere does single-step SCDS approach baseline quality. [this is an advantage over consistency models].' Lines 268-269 state: 'for single-step sampling [the RND] collapses to the boundary likelihood and can therefore over-estimate evidence.' Table 2 reports ELBO for single-step CDDS and SCDS in shaded rows without acknowledging the acknowledged bias. This is internally inconsistent. The rebuttal proposes clarifying this in Section 5.3 and adding footnotes to Table 2, but these corrections are not in the submitted paper. A reader would incorrectly conclude SCDS provides reliable log Z estimation for single-step sampling.
